topics.t: Measurement, units and systems of units
topics.h: A cricket pitch is 22 yards, a sprint is 100 m and a fever is 102 °F: every measurement is just a number glued to an agreed unit.
p: Measuring a physical quantity means comparing it with a fixed, internationally accepted reference standard called a unit; the result is a number times a unit (e.g. 5 m).
Base (fundamental) quantities such as length, mass and time are independent; their units are base units.
Derived quantities (speed, force, pressure) are built from base quantities, so their units (m s⁻¹, N = kg m s⁻², Pa) are derived units.
A complete set of base units and derived units is a system of units. Older systems: CGS (centimetre, gram, second), FPS (foot, pound, second) and MKS (metre, kilogram, second).
Different countries using different systems caused confusion, so the world agreed on one system: the SI (Système Internationale d'Unités).

ex.q: A car covers 72 km in 1 h. Express its speed in the MKS/SI derived unit.

topics.rl: ISRO's launch data, Indian Railways' timetables and AIIMS lab reports all use SI units, so a value measured in Sriharikota means the same thing in Paris.

topics.t: SI base units and their modern definitions
topics.h: Since 2019, the kilogram is no longer a metal cylinder locked in a vault near Paris. It is fixed by Planck's constant, a number that is the same everywhere in the universe.
p: SI has seven base quantities: length (metre, m), mass (kilogram, kg), time (second, s), electric current (ampere, A), thermodynamic temperature (kelvin, K), amount of substance (mole, mol) and luminous intensity (candela, cd).
Each base unit is now defined by fixing the exact value of a fundamental constant.
Second: caesium-133 hyperfine frequency fixed at 9 192 631 770 Hz. Metre: speed of light in vacuum fixed at 299 792 458 m s⁻¹.
Kilogram: Planck constant h fixed. Ampere: elementary charge e fixed. Kelvin: Boltzmann constant k fixed. Mole: Avogadro constant N_A fixed.
Candela: luminous efficacy of monochromatic light of frequency 540 × 10¹² Hz fixed at 683 lm W⁻¹.

ex.q: Which constant fixes the metre, and how far does light travel in 1 s by that definition?
st: The metre is defined by fixing the speed of light in vacuum, c.
So in 1 s light travels exactly 299 792 458 m.

topics.rl: The National Physical Laboratory (CSIR-NPL) in New Delhi keeps India's national standards and supplies Indian Standard Time, linked to the caesium definition of the second.

topics.t: Radian, steradian and SI prefixes
topics.h: A camera's '24 mm lens', a '4 GB' file and a '5 µm' dust particle all use prefixes. Get them wrong and your answer is off by a factor of a thousand or more!
p: Plane angle dθ = ds/r (arc length/radius); its unit is the radian (rad). A full circle is 2π rad.
Solid angle dΩ = dA/r² (area on a sphere/radius squared); its unit is the steradian (sr). A full sphere subtends 4π sr.
Both are ratios of like quantities, so they are dimensionless.
Prefixes: pico p 10⁻¹², nano n 10⁻⁹, micro µ 10⁻⁶, milli m 10⁻³, centi c 10⁻², kilo k 10³, mega M 10⁶, giga G 10⁹, tera T 10¹².
Symbol rules: unit symbols are not plural and take no full stop (5 kg, not 5 kgs.); units named after people take a capital symbol (N, Pa, K) but are written in lowercase in full (newton).

ex.q: An arc of length 0.5 m is cut on a circle of radius 2 m. Find the angle in radians.

topics.rl: Chip makers quote transistor sizes in nanometres, and a hard disk of 1 TB holds 10¹² bytes. The steradian is used by lighting engineers designing stadium floodlights for IPL night matches.

topics.t: Non-SI units and unit conversions
topics.h: Astronomers love light years, chemists love ångströms, and physicists love electron volts. The trick is converting cleanly to SI.
p: Litre: 1 L = 10⁻³ m³ = 1000 cm³.
Ångström: 1 Å = 10⁻¹⁰ m; fermi: 1 fm = 10⁻¹⁵ m (nuclear sizes).
Light year (distance light travels in one year): 1 ly ≈ 9.46 × 10¹⁵ m. Astronomical unit (mean Earth–Sun distance): 1 AU ≈ 1.496 × 10¹¹ m.
Electron volt (energy gained by an electron through 1 V): 1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.
Convert by replacing each unit with its SI value: 1 cm² = 10⁻⁴ m², 1 g cm⁻³ = 1000 kg m⁻³, 1 J = 10⁷ erg.

ex.q: Convert the density of water, 1 g cm⁻³, into kg m⁻³.

topics.rl: ISRO's Mars Orbiter Mission distances are often given in AU and km, while a typical Indian household water tank holds 1000 L = 1 m³ of water.

topics.t: Significant figures and the counting rules
topics.h: Your lab partner writes 2.50 cm and you write 2.5 cm. Same length? Not quite: the extra zero says your partner measured more precisely.
p: Significant figures = all reliably known digits + the first uncertain digit. More significant figures means a more precise measurement.
All non-zero digits are significant; zeros between non-zero digits are significant (2008 has 4).
In a number less than 1, zeros before the first non-zero digit are NOT significant (0.0045 has 2).
Trailing zeros after a decimal point are significant (4.500 has 4). In a number without a decimal point, trailing zeros are ambiguous (4500 could have 2, 3 or 4).
The power of ten is never counted: 4.50 × 10³ has 3 significant figures.

ex.q: How many significant figures are in (a) 0.007020 (b) 30.040?
st: (a) Leading zeros 0.00 are not significant. Digits 7, 0, 2, 0 count: the middle zero lies between 7 and 2, the last zero is after the decimal point.
(b) All digits 3, 0, 0, 4, 0 count: zeros in between and the trailing zero after the decimal point.

topics.rl: AIIMS blood reports print haemoglobin as 13.5 g/dL, not 13.50 or 14, because the analyser's precision fixes the digits that can be trusted.

topics.t: Scientific notation, order of magnitude and exact numbers
topics.h: The mass of an electron and the mass of the Sun differ by about 60 powers of ten. Scientific notation lets you write both neatly.
p: Scientific notation: write a number as a × 10ᵇ with 1 ≤ a < 10. All digits of a are significant, so ambiguity about zeros disappears (4.700 × 10³ has 4).
Order of magnitude: if a ≤ 5 the order is b; if a > 5 the order is b + 1 (as in NCERT). The Earth's radius 6.4 × 10⁶ m has order 7.
Changing units does not change the number of significant figures: 2.308 cm = 0.02308 m = 23.08 mm, all with 4.
Exact numbers (counted items, or pure numbers like 2 in 2πr, ½ in ½mv²) have unlimited significant figures and never limit a result.

ex.q: Write 0.0004070 m in scientific notation and state its significant figures and order of magnitude.
st: a = 4.070 ≤ 5, so the order of magnitude is −4.

topics.rl: Indian census figures (about 1.4 × 10⁹ people) and India's GDP in rupees are easiest to compare when written as powers of ten.

topics.t: Arithmetic with significant figures
topics.h: Your calculator says the density is 8.571428571 g cm⁻³. Your ruler was never that good. Significant-figure rules tell you how much of that to keep.
p: Multiplication or division: keep as many significant figures as the factor with the FEWEST significant figures.
Addition or subtraction: keep as many decimal places as the term with the FEWEST decimal places.
Example: 4.237 g ÷ 2.51 cm³ = 1.688… → 1.69 g cm⁻³ (3 sig figs, like 2.51).
Exact numbers (like 4/3 in the sphere volume) do not limit the result.

ex.q: A rectangle measures 4.234 m by 1.005 m. Report its area with correct significant figures.

topics.rl: Pharmacists at Jan Aushadhi Kendras weigh doses carefully: a total can never be reported more precisely than the least precise weighing in it.

topics.t: Rounding off and uncertainty in results
topics.h: Should 2.745 round to 2.74 or 2.75? Physics has a clever tie-breaking rule that avoids always rounding up.
p: If the digit dropped is more than 5, add 1 to the preceding digit; if less than 5, leave it unchanged.
If the digit dropped is exactly 5 (nothing or only zeros after it): leave the preceding digit unchanged if it is even, add 1 if it is odd. So 2.745 → 2.74 and 2.735 → 2.74.
Relative error = Δx/x. For a product or quotient, relative errors add: ΔA/A = Δl/l + Δb/b for A = l × b.
In multi-step calculations, carry one extra digit in intermediate results and round only the final answer.

ex.q: A rectangle has l = 16.2 ± 0.1 cm and b = 10.1 ± 0.1 cm. Estimate the percentage error in its area.
st: Errors add for a product: about 0.6% + 1% ≈ 1.6%.
Area = 163.62 cm², reported as about 164 ± 3 cm².

topics.rl: Weather stations of the IMD round rainfall readings consistently, so monthly monsoon totals are not biased upward by always rounding 5s up.

topics.t: Dimensions of physical quantities
topics.h: Kilometres or miles, the 'nature' of a distance is still length. Dimensions capture that nature, ignoring numbers and units.
p: Dimensions of a quantity are the powers to which base quantities must be raised to represent it.
Base dimensions are written in square brackets: [M] mass, [L] length, [T] time, [A] electric current, [K] temperature, [cd] luminous intensity, [mol] amount of substance.
Volume = [L³], velocity = [L T⁻¹], acceleration = [L T⁻²], force = [M L T⁻²].
Dimensions do not depend on the numerical value or the unit: 5 km and 3 miles both have dimension [L].
In mechanics everything can be written using only [M], [L] and [T].

ex.q: Find the dimensions of acceleration starting from a = Δv/Δt.
st: = [L T⁻²], i.e. dimension 1 in length and −2 in time.

topics.rl: Whether Indian Railways quotes speed in km/h or ISRO quotes it in m/s, the dimension is the same, [L T⁻¹], which lets engineers compare them safely.

topics.t: Dimensional formulae and dimensionless quantities
topics.h: Work, energy and torque all share the same dimensional formula. Pressure and stress do too. Spotting twins like these is a favourite exam trick.
p: Dimensional formula: shows which base quantities, with which powers, make up a quantity, e.g. velocity [M⁰ L T⁻¹].
Dimensional equation: equating a quantity to its formula, e.g. [F] = [M L T⁻²].
From definitions: work/energy = F × d → [M L² T⁻²]; power = W/t → [M L² T⁻³]; pressure = F/A → [M L⁻¹ T⁻²]; momentum = mv → [M L T⁻¹]; density = m/V → [M L⁻³].
Dimensionless quantities (ratios of like quantities): angle, strain, refractive index, relative density. Their dimensional formula is [M⁰ L⁰ T⁰].

ex.q: Derive the dimensional formula of pressure.

topics.rl: Water-supply engineers in Indian cities quote pipe pressure in pascals and pump power in watts; checking dimensions keeps those design sheets error-free.

topics.t: Principle of homogeneity and checking equations
topics.h: You can't add 5 kg to 3 m, just like you can't add rupees to kilometres. That simple idea catches wrong formulas instantly.
p: Principle of homogeneity: only quantities with the same dimensions can be added, subtracted or equated.
So every term on both sides of a correct equation has the same dimensions.
Arguments of sin, cos, exponential and log functions must be dimensionless (e.g. ωt in sin ωt).
Check x = x₀ + v₀t + ½at²: [L], [L T⁻¹][T] = [L], [L T⁻²][T²] = [L]. All terms are [L], so it is consistent.
A dimensionally consistent equation may still be wrong (e.g. a missing ½), but a dimensionally inconsistent one is certainly wrong.

ex.q: Check whether v² = u² + 2as is dimensionally consistent.
st: All terms match, so the equation is dimensionally consistent.

topics.rl: Before simulations of a monsoon model run on IITM Pune's supercomputer, scientists check each equation term by term, exactly like this.

topics.t: Testing formulae and finding dimensions of constants
topics.h: In CBSE papers you are often given 'v = at + b/(t + c)' and asked for the dimensions of a, b and c. It is a quick 2–3 mark win once you see the trick.
p: To test an energy relation, compare dimensions: ½mv² → [M][L T⁻¹]² = [M L² T⁻²]; mgh → [M][L T⁻²][L] = [M L² T⁻²]. Both match energy.
To find a constant, make each added term match the left side, and quantities added together must have the same dimensions.
Example: v = at + b/(t + c). [c] = [T] (added to t); [at] = [v] → [a] = [L T⁻²]; [b/T] = [v] → [b] = [L].
To spot the wrong formula among several, check each term; any mismatch rules it out.

ex.q: In P = a/b + x/(b + t²), with P a pressure and t a time, find the dimensions of b.
st: b is added to t², so [b] = [t²] = [T²].
That is enough for b; a and x can be found similarly.

topics.rl: Engineers at BHEL quickly verify vendor formulas for turbine power by dimensions before using them in design.

topics.t: Deducing relations by dimensional analysis and its limits
topics.h: Without any calculus, you can predict that a pendulum twice as long ticks √2 times slower. Dimensional analysis is that powerful.
p: Assume the quantity depends on the others as a power law, e.g. T = k lᵃ gᵇ mᶜ, and equate powers of M, L and T on both sides.
Pendulum: [T] = [L]ᵃ [L T⁻²]ᵇ [M]ᶜ → c = 0, a + b = 0, −2b = 1 → b = −½, a = ½. So T = k√(l/g) (k = 2π from theory).
Unit conversion: n₂ = n₁[M₁/M₂]ᵃ[L₁/L₂]ᵇ[T₁/T₂]ᶜ for a quantity of dimensions [Mᵃ Lᵇ Tᶜ]. E.g. 1 N = 10⁵ dyne.

Limitations: dimensionless constants (like 2π) cannot be found; it fails for relations with sums/differences of terms or trigonometric/exponential functions, and when a quantity depends on more than three variables in mechanics (only three equations: M, L, T).

ex.q: Convert 1 J into erg using dimensions.
st: [Energy] = [M L² T⁻²], so a = 1, b = 2, c = −2.
M₁ = 1 kg = 10³ g, L₁ = 1 m = 10² cm, T₁ = T₂ = 1 s.

topics.rl: Before building costly wind tunnels, aerospace engineers at NAL Bengaluru use dimensional analysis to predict how forces scale with speed and size.

topics.t: Describing motion: position, path length and displacement
topics.h: A Mumbai local covers 30 km in a day and ends up back at Churchgate. Did it 'go' anywhere? Physics answers both yes and no.
p: Motion is the change of position of an object with time. Rectilinear motion is motion along a straight line.
An object can be treated as a point object when its size is much smaller than the distance it moves (a car on a 200 km trip).
Kinematics describes motion (position, velocity, acceleration) without asking what causes it.
Choose an origin O and a positive direction on the x-axis. Positions to the right are positive, to the left negative; displacement Δx = x₂ − x₁ can be positive, negative or zero.
Path length is the total distance travelled (always positive). Average velocity = Δx/Δt; average speed = path length/time. Average speed ≥ magnitude of average velocity.

ex.q: A cyclist goes from x = 0 to x = +500 m and then returns to x = +300 m, taking 100 s in all. Find path length, displacement, average speed and average velocity.

topics.rl: A runner completing one lap of a 400 m track at the Jawaharlal Nehru Stadium has a path length of 400 m but zero displacement.

topics.t: Instantaneous velocity and speed
topics.h: A speed camera on the Mumbai–Pune Expressway doesn't care about your average for the trip; it measures your velocity at one instant.
p: Instantaneous velocity is the limit of average velocity as the time interval shrinks to zero: v = lim(Δt→0) Δx/Δt = dx/dt.
On a position–time graph, v at an instant is the slope of the tangent to the curve at that point.
Numerical approach: compute Δx/Δt for smaller and smaller Δt; the values approach v (e.g. x = 0.1t³ gives 1.9, 1.261, 1.206 … → 1.2 m s⁻¹ at t = 2 s).
Instantaneous speed = magnitude of instantaneous velocity. But average speed over an interval can exceed the magnitude of average velocity.

ex.q: For x = 0.1t³ (x in m, t in s), find Δx/Δt from t = 2 s to t = 2.1 s, and the instantaneous velocity at t = 2 s.

topics.rl: A car's speedometer shows instantaneous speed, while the trip computer on the same dashboard shows average speed.

topics.t: Finding velocity and acceleration by differentiation
topics.h: Give a physicist one equation for position, and two quick derivatives later she knows the velocity and acceleration at every instant.
p: If x(t) is known, v = dx/dt. Use d(tⁿ)/dt = n tⁿ⁻¹ and d(constant)/dt = 0.
Instantaneous acceleration a = dv/dt = d²x/dt²; it is the slope of the v–t graph at that instant.
For x = a + bt²: v = 2bt and acceleration = 2b (constant).
To find when the body is momentarily at rest, set v = 0 and solve for t.

ex.q: x = 2.5 + 5t² (x in m, t in s). Find v and a at t = 2 s.
st: At t = 2 s, v = 20 m s⁻¹.
ex.a: v = 20 m s⁻¹, a = 10 m s⁻²

topics.rl: A modern train's onboard computer logs position many times a second; differentiating that data gives the speed and acceleration shown to the loco pilot.

topics.t: Acceleration: meaning, sign and x–t curvature
topics.h: A car slowing down while reversing has a POSITIVE acceleration. Sounds wrong? It's all about the chosen direction.
p: Average acceleration = (v₂ − v₁)/(t₂ − t₁) = Δv/Δt; SI unit m s⁻².
Velocity is a vector, so acceleration arises from a change in speed, in direction, or both.
The sign of acceleration depends on the chosen positive direction; it does not by itself say 'speeding up' or 'slowing down'.
On an x–t graph: curve bending upward (slope increasing) → a > 0; bending downward → a < 0; straight line → a = 0.

ex.q: A scooter's velocity changes from 5 m s⁻¹ to 25 m s⁻¹ in 4 s. Find its average acceleration.

topics.rl: When the Tejas jet lands at an air base and brakes hard, its acceleration points opposite to its velocity, which is why pilots lean forward.

topics.t: Velocity–time graphs and the area rule
topics.h: Give a CBSE examiner one v–t graph and they can ask you five questions: acceleration, displacement, distance, turning point and average speed.
p: On a v–t graph, slope = acceleration and area under the graph = displacement (area below the t-axis counts as negative).
Constant acceleration gives a straight-line v–t graph. If the line crosses v = 0, the body reverses direction there (e.g. a ball thrown up).
Distance travelled = sum of magnitudes of areas above and below the axis.
Real motion has no sharp kinks: x and v change continuously. Impossible graphs show two positions at one time, negative speed or path length, or time going backward.
Read graphs carefully: x–t slope gives v; v–t slope gives a, v–t area gives displacement.

ex.q: A car accelerates uniformly from rest to 20 m s⁻¹ in 4 s, moves steadily for 6 s, then decelerates uniformly to rest in 2 s. Find the total distance.

topics.rl: Metro trains on the Delhi Metro follow a trapezium-shaped v–t profile between stations: accelerate, cruise, brake.

topics.t: Deriving the kinematic equations
topics.h: Three short equations solve almost every 'uniform acceleration' question in your board paper. Derive them once and you'll never forget them.
p: From a = (v − v₀)/t: v = v₀ + at.
Area under the v–t graph (rectangle v₀t + triangle ½(v − v₀)t = ½at²): x = v₀t + ½at².
For uniform acceleration, average velocity = (v₀ + v)/2, so x = (v₀ + v)t/2.
Eliminate t: x = (v + v₀)/2 × (v − v₀)/a gives v² = v₀² + 2ax.

ex.q: A car moving at 10 m s⁻¹ accelerates at 2 m s⁻² for 5 s. Find its final velocity and displacement.
st: Check: average velocity = (10 + 20)/2 = 15 m s⁻¹; 15 × 5 = 75 m.

topics.rl: During an ISRO PSLV launch, engineers estimate the rocket's speed after a burn using exactly v = v₀ + at for short intervals of nearly constant acceleration.

topics.t: General forms, calculus method and when the equations work
topics.h: Toss a cricket ball straight up: at the top it has zero velocity for an instant, yet gravity is still pulling it at 9.8 m s⁻². Zero velocity, non-zero acceleration!
p: With initial position x₀: x = x₀ + v₀t + ½at² and v² = v₀² + 2a(x − x₀).
Calculus: a = dv/dt → ∫dv = ∫a dt → v = v₀ + at; v = dx/dt → ∫dx = ∫(v₀ + at)dt → x = x₀ + v₀t + ½at². Also v dv/dx = a gives v² = v₀² + 2a(x − x₀).
These equations hold ONLY for constant acceleration. The definitions v = dx/dt and a = dv/dt hold always.
Zero velocity does not mean zero acceleration (top of a vertical throw). Speeding up or slowing down depends on whether a and v have the same or opposite signs.

ex.q: A particle at x₀ = 5 m has v₀ = 3 m s⁻¹ and a = 2 m s⁻². Find its position at t = 4 s.

topics.rl: Self-driving test cars at IIT Madras's research park model braking with these equations only after checking that the deceleration is roughly constant.

topics.t: Free fall and Galileo's odd-number rule
topics.h: Drop a stone from Qutub Minar's top (about 72.5 m) and gravity takes under 4 seconds to bring it down. Air resistance aside, a feather would do the same.
p: Free fall: motion under gravity alone with constant acceleration g = 9.8 m s⁻² downward (ignoring air resistance).
Take upward as +y: a = −g. Then v = v₀ − gt, y = v₀t − ½gt², v² = v₀² − 2gy.
A ball thrown up and landing below the launch point: solve the whole flight with one equation (y negative at landing) or split it into 'up' and 'down' parts — both give the same time.
Galileo's law of odd numbers: for a body falling from rest, distances in successive equal time intervals are in the ratio 1 : 3 : 5 : 7 …

ex.q: A ball is thrown up at 10 m s⁻¹ from the top of a 15 m building (g = 10 m s⁻²). How long does it take to reach the ground?
st: Take up as +, origin at the top: landing y = −15 m.
Check by splitting: up for 1 s rising 5 m, then falls 20 m in 2 s: total 3 s.

topics.rl: Paragliders over Bir Billing feel close to free fall for a moment after jumping, before the canopy fills with air.

topics.t: Stopping distance, reaction time and kinematics numericals
topics.h: Double your speed on a highway and your braking distance becomes FOUR times longer. That single fact is why speed limits exist.
p: Braking from v₀ with deceleration a: 0 = v₀² − 2a·d_s, so stopping distance d_s = v₀²/(2a) ∝ v₀².
Reaction time with a falling ruler: the ruler falls d = ½gt² before you catch it, so t = √(2d/g).
Strategy: list known quantities (v₀, v, a, x, t) with signs, pick the equation that contains the unknown and three knowns.
Units first: convert km h⁻¹ to m s⁻¹ (divide by 3.6) before using the equations.

ex.q: A friend drops a ruler and you catch it after it falls 19.6 cm (g = 9.8 m s⁻²). Find your reaction time.

topics.rl: Indian Railways' signal spacing depends on braking distance: a train at 90 km h⁻¹ needs far more track to stop than one at 45 km h⁻¹.

topics.t: Scalars and vectors
topics.h: Tell a pilot '500 km' and she'll ask: 'Which way?' Many quantities need a direction to make sense.
p: Motion in two or three dimensions needs vectors to describe position, velocity and acceleration. This chapter builds vector tools, then applies them to constant-acceleration motion, projectiles and uniform circular motion.
Scalars have only magnitude and combine by ordinary algebra: mass, time, temperature, work, energy, speed.
Vectors have magnitude and direction and add by the triangle or parallelogram law: displacement, velocity, acceleration, force, momentum.
Notation: a vector is written in bold (A) or with an arrow (A⃗). Its magnitude is |A| or simply A, always non-negative.

ex.q: A box of mass 5 kg and another of 3 kg are put together. Two forces of 5 N and 3 N act on a body. Why is the total mass surely 8 kg but the total force not surely 8 N?
st: Mass is a scalar: masses add by ordinary algebra, 5 + 3 = 8 kg.
Force is a vector: the result depends on the angle between the forces.
It can be anything from 2 N (opposite) to 8 N (same direction).
ex.a: Mass adds simply; forces add as vectors (2 N to 8 N)

topics.rl: Air-traffic controllers at Delhi's IGI Airport give pilots headings and speeds: velocity vectors, not just speeds.

topics.t: Position and displacement vectors, equality and scaling
topics.h: Whether you take the highway or the village road from Jaipur to Ajmer, your displacement vector is exactly the same.
p: The position vector r of a point P is the arrow from the origin O to P.
Displacement is the vector from the initial position P to the final position Q: Δr = r_Q − r_P. It depends only on the end points, not on the path.
Two vectors are equal if they have the same magnitude and the same direction. Such free vectors can be shifted parallel to themselves.
λA: if λ > 0, the magnitude becomes λ|A| and the direction is unchanged. If λ < 0, the magnitude becomes |λ||A| and the direction reverses.

ex.q: A = 3 m due east. Describe 2A and −1.5A.
st: The minus sign reverses the direction: west.

topics.rl: Google Maps may show three routes from Bengaluru to Mysuru with different distances, but the straight-line displacement between the cities is fixed.

topics.t: Graphical addition of vectors
topics.h: Ships at Visakhapatnam port used to plot courses with rulers and protractors: arrows placed head to tail on a chart.
p: Multiplying a vector by a scalar with dimensions gives a new physical quantity: velocity v × time t = displacement; mass × velocity = momentum.
Triangle (head-to-tail) method: place the tail of B at the head of A; the resultant R = A + B runs from the tail of A to the head of B.
Parallelogram method: draw A and B from a common point; the diagonal from that point is A + B. It gives the same result as the triangle method.
Addition is commutative (A + B = B + A) and associative ((A + B) + C = A + (B + C)).
Null vector 0 has zero magnitude: A + 0 = A, λ0 = 0, 0A = 0. Also A + (−A) = 0.

ex.q: A car moves at 20 m s⁻¹ due north for 30 s. What displacement vector results?
st: Displacement = v × t (vector × scalar with dimension of time).

topics.rl: Rowing teams on the Hooghly feel vector addition directly: the boat's velocity relative to water adds to the river's flow.

topics.t: Vector subtraction and the rain–umbrella problem
topics.h: Standing at a bus stop in a Mumbai monsoon with the wind blowing? Vector addition tells you exactly how to tilt your umbrella.
p: Subtraction is addition of the negative: A − B = A + (−B).
In the parallelogram of A and B, the second diagonal gives A − B (from the head of B to the head of A).
|A − B| = √(A² + B² − 2AB cos θ), where θ is the angle between A and B.

Rain falling vertically at v_r and wind blowing horizontally at v_w give the rain a resultant velocity at angle θ to the vertical with tan θ = v_w/v_r. Tilt the umbrella towards where the rain comes from, at angle θ from the vertical.

ex.q: Rain falls vertically at 8 m s⁻¹. Wind starts blowing from west to east at 6 m s⁻¹. How should you hold your umbrella?
st: The rain now has components 8 m s⁻¹ down and 6 m s⁻¹ eastward.
tan θ = 6/8 = 0.75, θ ≈ 37° from the vertical.
The rain comes from the west, so tilt the umbrella towards the west at about 37° from the vertical.
ex.a: Tilted ~37° from the vertical towards the west

topics.rl: During the Kerala monsoon, slanting rain against shopfronts is just the resultant of the falling speed and the wind velocity.

topics.t: Resolution of vectors and unit vectors
topics.h: A rope pulling a cart at an angle does two jobs at once: it drags it forward and lifts it slightly. Resolving the force reveals both.
p: Any vector in a plane can be written as a sum of two vectors along any two non-collinear directions: A = λa + μb.
Unit vectors î, ĵ, k̂ point along x, y, z, have magnitude 1 and no dimensions or units; they only show direction.
Rectangular components: Aₓ = A cos θ, A_y = A sin θ, where θ is the angle with the +x axis. A = Aₓî + A_yĵ.
Back from components: A = √(Aₓ² + A_y²), tan θ = A_y/Aₓ.
In 3D: A = Aₓî + A_yĵ + A_zk̂, A = √(Aₓ² + A_y² + A_z²); direction cosines cos α = Aₓ/A, cos β = A_y/A, cos γ = A_z/A, with cos²α + cos²β + cos²γ = 1.

ex.q: A force of 10 N acts at 30° above the +x axis. Find its components.

topics.rl: Civil engineers designing the cable-stayed Signature Bridge in Delhi resolve each cable's tension into vertical (holding the deck) and horizontal parts.

topics.t: Analytical addition of vectors
topics.h: A motorboat aiming straight across the Brahmaputra lands far downstream. The analytical method tells you exactly where.
p: Component method: if A = Aₓî + A_yĵ and B = Bₓî + B_yĵ, then R = (Aₓ + Bₓ)î + (A_y + B_y)ĵ.
Law of cosines: R² = A² + B² + 2AB cos θ, where θ is the angle between A and B.
Law of sines: R/sin θ = A/sin β = B/sin α, where α is the angle between R and A. Also tan α = B sin θ/(A + B cos θ).
Special cases: θ = 0 → R = A + B; θ = 180° → R = |A − B|; θ = 90° → R = √(A² + B²).

ex.q: A boat moves at 8 km h⁻¹ due north in still water. The river flows east at 6 km h⁻¹. Find the boat's resultant velocity.
st: tan α = 6/8 = 0.75, α ≈ 37° east of north.
ex.a: 10 km h⁻¹ at about 37° east of north

topics.rl: Ferries crossing from Mumbai's Gateway of India to Elephanta adjust their heading for the tidal current using this exact calculation.

topics.t: Position and velocity in a plane
topics.h: A drone delivering medicines in Telangana's 'Medicine from the Sky' project needs its x and y coordinates and velocity components every second.
p: Position vector r = xî + yĵ; displacement Δr = Δxî + Δyĵ.
Average velocity v̄ = Δr/Δt. Instantaneous velocity v = dr/dt = vₓî + v_yĵ, with vₓ = dx/dt and v_y = dy/dt.
Instantaneous velocity is always along the tangent to the path, in the direction of motion.
Speed |v| = √(vₓ² + v_y²) and direction tan θ = v_y/vₓ (θ measured from the x-axis).

ex.q: r = 3t î + 2t² ĵ (SI units). Find the velocity and speed at t = 1 s.
st: At t = 1 s: v = 3 î + 4 ĵ m s⁻¹.
Speed = √(9 + 16) = 5 m s⁻¹, at tan⁻¹(4/3) ≈ 53° to the x-axis.

topics.rl: A Formula Bharat student race car's GPS logs x and y every 0.1 s; dividing each Δr by Δt gives the velocity arrows shown on the team's laptop.

topics.t: Acceleration in a plane
topics.h: At the top of a cricket ball's flight, velocity is horizontal but acceleration is straight down: they can be at any angle.
p: Average acceleration ā = Δv/Δt. Instantaneous acceleration a = dv/dt = aₓî + a_yĵ, with aₓ = dvₓ/dt, a_y = dv_y/dt.
In two dimensions v and a can make any angle: 0° (speeding up straight), 180° (slowing straight), 90° (uniform circular motion), or anything else (projectile).
Recipe: from r(t), differentiate once for v(t), again for a(t); then find magnitudes with Pythagoras and directions with tan θ.
Acceleration is not necessarily along velocity; it points the way velocity is changing.

ex.q: r = 2t î + t³ ĵ (SI units). Find a at t = 1 s.
st: At t = 1 s, a = 6 ĵ m s⁻², i.e. 6 m s⁻² along +y.

topics.rl: A Chandrayaan orbiter's velocity is along its orbit while its acceleration points towards the Moon's centre: perpendicular, not parallel.

topics.t: Motion in a plane with constant acceleration
topics.h: A puck pushed across ice while a steady wind blows sideways: two simple 1D problems hiding inside one 2D problem.
p: With constant acceleration a: v = v₀ + at and r = r₀ + v₀t + ½at² (vector forms).
Component form: x = x₀ + v₀ₓt + ½aₓt² and y = y₀ + v₀ᵧt + ½a_yt². The x and y motions are independent; time t links them.
To find something at a given x-coordinate, first solve the x-equation for t, then use that t in the y-equations.
Speed = √(vₓ² + v_y²) at the required time.

ex.q: A particle starts from the origin with v₀ = 4 î m s⁻¹ and constant a = 2 ĵ m s⁻². Find its position and speed at t = 3 s.

topics.rl: Satellite launch trajectories from Sriharikota are split into downrange and altitude components, each solved with 1D kinematics in short steps.

topics.t: Projectile motion: independence and the parabolic path
topics.h: Hit a ball and drop another at the same instant from the same height: both land together. Horizontal speed doesn't change falling time.
p: A projectile moves under gravity alone after launch (air resistance ignored).
Horizontal motion is uniform (aₓ = 0); vertical motion is uniformly accelerated (a_y = −g). They are independent.
Launched with speed v₀ at angle θ₀: vₓ = v₀ cos θ₀ (constant), v_y = v₀ sin θ₀ − gt; x = (v₀ cos θ₀)t, y = (v₀ sin θ₀)t − ½gt².
Eliminating t: y = x tan θ₀ − gx²/(2v₀² cos²θ₀). This is of the form y = ax − bx², a parabola.

ex.q: A ball is projected at 20 m s⁻¹ at 30° (g = 10 m s⁻²). Find vₓ, v_y and the position at t = 1 s.

topics.rl: Javelin star Neeraj Chopra's throw follows a near-parabolic path; air drag and lift make the real path a bit shorter and lopsided.

topics.t: Time of flight, maximum height and range
topics.h: Why does a fielder's throw angle matter so much? Because range depends on sin 2θ, and for a launch from ground level without air resistance, 45° gives the maximum range.
p: Time to reach maximum height t_m = v₀ sin θ₀/g; total time of flight T_f = 2v₀ sin θ₀/g.
Maximum height h_m = v₀² sin²θ₀/(2g).
Horizontal range R = v₀² sin 2θ₀/g. It is maximum at θ₀ = 45°: R_max = v₀²/g.
Complementary angles θ and (90° − θ) give the same range (sin 2θ = sin(180° − 2θ)), but different heights and flight times.
Real throws (cricket ball, javelin) face air resistance, which reduces range and height; the best angle is then a little less than 45°.

ex.q: A cricketer can throw a ball to a maximum horizontal distance of 100 m. How high can he throw it vertically with the same speed? (g = 10 m s⁻²)
st: R_max = v₀²/g = 100 m → v₀² = 1000 m² s⁻².

topics.rl: A fielder's throw from the boundary at the Eden Gardens is slightly flatter than 45° because air drag steals more range from higher throws.

topics.t: Horizontal projection and target problems
topics.h: A relief helicopter over flooded Assam must release a food packet BEFORE it is directly above the target. Here's why.
p: Thrown horizontally from height h with speed u: x = ut, y = ½gt² (measuring downward).
Time to land t = √(2h/g); horizontal distance = u√(2h/g); speed on landing = √(u² + (gt)²).
A packet dropped from a moving aircraft keeps the aircraft's horizontal velocity, so (without air drag) it stays vertically below the aircraft while falling.
To hit a target at the same level, a bullet must be aimed slightly above it, because it falls ½gt² during flight time t. A gun can reach a target only if its distance ≤ R_max = v₀²/g.

ex.q: A stone is thrown horizontally at 10 m s⁻¹ from a 45 m high cliff (g = 10 m s⁻²). Find the time of flight and where it lands.
st: x = ut = 10 × 3 = 30 m from the foot of the cliff.
At impact v_y = gt = 30 m s⁻¹, speed = √(100 + 900) ≈ 31.6 m s⁻¹.

topics.rl: Indian Air Force supply drops in Ladakh use this physics (plus parachutes and wind corrections) to land loads on target.

topics.t: Uniform circular motion: angular speed, period and frequency
topics.h: A ceiling fan, a Ferris wheel at a Dussehra mela and the Earth's spin all share one set of simple formulas.
p: Uniform circular motion (UCM): constant speed on a circle. Speed is constant but velocity keeps changing direction.
Angular displacement Δθ (in radians); angular speed ω = dθ/dt (rad s⁻¹). Linear speed v = Rω.
Period T is the time for one revolution; frequency ν = 1/T (Hz or rev s⁻¹). ω = 2π/T = 2πν, v = 2πRν.
Centripetal acceleration a_c = v²/R = ω²R = 4π²ν²R.

ex.q: A stone tied to a 0.5 m string is whirled at ω = 4 rad s⁻¹. Find its speed and centripetal acceleration.

topics.rl: A washing machine's drum spinning at 1200 rpm (20 rev s⁻¹) has ω = 40π rad s⁻¹, enough to fling water out of clothes.

topics.t: Centripetal acceleration: derivation and nature
topics.h: A centrifuge at an AIIMS blood bank can produce accelerations over 1000 times g, all pointing towards the centre.
p: Derivation: in time Δt the velocity turns through Δθ; the triangle of velocity vectors is similar to the triangle of position vectors, so |Δv|/v = |Δr|/R.
Dividing by Δt and letting Δt → 0: a = v·(v/R) = v²/R, directed towards the centre (Δv points inward in the limit).
Magnitude v²/R is constant, but the direction keeps changing (always towards the centre), so the centripetal acceleration is NOT a constant vector.
Only in uniform circular motion is the net acceleration purely radial; if speed changes, there is also a tangential component.

ex.q: A centrifuge spins a tube at radius 0.1 m with ω = 100 rad s⁻¹. Find the centripetal acceleration in units of g (g = 10 m s⁻²).

topics.rl: The Moon's centripetal acceleration towards the Earth is only about 0.0027 m s⁻², yet it keeps the Moon in orbit around us.

topics.t: Force, Aristotle's fallacy and Galileo's inclines
topics.h: Stop pedalling your cycle and it slows down. For 2000 years people concluded that motion needs a constant push. They were wrong.
p: Kinematics describes motion; dynamics asks what causes motion and changes in motion. The answer is force.
A force is needed to change a body's velocity (speed or direction), not to keep it moving. Forces may act by contact (push, friction, tension) or at a distance (gravity, magnetic, electric).
Aristotle's fallacy: an external force is needed to keep a body moving uniformly. Wrong, because he missed friction and air resistance, which oppose motion; the push only cancels them.
Galileo's inclined planes: a ball speeds up rolling down, slows down rolling up, and on a horizontal plane its speed should stay constant if there is no friction.

ex.q: A cart is pushed along a road at constant speed with a 50 N force. Why does it need the push at all, and what does that say about Aristotle's idea?
st: At constant velocity, the net force on the cart is zero.
So the 50 N push must be balanced by 50 N of friction and air resistance.
The push cancels opposing forces; it is not needed for motion itself. Aristotle's view overlooked friction.
ex.a: The push only balances friction; net force is zero

topics.rl: A hockey puck on smooth ice at an indoor rink in Gurugram glides far without any push because friction is tiny.

topics.t: Inertia and Newton's first law
topics.h: Pull a tablecloth fast enough and the dishes stay put. That stubbornness of matter has a name: inertia.
p: Galileo's double incline: a ball rolling down one incline climbs the other to nearly the same height. Make the second incline gentler and it travels farther; make it horizontal and, without friction, it would roll forever.
So rest and uniform straight-line motion are equivalent states: in both, no net force acts.
Inertia is the resistance of a body to any change in its state of rest or uniform motion. Mass is the measure of inertia.

Ancient Indian thought: the Vaisheshika idea of 'vega' (a tendency to keep moving in a straight line) came close to inertia, and Bhaskara II's (1150 CE) 'tatkaliki gati' anticipated instantaneous motion.
Newton's first law: every body continues in its state of rest or of uniform motion in a straight line unless compelled by an external net force to change that state.

ex.q: In Galileo's double incline, the first plane is released from 20 cm height. The second plane is made less steep. What happens?
st: Without friction, the ball rises to the same 20 cm height.
A gentler slope means a longer path to reach 20 cm.
With the slope reduced to zero, it never reaches 20 cm, so it rolls on forever.
ex.a: It travels farther; on a level plane it would never stop

topics.rl: When a spent stage of an ISRO rocket separates in space, it keeps coasting at the velocity it had: inertia at work.

topics.t: First law in action, and momentum
topics.h: A cricket ball and a tennis ball at the same speed: one you can catch bare-handed, the other stings. The difference is momentum.
p: First law, equivalent form: if the net external force on a body is zero, its acceleration is zero (and vice versa).
A book on a table: weight down is balanced by the normal force up, so a = 0. A spaceship far from all stars needs no engine to keep moving uniformly.
Passengers lurch backward when a bus starts suddenly and forward when it brakes: their bodies tend to keep their earlier state.
An astronaut who leaves an accelerating spaceship has zero acceleration the moment he is outside (no force from the ship, gravity negligible in deep space).
Momentum p = mv is a vector along v. Catching a fast ball, stopping a bullet, or a karate chop all show that the effect of a blow depends on momentum and on how fast it changes.

ex.q: A spaceship in deep space accelerates at 100 m s⁻². An astronaut drifts out of the hatch. What is his acceleration just after leaving?
st: Inside, the ship's floor pushes him, giving 100 m s⁻².
Outside, nothing pushes him and gravity from distant stars is negligible.
Net force = 0, so his acceleration is 0 (he keeps the velocity he had).

topics.rl: In a crowded DTC bus, standing passengers grab the handle when it suddenly brakes, because their bodies keep moving forward by inertia.

topics.t: Newton's second law: F = dp/dt and F = ma
topics.h: Push a shopping trolley at a supermarket: empty, it zips; loaded, it crawls. Same push, different acceleration.
p: Second law: the rate of change of momentum of a body equals the net applied force and takes place in the direction of the force: F = dp/dt.
For constant mass, F = m dv/dt = ma. 1 newton = force that gives 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m s⁻²: 1 N = 1 kg m s⁻².
F = 0 gives a = 0, so the second law agrees with the first.
Component form: Fₓ = maₓ, F_y = ma_y, F_z = ma_z. A force changes only the velocity component along it (a force ⊥ v changes direction, not speed).
The law is local: the acceleration at an instant depends on the net force at that same instant, not on past forces.

ex.q: A net force of 20 N acts on a 4 kg block. Find the acceleration and the velocity after 3 s, starting from rest.

topics.rl: When a cricket ball leaves the bowler's hand, its acceleration depends only on the forces at that instant (gravity and air), not on the bowler's push a moment ago.

topics.t: Second law in action: bullets, impulse and batsmen
topics.h: A batsman meets a 140 km/h bouncer for a few milliseconds. In that blink, the force on the bat can reach thousands of newtons.
p: The second law applies to a particle, and also to a rigid body or a whole system, using the net EXTERNAL force and the acceleration of the system.
Impulse = F × Δt = change in momentum Δp. Impulsive forces are large and act for a very short time (bat on ball, hammer on nail); we measure their effect by Δp.
Bullet stopped in a block: find a from v² = u² + 2as, then F = ma.
If y = ut + ½gt² describes a particle (x-motion uniform), then a = g along y, so F = mg along y: a constant force gives a parabolic path.
Ball hit straight back at the same speed: Δp = m(v − (−v)) = 2mv.

ex.q: A 0.15 kg cricket ball moving at 20 m s⁻¹ is hit straight back at 20 m s⁻¹. Find the impulse and the average force if contact lasts 0.01 s.
st: Take the ball's return direction as +: initial p = −0.15 × 20 = −3 kg m s⁻¹, final p = +3 kg m s⁻¹.

topics.rl: Fielders pull their hands back while catching to increase the contact time, reducing the force for the same change in momentum.

topics.t: Newton's third law
topics.h: When you push a wall, the wall pushes you back just as hard. Then why don't the two pushes cancel? This is the most misunderstood law in physics.
p: Third law: to every action there is always an equal and opposite reaction. F_AB = −F_BA (force on A by B equals minus force on B by A).
Action and reaction act at the same instant on DIFFERENT bodies, so they never cancel each other.
There is no cause and effect between them: either force can be called the action.
In a system of bodies, internal forces come in third-law pairs and cancel; so only external forces affect the motion of the whole system.
Two colliding billiard balls exert equal and opposite forces for the same time, so they receive equal and opposite impulses.

ex.q: A 50 kg girl on skates pushes a 25 kg boy on skates with 100 N. Find each one's acceleration.
st: The boy gets 100 N forward: a = 100/25 = 4 m s⁻².
By the third law, the girl gets 100 N backward: a = 100/50 = 2 m s⁻² backward.
Equal forces, unequal accelerations, because masses differ.
ex.a: Boy 4 m s⁻², girl 2 m s⁻² opposite

topics.rl: When an Indian Navy sailor fires a deck gun, the gun recoils: the shell pushes back on the gun with the same force the gun pushes the shell.

topics.t: Rockets, recoil and conservation of momentum
topics.h: Chandrayaan-3's rocket had nothing to 'push against' in space. It moved by throwing gas backward: momentum must be conserved.
p: Third-law examples: walking (foot pushes ground back, ground pushes you forward), rowing (oar pushes water back), rocket (rocket pushes gas backward, gas pushes rocket forward), gun recoil.
Law of conservation of momentum: the total momentum of an isolated system (no net external force) stays constant.
Derivation for a collision: F_AB Δt = Δp_A and F_BA Δt = Δp_B; since F_AB = −F_BA, Δp_A + Δp_B = 0.
Recoil of a gun (initially at rest): 0 = m_b v_b + M V → V = −m_b v_b/M.
A shell exploding in flight: internal forces cannot change the total momentum; the fragments' momenta add up to the shell's momentum just before the explosion.

ex.q: A 4 kg gun fires a 0.02 kg bullet at 400 m s⁻¹. Find the recoil velocity of the gun.
st: V = −8/4 = −2 m s⁻¹ (opposite to the bullet).

topics.rl: ISRO's PSLV and GSLV rockets throw out exhaust gases at kilometres per second; the forward momentum of the rocket equals the backward momentum of the gas.

topics.t: Equilibrium of a particle
topics.h: A street lamp hangs perfectly still from two wires. The wires' pulls and the lamp's weight form a perfect closed triangle.
p: A particle is in equilibrium when the net external force on it is zero (it is at rest or moving uniformly).
Two forces in equilibrium must be equal in magnitude and opposite in direction along the same line.
Three concurrent forces in equilibrium can be drawn head to tail as a closed triangle (triangle law of forces); many forces form a closed polygon.
Component conditions: ΣFₓ = 0, ΣF_y = 0, ΣF_z = 0.
Method: draw the forces on the point (e.g. the knot), resolve them along x and y, and solve ΣFₓ = 0 and ΣF_y = 0.

ex.q: A 4 kg mass hangs from a string. A horizontal force F pulls the mass aside until the string makes θ with the vertical, where tan θ = 0.75. Find F and the tension (g = 10 m s⁻²).
st: Vertical: T cos θ = mg = 40 N.

topics.rl: Engineers designing the overhead electric lines for Indian Railways' electrified tracks balance the tensions and weights at every support point.

topics.t: Common forces: gravity, normal, tension and spring
topics.h: When you sit on a chair, the chair pushes up on you with exactly your weight. Where does that push come from? From electric forces between atoms!
p: Gravity acts at a distance; most other mechanical forces (normal, friction, tension, spring) are contact forces.
Normal reaction N is the component of contact force perpendicular to the surfaces in contact.
Tension acts along a string, pulling on the bodies attached; for a massless string it is the same throughout.
Spring force F = −kx: a restoring force proportional to extension or compression x, directed opposite to it (k is the spring constant).
Contact forces ultimately come from electrical forces between the charged particles (electrons and nuclei) of the surfaces.

ex.q: A spring of spring constant 200 N m⁻¹ is stretched by 5 cm. Find the restoring force.
st: Magnitude 10 N, directed back towards the natural length.

topics.rl: The shock absorbers of a motorbike and the spring balance at a sabzi mandi both rely on F = −kx.

topics.t: Static, kinetic and rolling friction
topics.h: Push a heavy almirah: nothing happens, then suddenly it jerks into motion. Static friction just gave up its maximum value.
p: Static friction f_s opposes impending relative motion. It is self-adjusting: it equals the applied force up to a limit f_s(max) = μ_s N.
Laws of friction: limiting friction is independent of the area of contact and proportional to the normal reaction N.
Kinetic friction f_k = μ_k N acts once sliding begins, opposing relative motion. μ_k < μ_s, and f_k is roughly independent of speed.
Angle of repose: a block on an incline is just about to slide when tan θ = μ_s.
Rolling friction is much smaller than sliding friction; that's why wheels and ball bearings are used.

ex.q: A 10 kg box rests on a floor with μ_s = 0.5 and μ_k = 0.4 (g = 10 m s⁻²). What friction acts if you push with (a) 30 N, (b) 60 N?
st: (a) 30 N < 50 N: box stays; static friction = 30 N.
(b) 60 N > 50 N: box slides; kinetic friction = 0.4 × 100 = 40 N.

topics.rl: Ball bearings in the wheels of Indian Railways' bogies replace sliding with rolling, saving huge amounts of energy.

topics.t: Friction at work: walking, trucks, connected blocks and lifts
topics.h: Without friction you couldn't walk, a car couldn't move, and a lift ride would feel very strange. Let's put forces to work.
p: Friction is essential: static friction from the road drives a car forward and lets us walk. Lubricants and ball bearings reduce unwanted friction in machines.
A box on a truck floor (μ_s) stays put as long as the truck's acceleration a ≤ μ_s g, because static friction is the only horizontal force on the box.
Block m₁ on a table (μ_k) tied over a pulley to a hanging m₂: a = (m₂ − μ_k m₁)g/(m₁ + m₂) and T = m₂(g − a).
Atwood machine (m₁ > m₂): a = (m₁ − m₂)g/(m₁ + m₂), T = 2m₁m₂g/(m₁ + m₂).
Lift: apparent weight N = m(g + a) when accelerating up, m(g − a) when accelerating down, 0 in free fall, and mg at constant velocity.

ex.q: A 2 kg block on a table (μ_k = 0.1) is tied by a string over a pulley to a hanging 3 kg block (g = 10 m s⁻²). Find a and T.
st: a = (m₂g − μ_k m₁g)/(m₁ + m₂) = (30 − 2)/5 = 5.6 m s⁻².
Hanging block: m₂g − T = m₂a → T = 3(10 − 5.6) = 13.2 N.
Check table block: T − 2 = 2 × 5.6 → T = 13.2 N ✓.

topics.rl: Riding a lift at a Mumbai high-rise, you feel heavier as it starts upward and lighter as it starts downward: the normal force from the floor changes.

topics.t: Circular motion: centripetal force and level roads
topics.h: A motorbike rider taking a sharp turn on a wet road skids out. The road's friction simply could not supply enough centripetal force.
p: Circular motion needs a net force towards the centre: f_c = mv²/R (the centripetal force).
Centripetal force is not a new kind of force. It is supplied by existing forces: tension (stone on string), gravity (planets), friction (car on road), normal force (wall of death).
Car on a level road: static friction provides mv²/R, so mv²/R ≤ μ_s mg → v_max = √(μ_s R g), independent of mass.
Cyclist or car on a level turn: if v² > μ_s R g, it skids outward. Slow down or reduce sharpness (increase R).

ex.q: A car takes a level turn of radius 20 m with μ_s = 0.5 (g = 10 m s⁻²). What is the maximum safe speed?

topics.rl: Road signs on ghat roads of the Western Ghats warn of sharp curves because the friction available limits safe turning speed.

topics.t: Banked roads: optimum and maximum safe speed
topics.h: Ever noticed that the outer edge of a highway curve is raised? That tilt lets the road itself help steer the car.
p: On a road banked at θ, the normal force N tilts inward. Equations (friction f down the slope): N cos θ = mg + f sin θ and N sin θ + f cos θ = mv²/R.
With f ≤ μ_s N, the maximum safe speed is v_max = √[Rg(μ_s + tan θ)/(1 − μ_s tan θ)].
Optimum speed (no friction needed): v₀ = √(Rg tan θ). At this speed, wear on tyres is least.
Banking raises v_max above the level-road value √(μ_s R g), which is why race tracks and highway curves are banked.

ex.q: A curve of radius 90 m is banked with tan θ = 1/3, and μ_s = 0.5 (g = 10 m s⁻²). Find the optimum and maximum safe speeds.
ex.a: v₀ ≈ 17.3 m s⁻¹, v_max = 30 m s⁻¹

topics.rl: Cycle velodromes have steeply banked tracks, and highway curves are gently banked, so that vehicles can corner faster and more safely than on flat ground.

topics.t: Solving mechanics problems with free-body diagrams
topics.h: Most mistakes in mechanics come from one thing: forgetting a force or adding one that isn't there. Free-body diagrams fix that.
p: Step 1: draw a schematic diagram showing all bodies, supports and connections (strings, pulleys, springs).
Step 2: choose a convenient part as your system and draw its free-body diagram (FBD) showing only that body.
Step 3: show all EXTERNAL forces on it (weight, normal, tension, friction, applied), known and unknown, with directions. Do not include forces the body exerts on others.
Step 4: apply F = ma to the chosen system. When switching to another body, use the third law for the force between them.
Example: block B (3 kg) resting on block A (5 kg) on the floor (g = 10 m s⁻²): B pushes A down with 30 N; the floor pushes A up with 80 N.

ex.q: A 3 kg block B rests on a 5 kg block A, which rests on the floor (g = 10 m s⁻²). Find the forces on A.
st: FBD of B: weight 30 N down, normal from A 30 N up.
Third law: B pushes A down with 30 N.
FBD of A: weight 50 N down, 30 N down from B, floor's normal N up.
ex.a: 30 N down from B, 50 N weight, 80 N up from floor

topics.rl: IIT JEE toppers swear by one habit: draw the FBD before writing any equation. It works just as well for your CBSE paper.

topics.t: The scalar (dot) product
topics.h: A coolie carrying a heavy bag on his head across a level platform is tired, yet in physics he did zero work on the bag. The dot product explains why.
p: In everyday language 'work', 'energy' and 'power' are loose words; in physics they have exact definitions built on the scalar product.
Scalar (dot) product: A·B = AB cos θ, where θ is the angle between A and B. The result is a scalar.
Properties: commutative (A·B = B·A) and distributive (A·(B + C) = A·B + A·C).
Unit vectors: î·î = ĵ·ĵ = k̂·k̂ = 1 and î·ĵ = ĵ·k̂ = k̂·î = 0.
Component form: A·B = AₓBₓ + A_yB_y + A_zB_z.

ex.q: Find A·B for A = 2î + 3ĵ − k̂ and B = 4î − ĵ + 2k̂.

topics.rl: Solar panel installers in Rajasthan tilt panels so that the sunlight direction and the panel's normal have the largest dot product, maximising captured energy.

topics.t: Work done by a constant force
topics.h: Pulling a suitcase by its handle at an angle: only the part of your pull along the floor does work.
p: Angle between vectors: cos θ = A·B/(AB).
Component of F along d = F·d/|d| = F cos θ.
Work by a constant force: W = F·d = Fd cos θ. It is a scalar; SI unit joule (1 J = 1 N m).

Zero work in three cases: no displacement (pushing a wall), no force (a body moving uniformly in free space), or force perpendicular to displacement (θ = 90°: coolie carrying a load horizontally, gravity on a body moving horizontally).

ex.q: F = 2î + ĵ + 2k̂ N and d = 2î − 2ĵ + k̂ m. Find the work done and the angle between F and d.

topics.rl: Porters at Indian railway stations do zero work (in physics) on a head-load while walking on the level, but plenty of work while climbing the stairs to the foot-over-bridge.

topics.t: Positive and negative work, and units of energy
topics.h: When you lower a heavy suitcase from a train's upper berth, gravity does positive work and your hands do negative work.
p: 0° ≤ θ < 90°: W > 0 (force helps motion). 90° < θ ≤ 180°: W < 0 (force opposes motion).
Kinetic friction opposes relative motion, so it does negative work on a sliding body.
Units of work and energy: joule (J); erg = 10⁻⁷ J; electron volt eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J; kilowatt hour kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J; calorie = 4.186 J.
Net work = sum of works by all forces (each with its sign).

ex.q: A 50 N push moves a box 5 m on a floor where friction is 20 N. Find the work done by each force and the net work.

topics.rl: Your electricity bill counts energy in 'units', and 1 unit = 1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J. A 2 kW geyser running for 30 minutes uses 1 unit.

topics.t: Kinetic energy and the work–energy theorem
topics.h: A raindrop falling from a cloud a kilometre up should hit you at over 140 m s⁻¹. It doesn't, because air resistance does a lot of negative work.
p: Start with v² − u² = 2as and multiply by m/2: ½mv² − ½mu² = mas = Fs.
Kinetic energy K = ½mv² (a scalar, never negative).
Work–energy theorem: the change in kinetic energy equals the net work done by all forces: K_f − K_i = W_net.
Typical kinetic energies span a huge range: a falling raindrop ~10⁻³ J, a running person ~10³ J, a car on a highway ~10⁵–10⁶ J.

ex.q: A 2 g raindrop falls 500 m and lands at 20 m s⁻¹ (g = 10 m s⁻²). Find the work done by gravity and by air resistance.

topics.rl: A Vande Bharat train of about 4 × 10⁵ kg at 30 m s⁻¹ carries nearly 2 × 10⁸ J of kinetic energy, which its brakes must remove to stop.

topics.t: Work done by a variable force
topics.h: Stretching a resistance band at the gym gets harder the further you pull. You can't just use W = Fd here.
p: For a force that changes with position, break the displacement into small steps Δx where F is nearly constant: W ≈ Σ F(x)Δx.
In the limit Δx → 0: W = ∫ F(x) dx from x_i to x_f.
Graphically, work done = area under the force–displacement (F–x) graph; area below the x-axis is negative work.
Use simple shapes (rectangles, triangles, trapeziums) to find areas for piecewise-linear graphs.

ex.q: A woman pushes a trunk with 100 N for the first 10 m; then her push falls linearly to 50 N over the next 10 m. Find the work done by her.

topics.rl: Engineers testing car crash barriers at the Automotive Research Association of India (ARAI), Pune, find the energy absorbed from the area under force–crush graphs.

topics.t: Work–energy theorem for variable forces and its uses
topics.h: A bullet punching through a plank loses most of its energy in a split second. The work–energy theorem tells you how much without knowing the messy force.
p: Proof for a variable force: dK/dt = mv dv/dt = Fv = F dx/dt, so dK = F dx. Integrating, K_f − K_i = ∫F dx = W.
The theorem is the integral form of Newton's second law. It is a scalar equation (no direction needed) and holds in inertial frames.
It is powerful when the force is complicated: you only need the work.
Bullet through a plank: kinetic energy lost = work done by the plank's resistance. Block entering a rough region: K_f = K_i + W_friction (W_friction < 0).

ex.q: A 20 g bullet enters a plank at 300 m s⁻¹ and emerges at 100 m s⁻¹. Find the kinetic energy lost and the fraction lost.

topics.rl: Bulletproof jackets used by the CRPF are tested by how much kinetic energy their layers absorb, which is the work done against the bullet.

topics.t: Potential energy and conservative forces
topics.h: Water held behind the Bhakra Dam stores energy simply because of where it is. Release it and the turbines spin.
p: Potential energy is stored energy due to position or configuration (a raised stone, a stretched bow).
Near the Earth's surface, gravitational PE V = mgh (taking V = 0 at the reference level). In 1D, F = −dV/dx (force points towards lower PE).
A force is conservative if the work done by it depends only on the initial and final positions (not on the path), and is zero over any closed path. Gravity and spring force are conservative.
Friction is non-conservative: its work depends on the path and is not zero over a closed path, so no potential energy can be defined for it.
PE has the same dimensions [M L² T⁻²] and unit (joule) as kinetic energy.

ex.q: A 2 kg stone is raised 5 m (g = 9.8 m s⁻²). Find its gain in PE, and show F = −dV/dx gives its weight.
st: The minus sign means the force points downward (towards lower V).

topics.rl: In pumped-storage plants like Tehri, water is pumped uphill at night (storing PE) and released through turbines during peak demand.

topics.t: Conservation of mechanical energy
topics.h: A coconut falling from a 20 m palm tree trades potential energy for kinetic energy all the way down. The total? Unchanged.
p: If only conservative forces act, total mechanical energy E = K + V remains constant.
Derivation: for a conservative force, W = −ΔV; by the work–energy theorem W = ΔK. So ΔK = −ΔV, i.e. Δ(K + V) = 0.
Ball dropped from height H: at height h, V = mgh and K = mg(H − h); just before the ground, K = mgH and v = √(2gH).
With friction or air resistance, mechanical energy is not conserved: some becomes heat.

ex.q: A 1 kg coconut falls from a 20 m tree (g = 10 m s⁻²). Find its kinetic energy and speed at 5 m above the ground.

topics.rl: A child on a swing at a village fair keeps converting PE at the ends to KE at the bottom; friction and air drag slowly steal energy, so someone has to keep pushing.

topics.t: Vertical circles and potential-energy graphs
topics.h: A 'loop-the-loop' ride at an amusement park is designed so the car is fast enough at the top. Energy conservation decides how fast it must be at the bottom.
p: Bob on a string of length L in a vertical circle: at the top, tension ≥ 0 needs mv_t²/L ≥ mg, so v_top(min) = √(gL).
Energy conservation between bottom and top (height 2L): v_b² = v_t² + 4gL. So v_bottom(min) = √(5gL).
With v_b = √(5gL): tension at the bottom = mg + mv_b²/L = 6mg; tension at the top = 0.
Potential-energy graph: K = E − V(x) ≥ 0. Regions where V(x) > E are forbidden; the particle turns back where V = E (turning points).

ex.q: A 0.2 kg bob on a 1 m string must just complete a vertical circle (g = 10 m s⁻²). Find the minimum speeds at the top and bottom.

topics.rl: Stunt riders in a 'maut ka kuan' (wall of death) at Indian melas must keep their speed above a minimum, or gravity wins.

topics.t: Spring potential energy
topics.h: Railway platforms end in spring buffers. A slow-moving coach that overshoots is stopped by a spring that stores its kinetic energy.
p: Spring force (Hooke's law): F = −kx, where k is the spring constant (N m⁻¹) and x is the extension or compression.
Work done in stretching from 0 to x = area of triangle under the F–x line = ½kx².
Spring PE: V = ½kx². The spring force is conservative (work depends only on start and end x).
Energy swaps between ½mv² and ½kx²: speed is maximum at x = 0 (equilibrium), v_max = x_m √(k/m).
Car hitting a spring: ½mv² = ½kx_m²; with friction μ, ½mv² = ½kx_m² + μmg x_m.

ex.q: A 1000 kg car hits a spring buffer (k = 16000 N m⁻¹) at 4 m s⁻¹. Find the maximum compression (ignore friction).

topics.rl: Scooter suspensions and the bogie springs of a Rajdhani coach store and release elastic potential energy with every bump.

topics.t: Power
topics.h: Two students climb the same stairs. Same work, but the one who sprints up uses more power. Power is about speed of doing work.
p: Average power P = W/t; instantaneous power P = dW/dt.
Since dW = F·dr, P = F·v.
SI unit: watt (1 W = 1 J s⁻¹). 1 horsepower (hp) = 746 W.
Kilowatt hour (kWh) is a unit of ENERGY: 1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J.
Lifting a load at constant speed against friction: P = (mg + f)v.

ex.q: A 1000 kg lift moves up at constant 3 m s⁻¹ against a friction force of 2000 N (g = 10 m s⁻²). Find the motor's power.

topics.rl: BEE star labels on Indian ACs and fridges compare power ratings and yearly energy use in kWh to show which appliance saves more electricity.

topics.t: Collisions: elastic, inelastic and perfectly inelastic
topics.h: When two kabaddi players crash and grab each other, they move off together. Momentum survives the crash; kinetic energy doesn't.
p: In every collision where external forces are negligible during the brief impact, total momentum is conserved.
Elastic collision: total kinetic energy is also conserved (e.g. ideal billiard balls, atomic collisions). Inelastic: some KE is converted to heat, sound or deformation.
Perfectly inelastic: the bodies stick together. Common velocity v = (m₁u₁ + m₂u₂)/(m₁ + m₂).
KE lost in a perfectly inelastic collision: ΔK = ½ [m₁m₂/(m₁ + m₂)] (u₁ − u₂)².
Total energy is always conserved; it is only kinetic energy that may not be.

ex.q: A 2 kg trolley at 6 m s⁻¹ hits a 1 kg trolley at rest and they stick. Find the common velocity and the KE lost.

topics.rl: Railway wagons coupling in a shunting yard are a perfectly inelastic collision: they move off together and some kinetic energy becomes sound and heat.

topics.t: Elastic collisions in one dimension and neutron moderators
topics.h: Nuclear reactors in Kudankulam use water to slow down fast neutrons. Why water and not lead? One-dimensional collisions explain it.
p: For m₁ moving at u₁ hitting m₂ at rest elastically: v₁ = (m₁ − m₂)u₁/(m₁ + m₂), v₂ = 2m₁u₁/(m₁ + m₂).
Equal masses: v₁ = 0, v₂ = u₁. They exchange velocities.
Heavy hits light (m₁ ≫ m₂): v₁ ≈ u₁, v₂ ≈ 2u₁. Light hits heavy (m₁ ≪ m₂): v₁ ≈ −u₁ (bounces back), v₂ ≈ 0.
Moderator: a neutron loses most KE when it hits a nucleus of similar mass. Fraction of KE kept = [(m₁ − m₂)/(m₁ + m₂)]². With deuterium (2m) it keeps 1/9; with carbon (12m) it keeps (11/13)² ≈ 0.72.

ex.q: A 2 kg ball at 6 m s⁻¹ collides elastically head-on with a 1 kg ball at rest. Find the final velocities.
st: Check KE: 36 J before; ½·2·4 + ½·1·64 = 4 + 32 = 36 J ✓.
ex.a: v₁ = 2 m s⁻¹, v₂ = 8 m s⁻¹

topics.rl: India's pressurised heavy-water reactors (PHWRs), like those at Rawatbhata, use heavy water (deuterium) as the moderator.

topics.t: Collisions in two dimensions
topics.h: On a carrom board, the striker hits a coin off-centre and both fly away at an angle. Momentum is conserved along x and y separately.
p: In 2D, conserve momentum along each axis: m₁u₁ = m₁v₁ cos θ₁ + m₂v₂ cos θ₂ and 0 = m₁v₁ sin θ₁ − m₂v₂ sin θ₂ (target at rest, angles on opposite sides).
With the KE equation for elastic collisions, there are 3 equations but 4 unknowns (v₁, v₂, θ₁, θ₂), so one quantity (e.g. an angle) must be given.
Equal masses, elastic, one at rest: the two final velocities are perpendicular, θ₁ + θ₂ = 90°.
Billiards: if the cue ball is deflected by 37°, the target ball moves off at 53° on the other side.

ex.q: A billiard ball hits an identical ball at rest elastically and is deflected by 30°. At what angle does the target ball move?
st: Equal masses, elastic, target at rest: θ₁ + θ₂ = 90°.
θ₂ = 90° − 30° = 60°, on the other side of the original line.

topics.rl: Snooker players use the 90° rule: when the cue ball (without spin) hits an identical object ball glancingly, the two balls separate at nearly right angles.

topics.ch: System of Particles and Rotational Motion
topics.t: Rigid bodies and the kinds of motion
topics.h: A rolling cricket ball, a spinning ceiling fan and a car on a highway: one translates, one rotates, one does both. Rigid-body physics handles all three.
p: An extended body is a system of particles. A rigid body is an idealisation in which the distances between all pairs of particles stay fixed.
Pure translation: every particle has the same velocity at every instant (a block sliding down an incline).
Rotation about a fixed axis: every particle moves in a circle in a plane perpendicular to the axis, with its centre on the axis (ceiling fan, potter's wheel).
Rotation about a fixed point (not a fixed axis): e.g. a spinning top whose axis itself swings around a vertical line (precession).
General motion of a rigid body = translation (of a reference point, like the centre of mass) + rotation about an axis through it (a rolling wheel).

ex.q: A cylinder rolls down an incline without slipping. Is its motion pure translation?
st: Points at the top, centre and bottom of the cylinder have different velocities at the same instant.
So it cannot be pure translation.
It is translation of the centre plus rotation about the axis through the centre.

topics.rl: A giant wheel at a Dussehra mela rotates about a fixed axis, while a bullock-cart wheel on a village road both translates and rotates.

topics.ch: System of Particles and Rotational Motion
topics.t: Centre of mass of particles and laminas
topics.h: A gymnast's centre of mass can even lie outside her body during a back-bend. It is a point defined by maths, not by matter.
p: Two particles on a line: X = (m₁x₁ + m₂x₂)/(m₁ + m₂). For equal masses it is midway.
n particles in 3D: R = Σmᵢrᵢ/M, i.e. X = Σmᵢxᵢ/M, Y = Σmᵢyᵢ/M, Z = Σmᵢzᵢ/M.
Continuous bodies: X = (1/M)∫x dm etc. For a uniform symmetric body (rod, ring, disc, sphere, cube) the CM lies at the geometric centre.
Uniform triangular lamina: CM at the centroid (intersection of medians).
Composite shapes (e.g. an L-shaped lamina of three equal squares): treat each part as a point mass at its own centre, then combine.

ex.q: Masses 1 kg at (0, 0), 1 kg at (4 m, 0) and 2 kg at (0, 4 m). Find the centre of mass.

topics.rl: Truck loaders in Indian mandis keep heavy sacks low and centred so that the vehicle's centre of mass stays low and it doesn't topple on turns.

topics.ch: System of Particles and Rotational Motion
topics.t: Motion of the centre of mass
topics.h: A Diwali rocket bursts into sparks high in the sky. The sparks fly everywhere, but their centre of mass calmly continues on the same parabola.
p: Differentiating MR = Σmᵢrᵢ: MV = Σmᵢvᵢ and MA = Σmᵢaᵢ.
MA = F_ext: the CM moves like a single particle of mass M acted on by the total external force.
Internal forces between particles cancel in third-law pairs, so they cannot affect the motion of the CM.
Exploding projectile: the explosion forces are internal, so the CM keeps following the original parabola (until fragments hit the ground).
The translational motion of a system is the motion of its CM; the rest is motion relative to the CM.

ex.q: A shell fired as a projectile explodes into two equal parts at the top of its path. One part falls straight down. Where does the CM land, and where does the other part land?
st: The CM continues on the original parabola, so it lands at the original range R.
One half lands at R/2 (below the top).
Since the CM is midway between equal halves, the other half lands at 3R/2.
ex.a: CM at R; other piece at 3R/2

topics.rl: In space-station docking, the internal pushes between astronauts and modules never change the motion of the station's overall centre of mass.

topics.ch: System of Particles and Rotational Motion
topics.t: Linear momentum of a system and its conservation
topics.h: Two stars orbit each other in a binary system. They whirl around wildly, yet their centre of mass glides through space in a straight line.
p: Total momentum P = Σmᵢvᵢ = MV.
dP/dt = F_ext: only external forces change the total momentum.
If F_ext = 0, P is constant, so the CM moves with constant velocity (or stays at rest).
Radioactive decay of a nucleus at rest: the products fly apart in opposite directions so that the CM stays at rest.
Binary stars: under their mutual gravity (internal), the CM moves uniformly while the stars orbit around it.

ex.q: A uranium-238 nucleus at rest decays into a thorium nucleus (234 u) and an alpha particle (4 u) moving at 1.17 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹. Find the thorium speed.
st: Initial P = 0, so the products' momenta are equal and opposite.
v = 2 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹, opposite to the alpha particle.

topics.rl: Astronomers at the Indian Institute of Astrophysics use the wobble of a star about the common CM to detect unseen companion planets.

topics.ch: System of Particles and Rotational Motion
topics.t: The vector (cross) product
topics.h: Tighten a screw clockwise and it goes in. That everyday rule is exactly how the direction of a cross product is decided.
p: a × b = ab sin θ n̂, where n̂ is perpendicular to both a and b. Direction by the right-hand rule (fingers from a to b, thumb gives a × b) or a right-handed screw.
Properties: anticommutative (a × b = −b × a), distributive, and a × a = 0.
Unit vectors: î × ĵ = k̂, ĵ × k̂ = î, k̂ × î = ĵ; reversing the order gives a minus sign; î × î = 0.
Component (determinant) form: a × b = (a_yb_z − a_zb_y)î + (a_zbₓ − aₓb_z)ĵ + (aₓb_y − a_ybₓ)k̂.
Under reflection, ordinary (polar) vectors change sign but a × b does not: the cross product is an axial (pseudo) vector.

ex.q: Find a·b and a × b for a = î + 2ĵ and b = 3î + ĵ.

topics.rl: Mechanics at a two-wheeler service centre know 'righty-tighty, lefty-loosey' without thinking: it's the right-handed screw rule.

topics.ch: System of Particles and Rotational Motion
topics.t: Angular velocity and angular acceleration
topics.h: Every point on a spinning CD turns through the same angle each second, but the outer rim races far faster than the inside.
p: Angular velocity ω is a vector along the axis of rotation; its direction follows the right-hand rule (curl fingers with the rotation, thumb gives ω).
Linear velocity of a particle: v = ω × r; magnitude v = ωr⊥, where r⊥ is the perpendicular distance from the axis.
All particles of a rigid body rotating about a fixed axis share the same ω; only v differs (∝ distance from axis). Points on the axis have v = 0.
Angular acceleration α = dω/dt. For rotation about a fixed axis, both ω and α lie along the axis.

ex.q: A disc rotates at ω = 10 rad s⁻¹. Find the speed of points 0.05 m and 0.15 m from the axis.

topics.rl: The Earth's angular velocity is the same everywhere (about 7.3 × 10⁻⁵ rad s⁻¹), but a person in Chennai moves faster than one in Srinagar because Chennai is farther from the axis.

topics.ch: System of Particles and Rotational Motion
topics.t: Torque and angular momentum of a particle
topics.h: Ever tried opening a door by pushing near its hinge? Same force, almost no turning. Torque depends on where you push.
p: Torque (moment of force): τ = r × F, magnitude τ = rF sin θ. SI unit N m (not written as joule). It is a vector along the axis by the right-hand rule.
τ = F × r⊥ (moment arm: perpendicular distance from the axis to the line of action of F) = r × F⊥.
Angular momentum of a particle: l = r × p, magnitude l = rp sin θ = r⊥ p.
Rotational analogue of F = dp/dt: dl/dt = τ.

ex.q: A force F = 3î N acts at r = î + 2ĵ m. Find the torque about the origin.
st: τ = −6k̂ N m (clockwise as seen from +z).

topics.rl: Spanners for truck wheel nuts in highway dhabas are long, so mechanics get a big moment arm and loosen tight nuts with modest force.

topics.ch: System of Particles and Rotational Motion
topics.t: Systems: dL/dt = τ_ext and conservation of angular momentum
topics.h: Planets sweep around the Sun for billions of years without slowing down because there is no external torque on them about the Sun.
p: For a system of particles, L = Σlᵢ and dL/dt = τ_ext. Internal torques cancel in pairs (internal forces are equal, opposite and along the same line).
Conservation: if τ_ext = 0, the total angular momentum L is constant (in magnitude and direction).
A particle moving with constant velocity has constant angular momentum about any point: l = r⊥ mv with r⊥ (distance of the line from the point) fixed.
Central forces (gravity of the Sun) produce no torque about the centre, so planets' angular momentum is conserved.

ex.q: Show that a 1 kg particle moving at 2 m s⁻¹ along the line y = 3 m has constant angular momentum about the origin.
st: x has dropped out, so l = −6k̂ kg m² s⁻¹ at all times.

topics.rl: ISRO's satellites use spinning momentum wheels: changing a wheel's spin makes the satellite turn the other way, keeping total angular momentum fixed.

topics.ch: System of Particles and Rotational Motion
topics.t: Equilibrium of a rigid body, couples and levers
topics.h: Turning a car's steering wheel with both hands applies a couple: it spins the wheel without pushing it anywhere.
p: Mechanical equilibrium of a rigid body: net external force = 0 (translational) AND net external torque = 0 (rotational).
In 3D these give six independent conditions: three force components and three torque components equal to zero.
A couple is a pair of equal and opposite forces with different lines of action. It produces rotation without translation; its torque = F × d (d = separation), the same about any point.
Principle of moments (lever): load × load arm = effort × effort arm. Mechanical advantage MA = load/effort = effort arm/load arm.

ex.q: A see-saw is balanced at its centre. A 30 kg child sits 2 m from the pivot. Where must a 40 kg child sit to balance it?
st: Principle of moments about the pivot: 30g × 2 = 40g × d.
Sit 1.5 m from the pivot on the other side.

topics.rl: A hand-pump in an Indian village is a lever: a long handle (effort arm) lets a small push lift a heavy column of water.

topics.ch: System of Particles and Rotational Motion
topics.t: Centre of gravity and equilibrium problems
topics.h: Tall structures, from the Qutub Minar to modern Mumbai skyscrapers, stand safely because their centre of gravity lies low and well within a wide base.
p: Centre of gravity (CG): the point where the total gravitational torque on the body is zero. In a uniform g, the CG coincides with the CM.
Finding CG of an irregular lamina: suspend it from a point and draw the vertical (plumb line); repeat from another point. The CG is where the lines cross.
Bar on two supports: use ΣF = 0 for the sum of reactions and Στ = 0 about one support for each reaction.
Ladder against a smooth wall: the wall gives only a horizontal push; the floor gives a vertical normal force and friction. Take torques about the foot.
Car on its wheels: take moments about one axle to split the weight between front and rear wheels.

ex.q: A uniform 1 m bar of 2 kg rests on supports at its ends A and B. A 4 kg load hangs 0.25 m from A (g = 10 m s⁻²). Find the reactions.
st: Weights: bar 20 N at 0.5 m, load 40 N at 0.25 m.

topics.rl: Truck designers place the engine and load so the weight is shared safely between the front and rear axles. Lab safety: when locating a lamina's CG by suspension, push the pin through a pre-made hole and keep fingers away from its sharp point.

topics.ch: System of Particles and Rotational Motion
topics.t: Moment of inertia and radius of gyration
topics.h: A tightrope walker carries a long pole. Spreading mass far from the axis makes her much harder to topple: that's moment of inertia.
p: Rotational KE: K = ½Iω², with moment of inertia I = Σmᵢrᵢ² (rᵢ = distance from the axis). Unit kg m².
I depends on the mass, its distribution, and the axis chosen. It is the rotational analogue of mass (measure of rotational inertia).
Thin ring about its axis (through centre, ⊥ plane): MR². Thin rod about a ⊥ axis through its centre: ML²/12.
Standard values: disc or solid cylinder about its axis MR²/2; hollow cylinder about its axis MR²; ring about a diameter MR²/2; disc about a diameter MR²/4; solid sphere about a diameter (2/5)MR².
Radius of gyration k: I = Mk², so k = √(I/M). For a ring about its axis k = R; for a disc about its axis k = R/√2.

ex.q: A ring of mass 2 kg and radius 0.5 m spins at 10 rad s⁻¹ about its axis. Find I and the rotational KE.

topics.rl: Kabaddi and wrestling coaches teach athletes to tuck limbs in to turn quickly: a smaller I means less effort to start rotation.

topics.ch: System of Particles and Rotational Motion
topics.t: Flywheels and kinematics of rotation
topics.h: Old bullock-driven sugarcane crushers and modern car engines both use heavy flywheels so the rotation doesn't jerk.
p: A flywheel has a large moment of inertia, so it resists changes in angular speed and smooths out the jerky torque of an engine.
Analogues: θ ↔ x, ω ↔ v, α ↔ a.
For constant α: ω = ω₀ + αt; θ = θ₀ + ω₀t + ½αt²; ω² = ω₀² + 2α(θ − θ₀).
Revolutions = θ/(2π); rpm to rad s⁻¹: multiply by 2π/60.

ex.q: A wheel starts from rest with α = 2 rad s⁻². Find ω and θ after 5 s, and the number of revolutions.

topics.rl: The flywheel on a single-cylinder motorbike engine keeps the single cylinder's power pulses from shaking the bike.

topics.ch: System of Particles and Rotational Motion
topics.t: Dynamics of rotation: τ = Iα, work and power
topics.h: Pull the rope of a well's pulley and the drum spins up. τ = Iα tells you exactly how fast.
p: For rotation about a fixed axis, only torque components along the axis matter; perpendicular components are balanced by the bearings.
Work done by a torque: dW = τ dθ, so W = τθ for constant τ. Power P = τω.
Second law for rotation: τ = Iα.
Analogues: m ↔ I, F ↔ τ, p = mv ↔ L = Iω, K = ½mv² ↔ ½Iω², W = Fx ↔ τθ, P = Fv ↔ τω.
Cord wound on a flywheel and pulled with F: τ = FR, α = FR/I; work done = F × length pulled = gain in ½Iω².

ex.q: A cord on the rim of a 10 kg disc flywheel (R = 0.2 m) is pulled with 20 N. Find α, and ω after 2 m of cord is pulled (from rest).
st: τ = FR = 4 N m; α = τ/I = 20 rad s⁻².
ex.a: α = 20 rad s⁻², ω = 20 rad s⁻¹

topics.rl: Ceiling-fan makers in India rate motors by power: P = τω tells how much torque the motor supplies at its running speed.
