topics.ch: System of Particles and Rotational Motion
topics.t: Angular momentum about a fixed axis and its conservation
topics.h: A Bharatanatyam dancer spinning on one foot pulls her arms in and suddenly whirls faster. No push, just angular momentum conservation.
p: For rotation about a fixed axis: L = Iω, and dL/dt = τ (axial component).
If the external torque is zero, Iω = constant: I₁ω₁ = I₂ω₂.
Examples: a person on a rotating stool pulling in arms (I decreases, ω increases); a diver tucking in to somersault faster; a skater spinning.
Rotational KE changes: K = L²/(2I). With L fixed, reducing I increases K; the extra energy comes from the work done by the person's muscles.
Typical numericals: torque on a disc from τ = Iα, L = Iω, and K = ½Iω².

ex.q: A child on a turntable has I = 6 kg m² with arms out, spinning at 2 rad s⁻¹. Folding arms makes I = 2 kg m². Find the new ω and the ratio of KE.
st: I₁ω₁ = I₂ω₂ → 6 × 2 = 2 × ω₂ → ω₂ = 6 rad s⁻¹.
KE triples; the child's muscles supply the extra 24 J.

topics.rl: Divers at national aquatics championships tuck tightly to complete multiple somersaults, then open out to slow the spin before entering the water.

topics.t: From geocentric skies to Kepler's law of orbits
topics.h: The same force that makes a mango drop from a tree in Malihabad keeps the Moon circling the Earth. It took humanity two thousand years to see that.
p: Everything near the Earth tends to fall towards it. The motion of planets puzzled thinkers for centuries: Ptolemy's geocentric model put the Earth at the centre.
Aryabhata (5th century CE) described the Earth rotating on its axis; Copernicus (16th century) proposed the heliocentric model with the Sun at the centre.

Tycho Brahe made precise naked-eye records of planetary positions; Kepler analysed them to find three laws; Galileo showed all bodies fall with the same acceleration; Newton explained it all with universal gravitation.
Kepler's first law (law of orbits): every planet moves in an ellipse with the Sun at one focus.
Perihelion: the point of closest approach to the Sun; aphelion: the farthest point.

ex.q: A planet's orbit has perihelion distance 1.0 AU and aphelion distance 1.5 AU. Find the semi-major axis.
st: The major axis = perihelion + aphelion distance = 2.5 AU.

topics.rl: Jantar Mantar observatories built in Jaipur and Delhi were used to track the Sun, Moon and planets with remarkable precision long before telescopes were common in India.

topics.t: Kepler's laws of areas and periods
topics.h: The Earth moves fastest in early January, when it is closest to the Sun. Kepler's second law predicted this centuries ago.
p: Second law (law of areas): the line joining a planet to the Sun sweeps out equal areas in equal intervals of time.
Reason: gravity is a central force, so it exerts no torque about the Sun and the planet's angular momentum L is conserved. Areal velocity dA/dt = L/(2m) = constant.
Hence a planet moves faster near perihelion and slower near aphelion: v_p r_p = v_a r_a.
Third law (law of periods): T² ∝ a³, where a is the semi-major axis. T²/a³ is nearly the same for all planets of the Sun.

ex.q: A comet's speed at perihelion (r = 1 AU) is 60 km s⁻¹. Find its speed at aphelion (r = 5 AU).
st: Angular momentum is conserved: v_p r_p = v_a r_a.

topics.rl: ISRO's Mars Orbiter Mission moved in a highly elliptical orbit around Mars, speeding up near periapsis exactly as the law of areas predicts.

topics.t: Newton's universal law of gravitation
topics.h: You and the person next to you attract each other gravitationally right now. The force is about a millionth of a newton, far too tiny to feel.
p: Every particle attracts every other particle with F = Gm₁m₂/r², along the line joining them.
Vector form: the force on m₂ due to m₁ is F₂₁ = −(Gm₁m₂/r²) r̂₁₂, where r̂₁₂ points from m₁ to m₂; the minus sign shows attraction.
Gravitational force is always attractive, central (along the line of centres) and obeys superposition: the net force is the vector sum of forces from each mass.
Three equal masses at the vertices of an equilateral triangle exert zero net force on a mass at the centroid (by symmetry).

ex.q: Find the gravitational force between two 100 kg spheres whose centres are 1 m apart (G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²).
st: Tiny compared with their weights (about 980 N each).

topics.rl: The tides at the Gulf of Khambhat, among the highest in India, are driven by the Moon's and Sun's gravitational pull on the oceans.

topics.t: Shell theorem, Newton's Moon test and measuring G
topics.h: Newton asked: if gravity reaches the apple, does it reach the Moon? He checked using nothing more than the Moon's orbit and the inverse-square law.
p: Shell theorem: a uniform spherical shell attracts an outside point mass as if all its mass were at its centre. Inside the shell, the net force is zero.
Moon test: the Moon is about 60 Earth radii away. Its centripetal acceleration a_m = 4π²R_m/T² ≈ 0.0027 m s⁻², and g/a_m ≈ 3600 = 60², just as the inverse-square law predicts.
Cavendish (1798) measured G with a torsion balance: two small lead spheres on a rod hung from a fine wire, attracted by two large spheres; the twist of the wire gave the force.
Accepted value: G ≈ 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻².

ex.q: Show that the Moon's acceleration agrees with the inverse-square law if the Moon is 60 Earth radii away.
st: At the surface (r = R), acceleration = g ≈ 9.8 m s⁻².
At r = 60R, acceleration should be g/60² = 9.8/3600.
= 0.0027 m s⁻², matching 4π²R_m/T² for the Moon.

topics.rl: Precise measurements of G are still being improved worldwide, because G is the least precisely known of the fundamental constants.

topics.t: Acceleration due to gravity at the Earth's surface
topics.h: Knowing just g, the Earth's radius and G, you can 'weigh' the entire Earth from your physics lab.
p: Treat the Earth as concentric uniform shells: for any outside point, the Earth acts as a point mass M_E at its centre.
At the surface: mg = GM_E m/R_E², so g = GM_E/R_E².
Mass of the Earth: M_E = gR_E²/G = 9.8 × (6.37 × 10⁶)²/(6.67 × 10⁻¹¹) ≈ 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg.
Weight W = mg. g does not depend on the mass of the falling body, so (without air) all bodies fall with the same acceleration.

ex.q: A planet has twice the Earth's mass and twice its radius. Compare g on it with g on the Earth.
st: So g on the planet is g/2.

topics.rl: Gaganyaan astronauts training in Bengaluru learn that their mass stays the same in orbit, while the weight they feel changes with g and with acceleration.

topics.t: Variation of g with height and depth
topics.h: Climbers on Mount Everest weigh about 0.3% less than at sea level, and in a deep mine g also drops. The surface is where g peaks.
p: Height h: g(h) = GM/(R + h)² = g(1 + h/R)⁻² ≈ g(1 − 2h/R) for h ≪ R.
Depth d: only the inner sphere of radius (R − d) attracts (the outer shell gives zero), so g(d) = g(1 − d/R).
g is maximum at the surface, decreases with height and with depth, and is zero at the centre.
At h = R, g becomes g/4; at d = R/2, g becomes g/2. Small heights: g falls by about twice as fast with height as with depth.

ex.q: A body weighs 72 N on the surface. Find its weight at height R/2 and at depth R/2.

topics.rl: Geologists of the Geological Survey of India use tiny variations of g (gravity surveys) to locate dense ore bodies and oil-bearing rocks underground.

topics.t: Gravitational potential energy
topics.h: Lifting a satellite to orbit costs energy. How much? You can't use mgh for thousands of kilometres; you need the general formula.
p: Gravitational force is conservative, so we can define potential energy: the work done by gravity depends only on start and end positions.
Near the surface (h ≪ R): the PE difference between heights h₁ and h₂ is mg(h₂ − h₁).
General expression, taking PE = 0 at infinity: W(r) = −GM_E m/r for r ≥ R_E. It is negative and increases (towards zero) as r increases.
Work needed to move m from r₁ to r₂ = W(r₂) − W(r₁) = GM_E m(1/r₁ − 1/r₂).

ex.q: Find the work needed to raise a 1 kg mass from the Earth's surface to a height R (in terms of GM/R).
st: = GMm/2R = ½ gR m (using GM = gR²).

topics.rl: PSLV launches to sun-synchronous orbits at about 700 km lift satellites high enough that mgh is no longer accurate: engineers use −GMm/r.

topics.t: Gravitational potential and systems of particles
topics.h: The total gravitational energy of a star cluster is the sum of the energy of every pair. Four particles? That's six pairs.
p: Gravitational potential V at a point = PE per unit mass: V = −GM/r (unit J kg⁻¹). It is a scalar.
Potentials from several masses add as scalars: V = −G Σ mᵢ/rᵢ.
PE of a system of particles = sum over all pairs: U = −G Σ mᵢmⱼ/rᵢⱼ (each pair counted once).
Four equal masses m at the corners of a square of side l: 4 sides and 2 diagonals (l√2), so U = −(Gm²/l)(4 + √2). Potential at the centre (distance l/√2 from each) = −4√2 Gm/l.

ex.q: Three equal masses m are at the vertices of an equilateral triangle of side a. Find the PE of the system.
st: Number of pairs = 3, each separated by a.

topics.rl: Astrophysicists at TIFR estimate whether a gas cloud will collapse into stars by comparing its total gravitational PE with its thermal energy.

topics.t: Escape speed
topics.h: Throw a ball up at 11.2 km s⁻¹ (ignoring air) and it never comes back. That's the Earth's escape speed.
p: A body escapes if its total energy is ≥ 0: ½mv² − GMm/R ≥ 0.
Minimum (escape) speed: v_e = √(2GM/R) = √(2gR). For the Earth (g = 9.8 m s⁻², R = 6.4 × 10⁶ m) v_e ≈ 11.2 km s⁻¹.
Escape speed does not depend on the mass of the body or the direction of launch (ignoring air).
The Moon's escape speed is only about 2.3 km s⁻¹. It is so low that the faster gas molecules escape over time, so the Moon has no atmosphere.
Between two fixed spheres: a projectile must reach the 'neutral point' where the two pulls balance; beyond it, the far sphere pulls it in.

ex.q: Calculate the Earth's escape speed with g = 9.8 m s⁻² and R = 6.4 × 10⁶ m.

topics.rl: Chandrayaan missions do not leave Earth at 11.2 km s⁻¹ directly; they raise their orbit step by step with engine burns, gaining energy gradually.

topics.t: Earth satellites: orbital speed and period
topics.h: A satellite skimming just above the Earth would circle the planet in about 85 minutes, faster than a cricket Test session!
p: Satellites are natural (the Moon) or artificial (INSAT, Cartosat). In a circular orbit, gravity provides the centripetal force: mv²/(R + h) = GMm/(R + h)².
Orbital speed v = √(GM/(R + h)); it decreases with height. Near the surface v ≈ √(gR) ≈ 7.9 km s⁻¹.
Period T = 2π√((R + h)³/GM), so T² ∝ (R + h)³: Kepler's third law for satellites.
For h ≪ R: T ≈ 2π√(R/g) ≈ 85 minutes.
From a moon's orbit we can find the planet's mass: M = 4π²r³/(GT²) (e.g. Mars from its moon Phobos; Earth from the Moon).

ex.q: Find the period of a satellite orbiting just above the Earth's surface (R = 6.4 × 10⁶ m, g = 9.8 m s⁻²).

topics.rl: ISRO's geostationary communication satellites like GSAT orbit at about 36000 km height with a 24-hour period, staying fixed over India.

topics.t: Energy of an orbiting satellite
topics.h: To move a satellite to a higher orbit, you must ADD energy, even though it will end up moving more slowly. Strange but true.
p: Kinetic energy in a circular orbit of radius r = R + h: K = GMm/(2r).
Potential energy: U = −GMm/r.
Total energy E = K + U = −GMm/(2r). It is negative for a bound orbit, and K = −E, U = 2E.
Energy to move from orbit r₁ to r₂: ΔE = (GMm/2)(1/r₁ − 1/r₂) > 0 for r₂ > r₁.
Conceptual points: gravity cannot be shielded by any material; weight changes with height and depth; g is slightly smaller at the equator than at the poles (Earth's rotation and bulge).

ex.q: A satellite in an orbit of radius 2R has total energy E. What is its energy in an orbit of radius 4R, and how much energy is needed to shift it?

topics.rl: Satellite operators at ISRO's ISTRAC in Bengaluru fire thrusters to raise orbits that slowly decay because of thin atmospheric drag.

topics.t: Elasticity and plasticity
topics.h: Stretch a rubber band and it snaps back; squeeze a lump of atta dough and it stays squashed. Same push, very different materials.
p: A rigid body is only an idealisation: every real body deforms (changes shape or size) when forces act on it.
Elasticity: the property of a body to regain its original size and shape when the deforming force is removed.
Plasticity: the body does not regain its shape and is permanently deformed.
Elastic examples: steel, rubber (within limits); nearly plastic examples: putty, wet clay, mud, dough.
Engineers must know elastic behaviour to design bridges, buildings, cranes, machines and even artificial body parts.

ex.q: A steel spring is stretched slightly and released; a clay ball is pressed and released. Classify each behaviour.
st: The spring returns to its original length: elastic.
The clay keeps its new dented shape: plastic.
So steel (within limits) is elastic and clay is plastic.

topics.rl: The pottery artisans of Khurja rely on the plasticity of wet clay to shape cups and vases on the wheel.

topics.t: Stress: longitudinal, shearing and hydraulic
topics.h: A heavy train crossing the Chenab rail bridge sets up stresses inside every steel member. Engineers calculate each one.
p: When a body is deformed, internal restoring forces appear. Stress = restoring force per unit area = F/A. SI unit N m⁻² = pascal (Pa).
Longitudinal stress: force normal to the cross-section. Tensile stress when stretched, compressive stress when compressed.
Shearing (tangential) stress: force parallel to the surface (e.g. pushing the top of a book sideways).
Hydraulic (volume) stress: equal force per unit area on all sides (e.g. a body deep in water); it equals the pressure.

ex.q: A steel rod of cross-section 2 × 10⁻⁴ m² supports a load of 4 × 10⁴ N. Find the stress.

topics.rl: The cables of the Bandra–Worli Sea Link carry tensile stress, while its pillars carry compressive stress.

topics.t: Strain and Hooke's law
topics.h: Hang a 1 kg mass on a 1 m steel wire and it stretches less than a hair's width. Strain measures that tiny change as a fraction.
p: Strain = fractional change in size or shape. Longitudinal strain = ΔL/L; shearing strain = Δx/L = tan θ ≈ θ; volume strain = ΔV/V.
Strain is a ratio of like quantities, so it has no units or dimensions.
Hooke's law: for small deformations, stress ∝ strain, i.e. stress = k × strain.
The proportionality constant k is the modulus of elasticity (Young's, shear or bulk modulus, depending on the type of stress).
Hooke's law is an empirical law and holds only within the elastic (proportional) limit.

ex.q: A 2 m wire stretches by 1 mm under a load. Find the longitudinal strain.

topics.rl: Strain gauges glued on the Howrah Bridge's members give live readings of tiny strains as traffic flows.

topics.t: The stress–strain curve
topics.h: Testing labs pull a steel rod until it snaps, plotting stress against strain. That curve tells engineers everything about the metal.
p: For a metal under tension, the curve starts as a straight line (O to A): Hooke's law holds up to the proportional limit.
Beyond A, up to the yield point (elastic limit) B, the body still returns to its shape but stress is no longer proportional to strain. The stress at B is the yield strength σ_y.
Beyond B is the plastic region: if the load is removed (say at C), the body does not return; the remaining strain is the permanent set.
Stress rises to a maximum, the ultimate tensile strength σ_u (point D); beyond it, the wire thins locally and breaks at the fracture point E, even with less stress.

ex.q: On a stress–strain curve, a wire is loaded to point C beyond the yield point and unloaded. What happens?
st: C lies in the plastic region.
When unloaded, the curve comes down roughly parallel to OA but does not reach O.
The wire keeps a permanent strain called the permanent set.

topics.rl: Steel plants grade TMT bars for Indian construction by their yield strength, e.g. 'Fe 500' means a yield strength of about 500 MPa.

topics.t: Ductile, brittle and elastomeric materials
topics.h: Copper can be drawn into thin wires; a glass rod just snaps. The stress–strain curve explains why.
p: Ductile materials (copper, aluminium, mild steel) have a large plastic region between the ultimate tensile strength and fracture; they can be drawn into wires.
Brittle materials (glass, cast iron, ceramics) fracture soon after the ultimate tensile strength is reached, with little plastic flow.
Elastomers (rubber, the tissue of the aorta) can be stretched to large strains and still return; their curve has no well-defined linear (Hooke's law) region.
Steel has a much larger Young's modulus than rubber, so for the same stress it strains far less. In the physics sense, steel is MORE elastic than rubber.

ex.q: Two wires of the same size, one of steel (Y = 2 × 10¹¹ Pa) and one of copper (Y = 1.1 × 10¹¹ Pa), carry equal loads. Which stretches more?
st: ΔL = FL/(AY), so ΔL ∝ 1/Y for the same F, L, A.

topics.rl: Electricians in India prefer copper wiring partly because copper is ductile: it bends without cracking during installation.

topics.t: Young's modulus
topics.h: The steel cables of a lift at a Mumbai high-rise stretch a few millimetres every time people step in. Young's modulus predicts exactly how much.
p: Young's modulus Y = longitudinal stress/longitudinal strain = (F/A)/(ΔL/L) = FL/(AΔL). Unit N m⁻² (Pa).
Elongation: ΔL = FL/(AY). Thicker, shorter, stiffer wires stretch less.
Typical values: steel about 2 × 10¹¹ Pa; copper about 1.1 × 10¹¹ Pa; aluminium about 7 × 10¹⁰ Pa. (B and G values are also tabulated for materials.)
Two wires joined end to end carrying a load: both have the same tension F. Stress in each = F/A for that wire; elongations add up.

ex.q: A 2 m steel wire (A = 10⁻⁶ m², Y = 2 × 10¹¹ Pa) holds a 100 N load. Find the elongation.

topics.rl: Indian Railways' overhead wire for electric locomotives is kept under carefully calculated tension, using Young's modulus to control sag and stretch.

topics.t: Shear modulus and bulk modulus
topics.h: At the deepest point of the Indian Ocean, water is under over 700 atmospheres of pressure, yet its volume shrinks by only about 3%.
p: Shear (rigidity) modulus G = shearing stress/shearing strain = (F/A)/(Δx/L) = FL/(AΔx). For most materials G ≈ Y/3.
Shear displacement of a slab: Δx = FL/(AG).
Bulk modulus B = −p/(ΔV/V) (the minus sign makes B positive, since volume decreases when pressure increases). Compressibility k = 1/B.
Solids have the largest B, liquids smaller, gases the smallest: gases are the most compressible.
Water has B ≈ 2.2 × 10⁹ Pa; glass about 3.7 × 10¹⁰ Pa.

ex.q: Water (B = 2.2 × 10⁹ Pa) is subjected to an extra pressure of 2.2 × 10⁷ Pa. Find the fractional decrease in volume.

topics.rl: Submarines of the Indian Navy are built to withstand enormous hydraulic stress; their hulls use materials with high bulk modulus.

topics.t: Poisson's ratio and elastic energy
topics.h: Stretch a rubber band and watch it get thinner. That sideways shrinking, compared with the stretch, is Poisson's ratio.
p: When a wire is stretched, it also gets thinner. Lateral strain = Δd/d; longitudinal strain = ΔL/L.
Poisson's ratio = lateral strain/longitudinal strain (magnitudes). It has no units or dimensions; for steel it is about 0.28–0.30.
Work done in stretching a wire is stored as elastic potential energy: U = ½ × stress × strain × volume = ½ F ΔL.
Energy density (per unit volume): u = ½ × stress × strain = ½ Y (strain)² = (stress)²/(2Y).

ex.q: A wire stretched by 2 mm under a final load of 100 N. Find the elastic energy stored.

topics.rl: Catapult (gulel) users in villages store elastic energy in stretched rubber; the energy is ½ × stress × strain × volume of the rubber.

topics.t: Applications of elastic behaviour
topics.h: Why are bridge girders shaped like the letter I, and why can't mountains on Earth be much taller than about 10 km? Elasticity answers both.
p: Crane ropes: the rope's area must keep stress below the yield strength, with a safety factor (say 10). Ropes are made of many thin wires twisted together for flexibility and strength.

Beams: sag of a beam (length l, breadth b, depth d) loaded at the middle: δ = Wl³/(4bd³Y). Increasing depth d reduces sag greatly (d³), so beams are deep; an I-section saves material and resists buckling.
Pillars with distributed (bevelled) ends carry more load than those with rounded ends.
Mountains: the rock at the base would flow under shear stress if a mountain were much taller than about 10 km on Earth.
Typical numericals: elongations with Y, shear displacements with G, volume changes with B, and ratios of elongations for different wires.

ex.q: A crane must lift 10⁴ kg. The rope's yield strength is 3 × 10⁸ Pa (g = 10 m s⁻²). Find the minimum cross-sectional area, and with a safety factor of 10.
st: With safety factor 10: A ≈ 3.3 × 10⁻³ m² (radius about 3 cm).

topics.rl: The I-shaped steel girders used in Delhi Metro's elevated viaducts are chosen to resist bending with minimum steel.

topics.t: Fluids, pressure and density
topics.h: A sharp needle pierces your skin with a gentle push, while a wide-footed elephant walks on soft ground. Same physics: pressure.
p: Fluids (liquids and gases) flow; they cannot resist a shear stress and take the shape of their container.
Liquids are nearly incompressible (fixed volume); gases are highly compressible.
Pressure P = F/A (normal force per unit area). It is a scalar; SI unit pascal (1 Pa = 1 N m⁻²).
Small area → large pressure (sharp knife, needle). Large area → small pressure (wide foundations, snowshoes, broad straps of a school bag).
Density ρ = m/V (kg m⁻³); water ≈ 1000 kg m⁻³, mercury ≈ 13.6 × 10³ kg m⁻³. Relative density = ρ/ρ_water (dimensionless).

ex.q: A 60 kg girl stands on one heel of area 1 cm². Find the pressure on the floor (g = 10 m s⁻²).

topics.rl: Railway tracks rest on wide concrete sleepers so the enormous weight of a goods train is spread out and the ground doesn't sink.

topics.t: Pascal's law and pressure at depth
topics.h: Divers in the Andaman Sea feel their ears pop just 3–4 m down. Every 10 m of water adds about one atmosphere of pressure.
p: Pascal's law: in a fluid at rest, pressure at a point is the same in all directions, and pressure is the same at all points at the same level (same depth).
Pressure at depth h below the open surface: P = P_a + ρgh, where P_a is atmospheric pressure.
The difference between two depths: P₂ − P₁ = ρg(h₂ − h₁).

Hydrostatic paradox: the pressure at the base depends only on the depth of liquid, not on the shape or volume of the vessel. Vessels of different shapes filled to the same height have equal pressure at the base.

ex.q: Find the absolute pressure on a swimmer 10 m below the surface of a lake (ρ = 1000 kg m⁻³, g = 10 m s⁻², P_a = 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa).

topics.rl: Dams like Sardar Sarovar are built much thicker at the base because water pressure (and hence force per unit area) grows with depth.

topics.t: Atmospheric pressure, barometers and manometers
topics.h: The air above you presses on your palm with the weight of about 100 kg! You don't feel it because the pressure acts on all sides.
p: Atmospheric pressure at sea level: 1 atm = 1.013 × 10⁵ Pa. It equals the pressure of a 76 cm (760 mm) column of mercury.
Torricelli's mercury barometer: a long tube of mercury inverted in a dish; mercury stands at h ≈ 76 cm, with near-vacuum above. P_a = ρgh. Units: 1 torr = 1 mm of Hg; 1 bar = 10⁵ Pa.
Open-tube manometer: a U-tube with liquid; the difference in levels h gives the gauge pressure: P − P_a = ρgh.
Atmospheric pressure decreases with height (air becomes thinner), roughly halving every 5–6 km near the Earth.

ex.q: Show that 76 cm of mercury corresponds to about 1.013 × 10⁵ Pa (ρ_Hg = 13.6 × 10³ kg m⁻³, g = 9.8 m s⁻²).

topics.rl: Mountaineers on the way to Ladakh's Khardung La notice breathlessness and chips packets puffing up: the outside air pressure is much lower up there.

topics.t: Hydraulic machines and forces on dams
topics.h: A mechanic in a garage lifts an SUV with one hand on a lever. The secret is Pascal's law of transmission of pressure.
p: Pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted undiminished to every part of the fluid and the walls (Pascal's law of transmission).
Hydraulic lift: pressure F₁/A₁ on the small piston appears at the large piston, giving F₂ = F₁(A₂/A₁). Force is multiplied by the area ratio.
Work is not multiplied: the small piston moves farther (d₁A₁ = d₂A₂).
Hydraulic brakes in cars use the same principle: a small push on the brake pedal produces large forces on the brake shoes of all wheels.
Typical problems: pressure on a swimmer at depth; force on a dam; two-piston lifts.

ex.q: In a hydraulic lift, the small piston has area 10 cm² and the large piston 1000 cm². What force on the small piston lifts a 1200 kg car? (g = 10 m s⁻²)

topics.rl: Hydraulic jacks carried by truck drivers on national highways let one person lift a loaded wheel to change a tyre.

topics.t: Streamline flow and the equation of continuity
topics.h: Press your thumb over a garden hose and the water shoots far. Narrow opening, faster flow: that's continuity.
p: Steady (streamline) flow: the velocity at each point does not change with time. Streamlines are the paths of fluid particles; they never cross.
A bundle of streamlines forms a flow tube. Above a critical speed, flow becomes turbulent (irregular, with eddies).
Equation of continuity (incompressible fluid, conservation of mass): A₁v₁ = A₂v₂ (volume flow rate is constant).
Where streamlines crowd together (narrower region), the fluid moves faster.

ex.q: Water flows at 2 m s⁻¹ through a pipe of area 10 cm² that narrows to 4 cm². Find the speed in the narrow part.

topics.rl: Rivers like the Ganga flow slowly where they are wide (near Varanasi's ghats) and rush through narrow gorges in the Himalayas.

topics.t: Bernoulli's principle
topics.h: During a cyclone in Odisha, roofs are lifted off houses. Fast wind over the roof means low pressure above, while the air inside is still.
p: Bernoulli's principle: along a streamline, P + ½ρv² + ρgh = constant (for steady, incompressible, non-viscous flow).
Derivation: apply the work–energy theorem to a fluid element in a tube of varying area and height. Work done by pressure forces = change in KE + change in gravitational PE.
Each term is energy per unit volume: pressure energy, kinetic energy and potential energy.
For a fluid at rest (v = 0), it reduces to P₁ − P₂ = ρg(h₂ − h₁), the pressure–depth relation.
Limitations: ignores viscosity (energy loss), compressibility and unsteady/turbulent flow.

ex.q: Water flows horizontally through a pipe; speed changes from 2 m s⁻¹ to 4 m s⁻¹. Find the pressure difference (ρ = 1000 kg m⁻³).
st: Same height, so P₁ + ½ρv₁² = P₂ + ½ρv₂².
= 6000 Pa (pressure is lower where the water is faster).

topics.rl: The venturi in older scooter carburettors uses Bernoulli's principle: fast air in the narrow throat lowers pressure and sucks in petrol.

topics.t: Torricelli's law, dynamic lift and Bernoulli in action
topics.h: A spin bowler makes the ball drift in the air; a passenger jet lifts hundreds of people off the runway at Delhi. Both are Bernoulli at work.
p: Speed of efflux (Torricelli's law): water from a small hole at depth h below the open surface of a large tank leaves at v = √(2gh), like a body falling freely through h.
Magnus effect: a spinning ball drags air around it; air moves faster on one side, so pressure is lower there and the ball swerves (dynamic lift).
Aerofoil (wing): air flows faster over the curved upper surface than below, so pressure above is lower; lift = ΔP × area = ½ρ(v_top² − v_bottom²)A.
Everyday effects: blowing over a strip of paper lifts it; an atomiser/spray uses fast air to suck liquid up; roofs are blown off in storms.

ex.q: Air flows over a wing at 50 m s⁻¹ and under it at 40 m s⁻¹ (ρ = 1.2 kg m⁻³). Find the lift on a wing of area 20 m².

topics.rl: Swing and drift in cricket owe a lot to air flow around the ball; spin bowlers use the Magnus effect to make the ball dip or drift.

topics.t: Viscosity
topics.h: Pour honey and water side by side: water races, honey crawls. The difference is viscosity, the fluid's internal friction.
p: Viscosity is internal friction between layers of a fluid in relative motion; it opposes the relative motion of layers.
In laminar flow, layers slide over each other with a velocity gradient v/l. Coefficient of viscosity η = (F/A)/(v/l), i.e. shear stress/strain rate.
SI unit: Pa s (also N s m⁻²); CGS unit poise (1 poise = 0.1 Pa s). Honey and glycerine have large η; water and air small η.
Temperature: viscosity of liquids decreases as temperature rises; viscosity of gases increases with temperature.
Example: a plate dragged over a thin oil film: η = Fl/(Av).

ex.q: A metal plate of area 0.1 m² is pulled at 0.5 m s⁻¹ over a 1 mm oil film with a force of 0.5 N. Find η.

topics.rl: Engine oils sold at Indian petrol pumps are graded by viscosity (like 20W-40) so they flow in a cold Shimla winter and still protect in hot Chennai summers.

topics.t: Stokes' law and terminal velocity
topics.h: Raindrops fall from clouds kilometres high but hit you gently. Air drag makes them stop accelerating and reach a steady terminal speed.
p: Stokes' law: a small sphere of radius a moving slowly at speed v through a fluid of viscosity η feels a drag force F = 6πηav.
As a sphere falls, drag grows with speed until weight = buoyancy + drag. Then acceleration is zero: terminal velocity v_t.
Balancing: (4/3)πa³ρg = (4/3)πa³σg + 6πηav_t gives v_t = 2a²(ρ − σ)g/(9η), where ρ is the sphere's density and σ the fluid's.
v_t ∝ a²: bigger drops fall faster. If ρ < σ (air bubble in water), v_t is negative: the bubble rises.

ex.q: A steel ball falls in oil and reaches terminal velocity 2 cm s⁻¹. What would be the terminal velocity of a ball of the same material with twice the radius?

topics.rl: Doctors at AIIMS use the Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR) test: red blood cells settle at a nearly constant speed governed by Stokes-type drag. Lab safety: if you time steel balls falling through glycerine or oil, wipe up spills at once (the floor gets slippery) and drop the balls gently so the glass jar doesn't crack.

topics.t: Surface tension and surface energy
topics.h: Water striders skate on ponds in Kerala's backwaters, and a steel needle can float on water. The surface acts like a stretched skin.
p: A liquid surface behaves like a stretched membrane. A molecule inside is pulled equally from all sides, but a surface molecule is pulled inward, so surface molecules have extra energy.
Surface energy: extra energy of the surface. To increase the surface area, work must be done.
Surface tension S = force per unit length acting along the surface, = surface energy per unit area (unit N m⁻¹ or J m⁻²).
Film on a wire frame with a movable slider of length l: the film has two surfaces, so F = 2Sl. Work to increase area by ΔA (each side) = S × 2ΔA.
Water at room temperature: S ≈ 0.072 N m⁻¹. Surface tension decreases as temperature rises.

ex.q: A soap film (S = 0.03 N m⁻¹) is held on a frame with a movable slider of length 10 cm. Find the force needed to hold the slider.
st: The film has two surfaces: F = 2Sl.

topics.rl: Hot water and detergents clean oily dishes better because both reduce surface tension, helping water spread and wet the grease.

topics.t: Angle of contact and wetting
topics.h: Water spreads on clean glass but beads up on a lotus leaf. The angle of contact decides whether a liquid wets a surface.
p: Angle of contact θ: the angle between the tangent to the liquid surface at the point of contact and the solid surface, measured inside the liquid.
θ < 90°: the liquid wets the surface and spreads (water on clean glass, θ ≈ 0°). θ > 90°: the liquid does not wet it and forms drops (mercury on glass, water on wax or lotus leaves).
Balance of interfacial tensions at the edge: S_sa = S_la cos θ + S_sl (solid–air, liquid–air, solid–liquid).
If S_sl < S_sa, cos θ > 0 and θ is acute; if S_sl > S_sa, θ is obtuse.
Soaps and detergents lower the contact angle, so water wets cloth and grease better; waterproofing agents raise it.

ex.q: For a liquid on a solid, S_sa = 0.05 N m⁻¹, S_sl = 0.02 N m⁻¹ and S_la = 0.06 N m⁻¹. Find cos θ and decide if the liquid wets the solid.
st: θ = 60° < 90°, so the liquid wets the solid.

topics.rl: Waterproof jackets used by trekkers in Meghalaya, one of the rainiest places on Earth, have coatings that make water's contact angle obtuse so it rolls off.

topics.t: Drops, bubbles and capillary rise
topics.h: Plants pull water up through tiny tubes, and a cloth wick soaks up oil in a diya. Capillary action at work.
p: Excess pressure inside a liquid drop (one surface): Pᵢ − Pₒ = 2S/r. An air bubble inside a liquid also has one surface: 2S/r.
Soap bubble in air has two surfaces: Pᵢ − Pₒ = 4S/r. Smaller bubbles have larger excess pressure.
Capillary rise: h = 2S cos θ/(ρgr). Concave meniscus (θ < 90°, water in glass) rises; convex meniscus (θ > 90°, mercury) is depressed.
h ∝ 1/r: narrower tubes, higher rise.
Small drops are spherical because surface tension minimises the area; surface energy problems use W = S ΔA.

ex.q: Water (S = 0.07 N m⁻¹, θ ≈ 0°) is in a glass tube of radius 0.7 mm (ρ = 1000 kg m⁻³, g = 10 m s⁻²). Find the capillary rise.

topics.rl: The wick of a traditional diya or kerosene lantern draws oil upward by capillary action between its fibres.

topics.t: Temperature, heat and thermal equilibrium
topics.h: A steel spoon and a wooden spoon in the same kitchen are at the same temperature, yet the steel one feels colder. Heat and temperature are not the same thing.
p: Thermal phenomena are everywhere: bodies get hot, expand, melt, boil and cool. To explain them we must separate heat from temperature.
Temperature is a relative measure of hotness or coldness of a body. SI unit: kelvin (K).
Heat is energy transferred from one system to another (or to its surroundings) because of a temperature difference. SI unit: joule (J).
Heat flows from higher to lower temperature until the temperatures are equal: the bodies are then in thermal equilibrium.
A body does not 'contain heat'; heat is energy in transit.

ex.q: A glass of cold water (10 °C) is left in a room at 30 °C. Describe what happens.
st: The room is hotter, so heat flows from the room into the water.
The water warms; the transfer slows as the difference shrinks.
It stops when the water reaches 30 °C: thermal equilibrium.
ex.a: Heat flows in until both are at 30 °C

topics.rl: A chai seller's kulhad cools in the winter air of Lucknow as heat flows out of it until it reaches the air's temperature.

topics.t: Thermometers and temperature scales
topics.h: A doctor says 98.6 °F, the weather app says 37 °C. Same body temperature, two different scales.
p: A thermometer uses a property that changes regularly with temperature: expansion of a liquid (mercury, alcohol) or the pressure of a gas at constant volume.
Two fixed points define a scale: ice point (freezing of pure water) and steam point (boiling of pure water) at 1 atm.
Celsius: ice point 0 °C, steam point 100 °C. Fahrenheit: 32 °F and 212 °F (180 divisions).
Linear relation: (t_F − 32)/180 = t_C/100, i.e. t_F = (9/5)t_C + 32.
The two scales read the same at −40°.

ex.q: Convert 37 °C into °F.

topics.rl: IMD weather bulletins in India report temperatures in °C, while many older clinical thermometers in Indian homes are still marked in °F.

topics.t: Gas laws, the ideal-gas equation and absolute temperature
topics.h: Cool a gas at constant volume and its pressure falls in a straight line. Extend that line and it hits zero pressure at −273.15 °C: absolute zero.
p: Boyle's law: PV = constant at fixed T. Charles' law: V/T = constant at fixed P. Combined: PV = μRT (ideal-gas equation), μ = number of moles, R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.
Constant-volume gas thermometer: at fixed volume, pressure varies linearly with temperature.
Extrapolating the P–t line to P = 0 (for any gas at low density) gives t = −273.15 °C: absolute zero.
Kelvin scale: T = t_C + 273.15. One kelvin equals one Celsius degree in size.
The triple point of water, 273.16 K, is used as the standard fixed point of the kelvin scale.

ex.q: A gas at 27 °C and 2 atm is heated at constant volume until its pressure becomes 3 atm. Find the new temperature.
st: At constant V, P/T is constant: T₂ = T₁ × P₂/P₁ = 300 × 3/2.

topics.rl: Tyre pressures of trucks on the Mumbai–Ahmedabad highway rise on hot afternoons: same volume, higher temperature, higher pressure.

topics.t: Thermal expansion of solids
topics.h: On a hot day, steel bridges like the Howrah Bridge grow a few centimetres longer. Engineers plan for it.
p: Most substances expand on heating: in length (linear), area (superficial) and volume (cubical).
Linear: ΔL = αLΔT, α = ΔL/(LΔT) (unit K⁻¹). Typical α: copper ≈ 1.7 × 10⁻⁵ K⁻¹, aluminium ≈ 2.5 × 10⁻⁵ K⁻¹; glass and invar are much smaller.
Area: ΔA = α_A AΔT; volume: ΔV = α_V VΔT.
For isotropic solids: α_A = 2α and α_V = 3α.
A hole in a plate expands on heating as if it were made of the plate material. Measuring tapes and rods read wrong at temperatures other than their calibration temperature.

ex.q: A 10 m copper wire (α = 1.7 × 10⁻⁵ K⁻¹) is heated by 50 K. Find the increase in length.

topics.rl: Blacksmiths in Moradabad heat iron rims before fitting them on cart wheels; the rim shrinks on cooling and grips tightly.

topics.t: Expansion of liquids and gases, and water's strange behaviour
topics.h: Lakes in Kashmir freeze from the top down in winter, and fish survive below. Water's anomalous expansion makes it possible.
p: Liquids and gases have only volume expansion; liquids generally expand more than solids, gases much more.
For an ideal gas at constant pressure, PV = μRT gives α_V = 1/T. At 0 °C (273 K), α_V ≈ 3.7 × 10⁻³ K⁻¹, far larger than for solids or liquids.
Anomalous expansion of water: from 0 °C to 4 °C, water CONTRACTS on heating; above 4 °C it expands. So water is densest at 4 °C.

In winter, surface water cools, becomes denser and sinks until the whole lake is at 4 °C. Further cooling makes the surface lighter; it freezes at the top, and the ice layer insulates the water below, letting aquatic life survive.

ex.q: Find the coefficient of volume expansion of an ideal gas at constant pressure at 27 °C.

topics.rl: The Dal Lake surface freezes in harsh winters, but water at about 4 °C below the ice keeps fish alive till spring.

topics.t: Thermal stress and uses of expansion
topics.h: A steel rail clamped tight on a summer afternoon can buckle with tremendous force. That's why old tracks had small gaps.
p: If a rod is prevented from expanding, a thermal stress develops: strain = αΔT, so thermal stress = YαΔT, and force = YAαΔT.
Example: a steel rail (Y = 2 × 10¹¹ Pa, α = 1.2 × 10⁻⁵ K⁻¹) clamped at both ends and heated by 20 K develops stress 2 × 10¹¹ × 1.2 × 10⁻⁵ × 20 = 4.8 × 10⁷ Pa.

Applications: gaps between rail sections, expansion joints in bridges; bimetallic strips (two metals with different α bend on heating) in thermostats and fire alarms; heating iron rims to fit on wheels.

ex.q: A brass rod (Y = 10¹¹ Pa, α = 2 × 10⁻⁵ K⁻¹, area 10⁻⁴ m²) is clamped between rigid walls and heated by 50 K. Find the stress and the force on the walls.

topics.rl: Modern Indian Railways tracks use long welded rails pre-stressed at a chosen temperature, plus special joints, to manage thermal stress.

topics.t: Heat capacity and specific heat
topics.h: Coastal Chennai has milder temperature swings than inland Nagpur. The sea's huge heat capacity acts like a giant thermal buffer.
p: Heat capacity of a body S = ΔQ/ΔT (unit J K⁻¹): heat needed to raise its temperature by 1 K.
Specific heat capacity s = ΔQ/(mΔT), unit J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. It depends on the substance and (slightly) on temperature.
Molar specific heat C = ΔQ/(μΔT), unit J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.
For gases, heat capacity depends on the conditions: C_p (constant pressure) > C_v (constant volume), because at constant pressure some heat goes into doing work.
Water has a very high specific heat (≈ 4186 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹). So it heats and cools slowly, moderates coastal climates, and is an excellent coolant in car radiators.

ex.q: How much heat raises 2 kg of water from 25 °C to 75 °C? (s = 4186 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹)

topics.rl: Car radiators use water-based coolant because water absorbs a lot of heat with only a small temperature rise.

topics.t: Calorimetry and the method of mixtures
topics.h: Mix hot and cold water in a bucket for a bath and you instinctively do calorimetry: heat lost by one equals heat gained by the other.
p: A calorimeter (often a copper vessel with a stirrer, inside an insulated jacket) keeps the system isolated so no heat is lost to the surroundings.
Principle of method of mixtures: heat lost by the hot body = heat gained by the cold body (and the calorimeter).
m₁s₁(T₁ − T) = m₂s₂(T − T₂) + m_c s_c(T − T₂), where T is the final common temperature.
Use it to find an unknown specific heat or a final temperature.

ex.q: 0.2 kg of water at 80 °C is mixed with 0.3 kg of water at 20 °C (ignore the container). Find the final temperature.
st: Heat lost = heat gained: 0.2 × s × (80 − T) = 0.3 × s × (T − 20).

topics.rl: In BIS testing labs, the specific heat of materials like cookware metals is found using the method of mixtures in calorimeters. Lab safety: lift the hot metal with tongs, transfer it quickly over the bench (not over your hands), and never touch the steam heater or boiling water.

topics.t: Change of state: melting, boiling and sublimation
topics.h: Dal takes longer to cook in Leh than in Delhi. At high altitude, water boils at a lower temperature, so food cooks slower.
p: Changes of state: melting/fusion (solid → liquid), freezing (liquid → solid), vaporisation/boiling (liquid → gas), condensation (gas → liquid), sublimation (solid → gas directly).
During a change of state, temperature stays constant even though heat is supplied; the heating curve of water shows flat steps at 0 °C and 100 °C.

Melting point decreases with increase of pressure for ice. Regelation: a weighted wire passes through an ice block (ice melts under the wire and refreezes above it); ice skating works partly this way.
Boiling point increases with pressure: it is lower at high altitudes and higher in a pressure cooker (about 120 °C).
Sublimation: dry ice (solid CO₂), iodine, naphthalene. At the triple point (water: 273.16 K), solid, liquid and vapour coexist.

ex.q: Ice at −10 °C is heated steadily until it becomes steam at 110 °C. Describe the temperature–time graph.

topics.rl: Pressure cookers in Indian kitchens raise the boiling point of water to about 120 °C, cooking rajma and chana much faster.

topics.t: Latent heat
topics.h: A burn from steam at 100 °C is far worse than one from boiling water at 100 °C. Latent heat is the hidden culprit.
p: Heat needed to change the state of mass m without changing temperature: Q = mL, where L is the latent heat (J kg⁻¹).
Water: latent heat of fusion L_f ≈ 3.33 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹; latent heat of vaporisation L_v ≈ 22.6 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹.
Steam at 100 °C releases its large latent heat (2.26 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹) on condensing on the skin, then more as the water cools, so it burns worse than water at 100 °C.
Ice at −t °C to steam: add the heats msΔT (ice) + mL_f + msΔT (water) + mL_v.
Mixing ice with warm water: first check whether all the ice can melt; if the heat available is less than mL_f, the final temperature is 0 °C with some ice left.

ex.q: Find the heat needed to turn 1 kg of ice at 0 °C into water at 0 °C, and then into steam at 100 °C (L_f = 3.34 × 10⁵, L_v = 22.6 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹, s = 4186 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹).

topics.rl: Matka water stays cool in Rajasthan summers because water seeping through the clay evaporates and takes away latent heat.

topics.t: Conduction of heat
topics.h: Steel cooking pots often have copper bottoms. Copper conducts heat many times better than steel, spreading the flame's heat evenly.
p: Heat is transferred by three modes: conduction, convection and radiation.
Conduction: heat flows through a material from hot to cold regions by molecular collisions, without bulk movement. Heat current H = KA(T_C − T_D)/L.
K is the thermal conductivity (W m⁻¹ K⁻¹). Metals are good conductors (copper ≈ 400); wood, glass and especially gases (air ≈ 0.024) are poor conductors (insulators).
Uses: copper-bottomed pots; insulating materials (glass wool, air gaps) in buildings and flasks; ice on lakes conducts poorly and protects water below.
Rods in series at steady state: the same heat current flows through each: K₁A(T₁ − T)/L₁ = K₂A(T − T₂)/L₂.

ex.q: Two rods of equal length and area are joined end to end. Rod A (K = 3K₀) is at 100 °C at its free end, rod B (K = K₀) is at 0 °C at its free end. Find the junction temperature.

topics.rl: Traditional mud-and-thatch houses in rural India stay cool because mud and straw are poor conductors of heat.

topics.t: Convection and radiation
topics.h: At Marina Beach, the afternoon breeze blows in from the sea; at night it reverses. That's convection on a giant scale.
p: Convection: heat transfer by actual (bulk) movement of a fluid. Natural convection is driven by density differences under gravity (hot fluid rises); forced convection uses a pump or fan.

Sea breeze (day): land heats faster, warm air over land rises, cooler air from the sea flows in. Land breeze (night): the reverse. Trade winds arise from convection between the hot equator and cooler regions, deflected by Earth's rotation.
Radiation: heat transfer by electromagnetic waves; needs no medium (the Sun's heat crosses empty space). It travels at the speed of light.
Good absorbers are good emitters. A black body absorbs all radiation falling on it. Dark clothes absorb more heat; white clothes reflect more.
Thermos flask: double glass walls with vacuum between (cuts conduction and convection), silvered surfaces (cut radiation).

ex.q: Explain why a land breeze blows at night.
st: At night, land cools faster than the sea (lower specific heat).
Air over the sea is warmer and rises.
Cooler air from the land flows towards the sea: a land breeze.
ex.a: Land cools faster; air flows from land to sea

topics.rl: White kurtas in Rajasthan summers and dark blankets in Himachal winters use the physics of absorption and reflection of radiation.

topics.t: Blackbody radiation: Wien's and Stefan's laws
topics.h: Astronomers at the Indian Institute of Astrophysics tell a star's surface temperature just by its colour. Wien's law makes it possible.
p: A black body emits radiation over all wavelengths; the energy distribution with wavelength depends only on its temperature.
Wien's displacement law: λ_m T = b, with b ≈ 2.9 × 10⁻³ m K. Hotter bodies peak at shorter wavelengths (red → white → blue-hot).
The Sun's spectrum peaks near 480–500 nm, giving a surface temperature of about 6000 K.
Stefan–Boltzmann law: power radiated H = σAT⁴ (black body), H = eσAT⁴ for a real body with emissivity e (0 ≤ e ≤ 1). σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴.
Net loss to surroundings at T_s: H_net = eσA(T⁴ − T_s⁴).

ex.q: A star's radiation peaks at λ_m = 290 nm. Estimate its surface temperature.

topics.rl: Thermal cameras used by Indian Army border patrols detect people at night because warm bodies radiate infrared strongly (λ_m ≈ 10 µm at body temperature).

topics.t: Newton's law of cooling
topics.h: Your chai cools from 90 °C to 70 °C quickly, but from 40 °C to 35 °C painfully slowly. Newton's law of cooling explains the slowdown.
p: For small temperature differences, the rate of loss of heat is proportional to the difference between the body and its surroundings.
dT/dt = −k(T − T_s), where k depends on the surface area and nature of the body. The temperature difference decays exponentially with time.
Approximate method for intervals: average rate (ΔT/Δt) ∝ (average temperature − T_s).
Lab activity: heat water in a calorimeter, record temperature every minute while it cools, and plot T against t (falling curve) and log(T − T_s) against t (straight line) to verify the law.
Typical numericals combine expansion, calorimetry, latent heat, conduction and cooling.

ex.q: A body cools from 90 °C to 70 °C in 5 min in a room at 20 °C. How long will it take to cool from 70 °C to 50 °C?
st: First interval: rate = 20/5 = 4 °C/min at average 80 °C (difference 60): 4 = k × 60 → k = 1/15 per min.

topics.rl: Hospital labs in India store blood samples in insulated boxes; Newton's law of cooling helps estimate how long the samples stay within the safe temperature range. Lab safety: pour hot water slowly, hold the calorimeter by its insulated jacket, and read the thermometer without lifting it out.

topics.t: Thermodynamic systems and thermal equilibrium
topics.h: A pressure cooker on a gas stove: heat goes in, steam pushes the weight up, work gets done. Thermodynamics is the science of exactly this.
p: Thermodynamics studies heat, temperature and the conversion of heat into work and vice versa, for macroscopic systems.
It uses macroscopic variables such as pressure, volume, temperature, mass and composition, not the motion of individual molecules (which is the microscopic description of kinetic theory).
A system is the part of the universe under study; everything else is the surroundings. Walls can be adiabatic (insulating: no heat flow) or diathermic (conducting: heat can flow).
A system is in equilibrium when its macroscopic variables do not change with time.
Two systems separated by a diathermic wall reach thermal equilibrium when their temperatures become equal and no further change happens.

ex.q: Gas A at 400 K and gas B at 300 K are in a box with a partition. What happens if the partition is (a) adiabatic (b) diathermic?
st: (a) Adiabatic: no heat flows; each gas keeps its own state.
(b) Diathermic: heat flows from A to B.
Their pressures and volumes adjust until temperatures are equal: thermal equilibrium.
ex.a: (a) No change (b) They reach a common temperature

topics.rl: Steel thermos flasks sold in every Indian market approximate adiabatic walls, while copper vessels act as diathermic walls.

topics.t: Zeroth law and internal energy
topics.h: When a doctor reads your fever from a thermometer, she relies on the zeroth law: you and the thermometer reach thermal equilibrium.
p: Zeroth law: if two systems A and B are each in thermal equilibrium with a third system C, then A and B are in thermal equilibrium with each other.
This law tells us there is a quantity that is equal for systems in thermal equilibrium: temperature. It makes thermometers meaningful.
Internal energy U of a system is the sum of the kinetic and potential energies of its molecules, measured in the frame where the system's centre of mass is at rest.
Bulk kinetic energy of the whole system (e.g. a moving gas container) is NOT part of its internal energy.
For an ideal gas, molecular interactions are negligible, so U is purely kinetic and depends only on temperature.

ex.q: A thermometer C reads 37 °C when touching A and also 37 °C when touching B. Are A and B in thermal equilibrium?
st: A is in thermal equilibrium with C.
B is in thermal equilibrium with C.
By the zeroth law, A and B are in thermal equilibrium with each other (same temperature).

topics.rl: Every digital thermometer in an Indian pharmacy works because of the zeroth law of thermodynamics.

topics.t: Heat, work and the first law
topics.h: Rub your palms together and they warm up; put a lid on boiling water and it rattles. Heat and work are two ways to change internal energy.
p: Internal energy U is a state variable: it depends only on the state (P, V, T), not on how the state was reached. Heat and work are NOT state variables; they depend on the process.
Energy can be transferred to a gas in a cylinder by heating it (heat) or by pushing the piston (work).
First law: ΔQ = ΔU + ΔW. Heat supplied to a system is used partly to increase its internal energy and partly to do work. It is the law of conservation of energy for thermodynamic systems.
Sign convention (NCERT): ΔQ > 0 when heat is supplied TO the system; ΔW > 0 when work is done BY the system; ΔU > 0 when internal energy increases.

ex.q: A gas absorbs 500 J of heat and does 200 J of work on the surroundings. Find ΔU.
st: ΔQ = +500 J (heat supplied); ΔW = +200 J (work by the gas).

topics.rl: The diesel engines of Indian Railways' WDM locomotives convert fuel's heat into work; the first law tracks every joule.

topics.t: Work at constant pressure and boiling water
topics.h: When water boils in an open pot, it pushes back the atmosphere as it turns into steam. A part of the heat you supply goes into that push.
p: Work done by a gas expanding at constant pressure P: ΔW = PΔV.
Boiling water at 1 atm: heat supplied ΔQ = mL; work done against the atmosphere ΔW = PΔV (ΔV = steam volume − water volume); increase in internal energy ΔU = ΔQ − ΔW.
Most of the latent heat goes into internal energy (breaking intermolecular bonds); a smaller part does work pushing back the air.
Work is positive for expansion, negative for compression.

ex.q: 2 g of water at 100 °C boils into steam at P = 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa (L = 2260 J g⁻¹); the volume increases by 3.4 × 10⁻³ m³. Find ΔW and ΔU.

topics.rl: A pressure cooker's whistle lifts because the steam does work PΔV pushing the weight up.

topics.t: Specific heat of solids and water, and the calorie
topics.h: Copper, aluminium and lead have very different specific heats per kilogram, but per mole they are all close to 25 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. Coincidence? No: energy sharing.
p: Specific heat capacity s = ΔQ/(mΔT); molar specific heat C = ΔQ/(μΔT).

For solids, each atom oscillates about its position with both kinetic and potential energy. Using equipartition: average energy per atom = 3k_BT, so U = 3RT per mole and C = 3R ≈ 24.9 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ (Dulong–Petit law).
Experimental values agree well at ordinary temperatures (C is lower for some light, hard solids such as carbon and at low temperatures).
Water's specific heat is about 4186 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. The calorie is the heat that raises 1 g of water by 1 °C (14.5 °C to 15.5 °C): 1 cal = 4.186 J.
Mechanical equivalent of heat: J = 4.186 J cal⁻¹ (Joule showed work and heat are equivalent).

ex.q: Using the Dulong–Petit law, estimate the heat needed to raise 2 mol of copper by 10 K (R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹).

topics.rl: Food labels in Indian supermarkets list energy in kcal; 1 kcal = 4186 J, the same calorie you meet in physics.

topics.t: Cp, Cv and Mayer's relation
topics.h: Heat a gas in a sealed steel can and in a balloon: the balloon needs more heat for the same temperature rise. The difference is exactly R per mole.
p: Molar specific heat at constant volume C_v: heat per mole per kelvin with V fixed (no work done).
Molar specific heat at constant pressure C_p: heat per mole per kelvin with P fixed (gas expands and does work).
Mayer's relation for an ideal gas: C_p − C_v = R.
Derivation: at constant V, ΔQ = ΔU = μC_vΔT. At constant P, ΔQ = ΔU + PΔV = μC_vΔT + μRΔT (since PΔV = μRΔT). So C_p = C_v + R.
γ = C_p/C_v > 1. For a monatomic gas C_v = 3R/2, C_p = 5R/2, γ = 5/3; for a diatomic gas (rigid) C_v = 5R/2, C_p = 7R/2, γ = 7/5.

ex.q: For 2 mol of an ideal monatomic gas heated by 10 K, find the heat needed at constant volume and at constant pressure (R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹).

topics.rl: Engineers designing gas turbines at BHEL Hyderabad use C_p and γ of air to predict temperatures in compressors and turbines.

topics.t: State variables, equation of state and quasi-static processes
topics.h: Two ways to compress a gas: slam the piston or ease it in over minutes. Only the slow one keeps the gas in equilibrium at every step.
p: Equilibrium states are described by state variables such as P, V, T and U. A relation among them is the equation of state.
For an ideal gas the equation of state is PV = μRT.
Extensive variables depend on the size of the system (volume, mass, internal energy). Intensive variables do not (pressure, temperature, density).
A quasi-static process is infinitely slow, so the system passes through a series of equilibrium states; P and T are well defined at every stage and differ only infinitesimally from the surroundings.

ex.q: A box of gas at P, V, T is divided into two equal halves by a partition. Which variables stay the same in each half?
st: Intensive variables P and T (and density) are unchanged.
Extensive variables V, mass and U are halved.
ex.a: P, T, density unchanged; V, m, U halved

topics.rl: Slowly pumping a bicycle tyre is closer to quasi-static than a sudden bang; that's why ideal-process formulas apply better to gentle changes.

topics.t: Isothermal and adiabatic processes
topics.h: Pump a bicycle tyre fast and the pump gets hot: nearly adiabatic compression. Do it slowly in contact with air: closer to isothermal.
p: Isothermal (T constant): PV = constant. For an ideal gas, ΔU = 0, so ΔQ = ΔW.
Work in isothermal expansion: W = μRT ln(V₂/V₁) = 2.303 μRT log₁₀(V₂/V₁). Heat absorbed equals work done.
Adiabatic (ΔQ = 0, insulated or very fast): PV^γ = constant (also TV^(γ−1) = constant). W = μR(T₁ − T₂)/(γ − 1). Expansion cools the gas; compression heats it.
On a P–V diagram, an adiabatic curve is steeper than an isothermal curve through the same point (slope ratio γ).
Typical comparisons: for the same compression from the same state, adiabatic compression needs more work and ends at a higher pressure and temperature.

ex.q: 1 mol of an ideal gas at 300 K expands isothermally to twice its volume (R = 8.31, ln 2 = 0.693). Find the work done and the heat absorbed.

topics.rl: Diesel engines in trucks ignite fuel without spark plugs: rapid (nearly adiabatic) compression heats the air above the fuel's ignition point.

topics.t: Isochoric, isobaric and cyclic processes
topics.h: An engine's cylinder goes through a cycle again and again. The work it delivers each cycle is simply the area enclosed on a P–V graph.
p: Isochoric (V constant): W = 0; heat supplied changes only U and T: ΔQ = ΔU = μC_vΔT.
Isobaric (P constant): W = P(V₂ − V₁) = μR(T₂ − T₁); ΔQ = μC_pΔT.
Cyclic process: the system returns to its initial state, so ΔU = 0 and net heat absorbed = net work done = area enclosed by the loop on the P–V diagram (clockwise loop: positive work by the gas).
Comparisons: for compression from the same state to the same volume, adiabatic needs more work than isothermal.
Reading indicator (P–V) diagrams: vertical line = isochoric, horizontal line = isobaric, hyperbola = isothermal, steeper curve = adiabatic.

ex.q: A gas goes round a rectangular cycle on a P–V diagram: P from 1 × 10⁵ to 3 × 10⁵ Pa and V from 1 × 10⁻³ to 4 × 10⁻³ m³ (clockwise). Find the net work.
st: Clockwise loop: 600 J of net work done by the gas (= net heat absorbed).

topics.rl: The indicator diagrams of steam engines in old Indian Railways workshops were literally drawn by a pen on the cylinder to measure work per cycle.

topics.t: The second law of thermodynamics
topics.h: A cup of tea never spontaneously heats itself by cooling the room. The first law wouldn't object, but the second law forbids it.
p: The first law allows many processes that never happen (e.g. heat flowing by itself from cold to hot, or a hot body converting all its internal energy to work). The second law rules them out.
Kelvin–Planck statement: no process is possible whose sole result is the absorption of heat from a reservoir and the complete conversion of this heat into work.
Clausius statement: no process is possible whose sole result is the transfer of heat from a colder object to a hotter object.
The two statements are equivalent: violating one would let us violate the other.
Consequence: no heat engine can have 100% efficiency; some heat must always be rejected to a colder reservoir.

ex.q: An inventor claims an engine that takes 1000 J from a hot reservoir and does 1000 J of work each cycle, rejecting nothing. Is this possible?
st: That means heat fully converted into work with no other effect.
This violates the Kelvin–Planck statement, so it is impossible.
ex.a: No, it violates the second law

topics.rl: Every power plant in India, coal or nuclear, rejects a large part of its heat to cooling towers and rivers because of the second law.

topics.t: Reversible and irreversible processes
topics.h: Drop ink into water and it spreads; it never gathers itself back into a drop. Most real processes run only one way.
p: A reversible process can be retraced so that both the system and the surroundings return to their original states, with no other change in the universe.
Reversible processes must be quasi-static and free of dissipative effects; they are idealisations.
Irreversibility arises from dissipative effects (friction, viscosity, electrical resistance) and from non-quasi-static changes (sudden, far from equilibrium).
Examples of irreversible processes: free expansion of a gas into vacuum, heat flow across a finite temperature difference, mixing of two gases, a block sliding to rest by friction.

ex.q: Is the free expansion of a gas into a vacuum reversible?
st: The gas rushes into the empty half; the process is sudden, not quasi-static.
To return it, an external agent must compress the gas, which changes the surroundings.
So the system and surroundings cannot both be restored: irreversible.

topics.rl: The brakes of a Delhi Metro train convert kinetic energy to heat by friction (irreversible), while its regenerative braking recovers part of it as electrical energy.

topics.t: Heat engines and the Carnot cycle
topics.h: Every car engine, steam turbine and thermal power plant follows the same plan: take heat from hot, do work, dump the rest to cold.
p: A heat engine uses a working substance that absorbs heat Q₁ from a hot reservoir (T₁), does work W, and rejects heat Q₂ to a cold reservoir (T₂) in a cycle. Efficiency η = W/Q₁ = 1 − Q₂/Q₁.
A Carnot engine is an ideal reversible engine working between two temperatures T₁ and T₂.

Carnot cycle (four reversible steps): (1) isothermal expansion at T₁, absorbing Q₁; (2) adiabatic expansion, T₁ → T₂; (3) isothermal compression at T₂, rejecting Q₂; (4) adiabatic compression, T₂ → T₁.
On a P–V diagram: two isotherms and two adiabats. Net work = area enclosed. Heat flows only in the isothermal steps; in the adiabatic steps work changes the temperature.

ex.q: An engine absorbs 1000 J from the hot reservoir and rejects 600 J to the cold reservoir per cycle. Find W and η.

topics.rl: NTPC's thermal power stations are huge heat engines: coal burning gives the hot reservoir, and rivers or cooling towers provide the cold reservoir.

topics.t: Carnot efficiency and Carnot's theorem
topics.h: Even a perfect engine between 500 K steam and 300 K river water cannot beat 40% efficiency. Carnot set that ceiling in 1824.
p: For a Carnot engine: Q₂/Q₁ = T₂/T₁, so η = 1 − T₂/T₁ (temperatures in kelvin).
Efficiency increases with a hotter source or a colder sink; it can reach 1 only if T₂ = 0 K, which is unattainable.
Carnot's theorem: (a) no engine working between two given temperatures can be more efficient than a Carnot engine; (b) the efficiency of a Carnot engine is independent of the working substance.
Problem types: first law, specific heats, work in processes, and Carnot efficiency.

ex.q: A Carnot engine works between 500 K and 300 K and absorbs 1000 J per cycle. Find η, W and Q₂.

topics.rl: Improving Indian thermal plants to 'supercritical' steam temperatures raises T₁, which raises the Carnot limit and cuts coal use per unit of electricity.

topics.t: Kinetic theory and the molecular nature of matter
topics.h: You can't see air molecules, yet the pressure in your bicycle tyre is just billions of them drumming on the rubber every second.
p: Kinetic theory explains the behaviour of gases from the motion of their molecules: a gas is a swarm of rapidly moving molecules, and pressure and temperature come from that motion. Boyle, Newton, Maxwell and Boltzmann helped build it.
Atomic hypothesis: matter is made of tiny particles. Kanada in ancient India and Democritus in ancient Greece proposed indivisible constituents of matter.
Dalton's atomic theory explained the laws of definite and multiple proportions in chemistry.
Gay-Lussac's law: gases combine in simple ratios by volume. Avogadro's law: equal volumes of all gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules.

ex.q: 2 L of hydrogen combine with 1 L of oxygen to give 2 L of water vapour (same T and P). How does Avogadro's law explain this?
st: Equal volumes contain equal numbers of molecules.
So 2 molecules of H₂ react with 1 molecule of O₂ to give 2 molecules of H₂O.
The simple volume ratio 2 : 1 : 2 reflects the molecular ratio.

topics.rl: The Vaisheshika school of ancient Indian philosophy, associated with Kanada, described matter as made of 'paramanu', tiny eternal particles.

topics.t: Molecular spacing and the ideal gas equation
topics.h: One mole of water is about 18 mL as a liquid, but over 30 litres as steam at 100 °C. Molecules in gases are far apart.
p: In solids, atoms are tightly packed (~2 Å apart); in liquids slightly farther; in gases the spacing is about ten times larger and interactions are weak.

Atoms are always in motion. In a liquid–vapour system in a closed container, molecules leave and return at equal rates: dynamic equilibrium. A molecule in a gas travels a certain average distance between collisions (the mean free path).
Ideal gas equation: PV = μRT = Nk_BT, where μ = number of moles, N = number of molecules, R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ and k_B = R/N_A = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹.
Avogadro's number N_A = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹. At STP (273 K, 1 atm), 1 mole of any gas occupies about 22.4 L.

ex.q: How many molecules are there in 11.2 L of a gas at STP?

topics.rl: LPG cylinders in Indian kitchens hold gas as a compressed liquid; when released it expands hugely because gas molecules are far apart.

topics.t: Gas laws, real gases and partial pressures
topics.h: A scuba diver's tank holds a mix of gases, and each gas contributes its own share of the pressure. That's Dalton's law.
p: Boyle's law (PV constant at fixed T and μ) and Charles' law (V ∝ T at fixed P and μ) are special cases of PV = μRT.
Real gases follow the ideal gas law closely only at low pressures and high temperatures (molecules far apart, weak interactions).
Dalton's law of partial pressures: in a mixture of ideal gases, P = P₁ + P₂ + …, where each partial pressure Pᵢ = μᵢRT/V is the pressure that gas would exert alone.
Molecular volume fraction: in water vapour at 100 °C (ρ ≈ 0.6 kg m⁻³), molecules take up only ρ_vapour/ρ_liquid ≈ 0.6/1000 = 6 × 10⁻⁴ of the volume.

ex.q: A 10 L vessel at 300 K contains 0.2 mol of N₂ and 0.3 mol of O₂. Find the total pressure (R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹).

topics.rl: Oxygen cylinders in Indian hospitals are rated by their gas pressure; Boyle's law tells how much volume of oxygen they supply at room pressure.

topics.t: Kinetic theory: assumptions and pressure
topics.h: Picture a cricket ball hitting a wall again and again. A gas is that, with trillions of tiny balls every microsecond.
p: Assumptions: molecules are point-like (negligible size), move randomly, collide elastically with each other and the walls, and exert no forces except during collisions.
A molecule of mass m with velocity component vₓ hitting a wall transfers momentum 2mvₓ. Counting the molecules that hit in time Δt gives P = n m vₓ² (average).
Isotropy: random motion means vₓ² = v_y² = v_z² = v²/3 (averages), so P = (1/3) n m v̄², where n = number density and v̄² is the mean of the squared speed.
Pressure is the same in all directions (Pascal's law) because molecular motion is random.
Mixture: each gas contributes (1/3)nᵢm v̄ᵢ², so the total pressure is the sum of partial pressures (Dalton's law).

ex.q: A gas has number density 2.5 × 10²⁵ m⁻³, molecular mass 5 × 10⁻²⁶ kg and mean square speed 2.4 × 10⁵ m² s⁻². Find its pressure.

topics.rl: Weather balloons launched by IMD expand as they rise because outside molecular bombardment (pressure) drops with height.

topics.t: Temperature, kinetic energy and rms speed
topics.h: Oxygen molecules in the air of your classroom zip around at nearly 500 m s⁻¹, faster than a passenger jet!
p: From P = (1/3)nmv̄² and PV = Nk_BT: average translational KE per molecule = ½m v̄² = (3/2)k_BT. Temperature is a measure of average molecular kinetic energy.
Total translational KE E of a gas: PV = (2/3)E.
Root mean square speed: v_rms = √(v̄²) = √(3k_BT/m) = √(3RT/M), M = molar mass in kg mol⁻¹.
At the same temperature, lighter molecules move faster: v_rms ∝ 1/√M. E.g. v_rms(H₂) = 4 × v_rms(O₂).
Isotope separation: ²³⁵UF₆ and ²³⁸UF₆ have rms speeds in the ratio √(352/349) ≈ 1.0043; the slight difference in diffusion rates is used to enrich uranium.

ex.q: Find the rms speed of oxygen molecules at 300 K (M = 0.032 kg mol⁻¹, R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹).

topics.rl: The nuclear fuel cycle at India's atomic facilities depends on uranium enrichment, which exploits tiny differences in molecular speeds of isotopes.

topics.t: Degrees of freedom and equipartition of energy
topics.h: A helium atom can only zip around; an oxygen molecule can also tumble. Every extra way to store energy changes how much heat a gas needs.
p: Degrees of freedom: independent ways a molecule can have energy. Translational (3 for motion along x, y, z), rotational, vibrational.
Monatomic molecule (He, Ar): 3 translational degrees of freedom. Rigid diatomic molecule (O₂, N₂): 3 translational + 2 rotational = 5.
A vibrational mode has both kinetic and potential energy, so it contributes two quadratic terms (2 × ½k_BT = k_BT).

Law of equipartition of energy: in thermal equilibrium, each quadratic energy term (each translational and rotational degree of freedom, and each of the two terms of a vibrational mode) has average energy ½k_BT per molecule.

ex.q: Find the average energy of a rigid diatomic molecule at temperature T, and the energy of 1 mol.

topics.rl: Nitrogen and oxygen, which make up most of the air we breathe in Delhi or Kochi, behave as rigid diatomic gases at room temperature.

topics.t: Specific heats of gases from equipartition
topics.h: Measured C_v for helium is 12.5 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ and for nitrogen about 20.8. Equipartition predicts both numbers almost perfectly.
p: Rigid diatomic: U = (5/2)RT, C_v = (5/2)R, C_p = (7/2)R, γ = 7/5 = 1.4. With vibration also active: C_v = (7/2)R, C_p = (9/2)R, γ = 9/7.
Polyatomic (3 translational, 3 rotational, f vibrational modes): C_v = (3 + f)R, C_p = (4 + f)R, γ = (4 + f)/(3 + f).
Predicted values agree well with measurements for monatomic and many diatomic gases at room temperature (e.g. He ≈ 12.5, N₂ ≈ 20.8 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹).

ex.q: Find C_v, C_p and γ for a rigid diatomic gas (R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹).
st: C_p = C_v + R = (7/2)R = 29.09 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.

topics.rl: The γ of air (≈ 1.4), used by engineers designing jet engines and wind tunnels, comes straight from the diatomic nature of N₂ and O₂.

topics.t: Specific heat of solids and gas mixtures
topics.h: At room temperature most solids need about 25 J to warm one mole by 1 K, but near absolute zero that number plunges. Classical physics can't explain why.
p: Solids: each atom oscillates in 3 dimensions. Each direction has KE and PE terms: 2 × ½k_BT per direction, so 3k_BT per atom.
Hence U = 3RT per mole and C = 3R ≈ 25 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ (Dulong–Petit law). At constant pressure and volume the values are nearly equal for solids.
At low temperatures, specific heats of solids (and the vibrational part for gases) fall below classical values. Explaining this needs quantum ideas (energy comes in discrete amounts).
Gas mixtures: C_v(mix) = (μ₁C_v1 + μ₂C_v2)/(μ₁ + μ₂). Heat for a gas in a cylinder: Q = μC_vΔT (rigid) or μC_pΔT (constant pressure).

ex.q: Find C_v of a mixture of 1 mol of helium and 1 mol of oxygen (rigid).

topics.rl: Cryogenic engines developed by ISRO handle materials near very low temperatures, where specific heats are far below the room-temperature 3R values.

topics.t: Mean free path
topics.h: Gas molecules move at hundreds of metres per second, yet a smell takes minutes to cross a room. They keep bumping into each other.
p: Mean free path l: the average distance a molecule travels between successive collisions.
l = 1/(√2 n π d²), where n is the number density and d the molecular diameter.
l decreases if the gas is denser (larger n) or the molecules are bigger (larger d). l ∝ 1/n, so at constant T, l ∝ 1/P.
Collision frequency ≈ v̄/l; time between collisions ≈ l/v̄. For air at STP, l ≈ 10⁻⁷ m, much larger than the molecular size (~10⁻¹⁰ m) and than the spacing (~3 × 10⁻⁹ m).
Typical estimates: average spacing (1/n)^(1/3), mean free path, and rms speed at a given temperature.

ex.q: Molecules of diameter d = 2 × 10⁻¹⁰ m have number density n = 2 × 10²⁵ m⁻³. Estimate the mean free path (π ≈ 3.14, √2 ≈ 1.414).

topics.rl: Vacuum chambers at ISRO's test facilities pump air down so far that the mean free path becomes metres long, mimicking space conditions for satellites.

topics.t: Periodic and oscillatory motion
topics.h: Your heartbeat, a jhoola at a mela, the hands of a clock and atoms in a crystal: all repeat their motion again and again.
p: Periodic and oscillatory motions are everywhere: swings, pendulums, heartbeats, vibrating strings and atoms in solids.
Oscillations underlie sound, waves of all kinds and alternating currents in electrical circuits.
Periodic motion repeats itself at regular intervals of time (the Earth's rotation, a clock's hands).

Oscillatory (vibratory) motion is to-and-fro motion about a mean (equilibrium) position. Every oscillatory motion is periodic, but not every periodic motion is oscillatory (uniform circular motion is periodic, not to-and-fro).
Oscillations happen because a restoring force acts towards the equilibrium position whenever the body is displaced.

ex.q: Classify (a) the Moon going round the Earth and (b) a swinging jhoola.
st: (a) The Moon repeats its path every 27.3 days, but does not move to and fro about a mean position: periodic, not oscillatory.
(b) The jhoola moves to and fro about its lowest point at regular intervals: oscillatory (and hence periodic).

topics.rl: The quartz crystal in a digital watch oscillates 32768 times a second, keeping time for millions of Indians' wrists.

topics.t: Period, frequency and periodic functions
topics.h: Indian classical tabla rhythms, alternating current at 50 Hz and a pendulum clock all have one thing in common: a definite period.
p: Period T: the smallest time after which the motion repeats. Frequency ν = 1/T (unit hertz, Hz = s⁻¹).
The displacement variable need not be a position. It can be an angle (pendulum), pressure (sound), voltage or current (AC), or electric and magnetic fields (light).
Any periodic function can be built as a sum of sines and cosines of different periods (Fourier's idea).

Checking periodicity: sin ωt, cos ωt and sin ωt + cos ωt are periodic with T = 2π/ω; sin²ωt is periodic with T = π/ω; sin ωt + cos 2ωt is periodic with T = 2π/ω (but not SHM); e^(−ωt) and log(ωt) are not periodic.

ex.q: Find the period of x(t) = sin ωt + sin 2ωt.
st: sin ωt has period 2π/ω; sin 2ωt has period π/ω.
The sum repeats only when both repeat.

topics.rl: India's electricity grid runs at 50 Hz, so voltage in your home's sockets repeats every 0.02 s.

topics.t: Simple harmonic motion: displacement, amplitude and phase
topics.h: A child on a spring rider at a park bounces up and down in a beautifully regular way. That motion is (nearly) simple harmonic.
p: SHM: displacement varies sinusoidally with time: x(t) = A cos(ωt + φ).
A = amplitude (maximum displacement, positive). (ωt + φ) = phase; φ = phase constant (epoch), the phase at t = 0. ω = angular frequency = 2π/T = 2πν.
On x–t graphs: a larger A gives taller curves; a different φ shifts the curve along the time axis; a larger ω squeezes it (shorter period).
To write the SHM equation, read A, T (hence ω) and the value of x at t = 0 (hence φ).

ex.q: A particle in SHM has amplitude 5 cm and period 2 s, and starts at x = +5 cm at t = 0. Write x(t).
st: A = 5 cm, ω = 2π/T = π rad s⁻¹.
At t = 0, x = A, so cos φ = 1 → φ = 0.

topics.rl: Seismographs at IMD stations record ground vibrations as sinusoids; their amplitude and period reveal an earthquake's strength and distance.

topics.t: SHM as the projection of uniform circular motion
topics.h: Shine a torch on a bead going round a turntable and watch its shadow on the wall: the shadow moves back and forth in perfect SHM.
p: If a particle moves uniformly on a circle, its projection (foot of the perpendicular) on any diameter executes SHM.
Reference circle: radius of the circle = amplitude A; angular speed of the particle = angular frequency ω of the SHM; initial angle = phase constant φ.
If the particle starts at angle φ from the x-axis and moves anticlockwise, its x-projection is x = A cos(ωt + φ) and its y-projection is y = A sin(ωt + φ).
Uniform circular motion = two perpendicular SHMs of equal amplitude with a phase difference of π/2.

ex.q: A particle moves anticlockwise on a circle of radius 3 cm at 2 rev s⁻¹, starting at 60° from the +x axis. Write the SHM of its x-projection.
st: A = 3 cm; ω = 2π × 2 = 4π rad s⁻¹; φ = π/3.

topics.rl: Try it at home: put a cup near the edge of a slowly turning lazy-susan tray and shine a torch across the tray, level with it. The cup's shadow on the wall slides to and fro in SHM.

topics.t: Velocity and acceleration in SHM
topics.h: A pendulum bob is fastest as it swings through the bottom and momentarily stops at the ends, where its acceleration is greatest.
p: Velocity: v = dx/dt = −ωA sin(ωt + φ). Maximum speed ωA at the mean position; zero at the extremes.
Speed in terms of displacement: v = ω√(A² − x²).
Acceleration: a = −ω²A cos(ωt + φ) = −ω²x. It always points towards the mean position; maximum magnitude ω²A at the extremes, zero at the mean position.
Phase relations: velocity leads displacement by π/2; acceleration leads displacement by π (opposite to x).
Typical problems: find v_max = ωA and a_max = ω²A.

ex.q: A body in SHM has A = 0.1 m and ω = 5 rad s⁻¹. Find its maximum speed, maximum acceleration, and speed at x = 0.06 m.

topics.rl: Earthquake engineers at IIT Roorkee design buildings for the maximum ground acceleration ω²A, not just the displacement.

topics.t: The force law: springs and SHM
topics.h: Stiffer shock absorbers on a mountain bike bounce faster. The period of a spring–mass system depends on the ratio m/k.
p: Force law for SHM: F = ma = −mω²x = −kx, with k = mω². The restoring force is linear in displacement and opposite to it.
So ω = √(k/m) and T = 2π√(m/k).
A block of mass m on a spring of constant k on a frictionless surface is a linear harmonic oscillator.
Two identical springs (each k) attached to a block on opposite sides: displacing the block by x stretches one and compresses the other, so F = −2kx, k_eff = 2k and T = 2π√(m/2k).
Typical problem: given k and m, find T, then a_max = (k/m)A and v_max = A√(k/m).

ex.q: A 1 kg block on a spring of k = 100 N m⁻¹ oscillates with amplitude 0.1 m. Find T, v_max and a_max (π = 3.14).
ex.a: T ≈ 0.63 s; 1 m s⁻¹; 10 m s⁻²

topics.rl: The suspension springs of an auto-rickshaw are chosen so that the bounce period is comfortable for passengers on bumpy roads.

topics.t: Energy in simple harmonic motion
topics.h: A swing at the top of its arc is all potential energy; at the bottom it's all kinetic. The total never changes (if there's no friction).
p: Kinetic energy K = ½mv² = ½kA² sin²(ωt + φ). Potential energy U = ½kx² = ½kA² cos²(ωt + φ).
