Total energy E = K + U = ½kA², constant. Energy keeps changing between kinetic and potential forms.
K and U each oscillate in time with period T/2 (twice per cycle), between 0 and ½kA².
Against displacement: U(x) = ½kx² is a parabola, K(x) = ½k(A² − x²) an inverted parabola; E is a horizontal line. K = U at x = ±A/√2.

ex.q: A block (k = 200 N m⁻¹) oscillates with A = 0.1 m. Find E, and K and U at x = 0.05 m.

topics.rl: Grandfather clocks in old Kolkata homes need winding because friction slowly drains the pendulum's total energy.

topics.t: The simple pendulum
topics.h: Galileo timed a swinging chandelier with his pulse and noticed something surprising: big or small swings, the time was the same.
p: A simple pendulum is a point mass (bob) hung from a light, inextensible string fixed at one end.
When displaced by θ, gravity gives a restoring torque τ = −mgL sin θ about the support.
For small angles, sin θ ≈ θ (in radians), so τ = −mgLθ: angular acceleration ∝ −θ, which is SHM.
Period T = 2π√(L/g). It is independent of the mass of the bob and (for small oscillations) of the amplitude.

ex.q: Find the period of a pendulum of length 0.4 m (g = 9.8 m s⁻², π = 3.14).

topics.rl: Pendulum clocks once kept time in Indian railway stations; adjusting the bob's height (L) corrected the clock.

topics.t: Seconds pendulum, measuring g and other SHMs
topics.h: The 'seconds pendulum' takes exactly one second for each swing from one side to the other. Its length on Earth works out to very nearly 1 metre.
p: A seconds pendulum has a period of 2 s (each swing, one side to the other, takes 1 s). Its length L = gT²/(4π²) ≈ 0.99 m ≈ 1 m.
Measuring g: time many oscillations to find T, then g = 4π²L/T². Plotting T² against L gives a straight line of slope 4π²/g.
In a lift accelerating upward at a, the effective g is (g + a), so T decreases; accelerating downward, (g − a), T increases; in free fall, the pendulum does not oscillate.
On the Moon (g_Moon ≈ g/6), T is √6 times longer.

Other SHMs: a ball rolling in a smooth bowl near the bottom, liquid oscillating in a U-tube, a mass on springs. The Earth's rotation is periodic but not SHM; a polyatomic molecule's general vibration is a superposition of SHMs.

ex.q: Find the length of a seconds pendulum where g = 9.8 m s⁻² (π² ≈ 9.87).

topics.rl: Students in CBSE physics labs across India find g by timing 20 oscillations of a pendulum of known length; the class average is usually close to 9.8 m s⁻². Lab safety: clamp the stand firmly so it can't tip, and keep the swing small and clear of faces.

topics.t: What a wave is
topics.h: A 'Mexican wave' sweeps around a packed Wankhede Stadium, yet no spectator leaves their seat. That's exactly how a wave works.
p: A wave transfers energy and information from one place to another without transporting matter as a whole.

Mechanical waves (sound, waves on strings, water waves, seismic waves) need a material medium. Electromagnetic waves (light, radio, X-rays) do not need a medium. Matter waves are associated with moving particles like electrons.
In a mechanical wave, each particle of the medium only oscillates about its mean position; it is the disturbance (pattern) that travels.
Wave propagation needs two properties of the medium: elasticity (restoring forces between neighbouring parts) and inertia (mass) of its parts.

ex.q: A paper boat floats on a pond as ripples pass. Does it move along with the ripples?
st: The ripples carry energy across the water.
Each water particle, and the boat on it, just moves up and down (and slightly to and fro) about its place.
So the boat bobs but is not carried along by the wave.
ex.a: No, it only bobs about its position

topics.rl: Mobile phone signals, Doordarshan broadcasts and the light from the Sun are electromagnetic waves; they travel even through the vacuum of space.

topics.t: Transverse and longitudinal waves
topics.h: During an earthquake, the first jolt (P-wave) squeezes and stretches the ground; the later, more destructive shaking (S-wave) moves it side to side.
p: Transverse waves: particles oscillate perpendicular to the direction of propagation (wave on a string, ripples on a stretched rope).
Longitudinal waves: particles oscillate along the direction of propagation, forming compressions and rarefactions (sound in air, P-waves).

Transverse mechanical waves need the medium to resist shear (shear modulus), so they travel in solids and along strings, but not through the bulk of liquids or gases. Longitudinal waves travel in solids, liquids and gases.
Water surface waves are a combination of both: water particles move in roughly circular paths.
Classify by asking: do particles move across (transverse) or along (longitudinal) the direction the wave travels?

ex.q: Classify: (a) sound from a sitar in air (b) the vibration of the sitar string (c) ripples on a lake.
st: (a) Air particles oscillate along the direction of travel: longitudinal.
(b) The string vibrates perpendicular to its length: transverse.
(c) Water particles move in circles: both transverse and longitudinal.

topics.rl: Seismologists at NCS (National Center for Seismology) use the arrival gap between P-waves and S-waves to locate earthquake epicentres.

topics.t: Equation of a progressive wave
topics.h: One compact equation, y = a sin(kx − ωt + φ), describes the wave on a sitar string at every point and every instant.
p: A sinusoidal wave travelling in +x: y(x, t) = a sin(kx − ωt + φ). In −x: y = a sin(kx + ωt + φ).
a = amplitude (maximum displacement). (kx − ωt + φ) = phase; φ = phase constant (initial phase at x = 0, t = 0).
Wavelength λ: distance between two consecutive points in the same phase (e.g. crests). Angular wave number k = 2π/λ (unit rad m⁻¹).
Period T: time for one oscillation of a particle; angular frequency ω = 2π/T; frequency ν = 1/T = ω/2π.
Reading a wave equation: match it with a sin(kx − ωt + φ) and identify a, k, ω, then λ = 2π/k, T = 2π/ω.

ex.q: y = 0.005 sin(80x − 3t) (SI units). Find amplitude, wavelength, period and frequency.

topics.rl: Engineers at All India Radio describe carrier waves by equations of exactly this form, with frequencies of hundreds of kHz.

topics.t: Wave speed and waves on strings
topics.h: Tighten a sitar string and the note rises. Higher tension makes waves travel faster along the string.
p: Following a point of constant phase (kx − ωt = constant) gives the wave speed v = ω/k = λ/T = νλ.
Wave speed depends on the properties of the medium (elasticity and inertia), not on the frequency of the source. Changing the source frequency changes λ, not v.
Transverse wave on a stretched string: v = √(T/μ), where T is the tension and μ the mass per unit length. Dimensional analysis gives this form (constant = 1 from full theory).
Example: a wire of μ = 0.01 kg m⁻¹ under 100 N tension carries waves at √(100/0.01) = 100 m s⁻¹.

ex.q: A 2 m wire of mass 0.04 kg is stretched with a tension of 50 N. Find the speed of a transverse pulse and the time to cross the wire.

topics.rl: Sitar and veena players tune strings by adjusting tension with the pegs: v = √(T/μ) sets the pitch.

topics.t: Speed of sound: Newton's formula and Laplace's correction
topics.h: Put your ear to a railway track and you hear the train long before the sound comes through the air. Sound is much faster in steel.
p: Speed of longitudinal waves: v = √(B/ρ) in a fluid (B = bulk modulus), v = √(Y/ρ) in a solid rod.
Sound is fastest in solids, slower in liquids, slowest in gases (e.g. roughly 5000 m s⁻¹ in steel, 1500 m s⁻¹ in water, 340 m s⁻¹ in air).
Newton assumed isothermal compressions: B = P, giving v = √(P/ρ) ≈ 280 m s⁻¹ for air at STP, about 15% too low.
Laplace correction: compressions are fast and adiabatic, so B = γP and v = √(γP/ρ). With γ = 1.4 for air, v ≈ 331 m s⁻¹ at 0 °C, matching experiment.
v ∝ √T (absolute temperature). At constant temperature, changing pressure does not change v (since P/ρ stays constant).

ex.q: Using Newton's formula, the speed of sound in air at STP comes out as 280 m s⁻¹. What does Laplace's correction give (γ = 1.4, √1.4 ≈ 1.183)?

topics.rl: In a Rajasthan summer at 47 °C, sound travels noticeably faster than on a cold Shimla winter morning, because v ∝ √T.

topics.t: Using sound speed, and the superposition principle
topics.h: During a monsoon storm, count the seconds between the lightning flash and the thunder, multiply by 340, and you know how far the strike was.
p: Echo: sound travels to the reflector and back, so distance d = vt/2.
Lightning–thunder: light arrives almost instantly, so distance ≈ v_sound × delay.
Principle of superposition: when two or more waves overlap, the net displacement at a point is the algebraic sum of the individual displacements: y = y₁ + y₂ + ….
Two pulses moving in opposite directions pass through each other and emerge unchanged; while overlapping, they add (a crest and an equal trough momentarily cancel).

ex.q: A girl shouts in front of a cliff and hears the echo after 2 s (v = 340 m s⁻¹). How far is the cliff?
st: Sound goes to the cliff and back: total path = vt = 340 × 2 = 680 m.

topics.rl: Bats over the forests of the Western Ghats use echoes to locate insects, timing returns to fractions of a millisecond.

topics.t: Interference of two harmonic waves
topics.h: Noise-cancelling headphones play a sound wave exactly opposite to the outside noise. The two add up to near silence.
p: Two waves of the same frequency and amplitude a, travelling in the same direction with phase difference φ: y₁ = a sin(kx − ωt), y₂ = a sin(kx − ωt + φ).
Resultant: y = 2a cos(φ/2) sin(kx − ωt + φ/2). The resultant amplitude is A = 2a cos(φ/2).
Constructive interference: φ = 0 (or 2nπ), A = 2a (intensity 4 times one wave).
Destructive interference: φ = π (or (2n + 1)π), A = 0.
Intermediate phases give amplitudes between 0 and 2a (e.g. φ = 2π/3 gives A = a).

ex.q: Two waves of amplitude 3 mm and the same frequency travel together with a phase difference of π/2. Find the resultant amplitude.

topics.rl: Concert halls like NCPA Mumbai are designed to avoid dead spots where reflected sound waves interfere destructively.

topics.t: Reflection and standing waves
topics.h: Shake a rope tied to a wall at just the right rate and it forms a still pattern of loops. Waves going and coming back create a standing wave.
p: Reflection at a rigid boundary (fixed end): the reflected wave has a phase change of π, so a crest returns as a trough (pulse inverted).
Reflection at an open (free) boundary: no phase change; a crest returns as a crest.
The incident and reflected waves superpose to form a standing (stationary) wave: y = 2a sin kx cos ωt.
Nodes: points of zero amplitude (sin kx = 0): x = nλ/2. Antinodes: points of maximum amplitude 2a: x = (n + ½)λ/2.
Distance between adjacent nodes (or adjacent antinodes) = λ/2; between a node and the next antinode = λ/4.

ex.q: A standing wave on a string has adjacent nodes 20 cm apart. Find the wavelength and the distance between a node and the nearest antinode.
st: Adjacent nodes are λ/2 apart: λ = 40 cm.
Node to next antinode = λ/4 = 10 cm.

topics.rl: Tabla and mridangam skins vibrate in standing-wave patterns; the black syahi patch shapes these modes to give their rich tones.

topics.t: Normal modes of strings and air columns
topics.h: A flute and a clarinet can play the same note, but they sound different. One is open at both ends, the other closed at one: different harmonics.
p: String fixed at both ends (nodes at both ends): λₙ = 2L/n, νₙ = nv/(2L), n = 1, 2, 3, … The lowest (n = 1) is the fundamental; all harmonics are present.
Air column closed at one end (node at closed end, antinode at open end): L = (2n − 1)λ/4, νₙ = (2n − 1)v/(4L). Only odd harmonics (1st, 3rd, 5th, …) are present.
Air column open at both ends (antinodes at both ends): νₙ = nv/(2L); all harmonics are present.
For the same length, the fundamental of a closed pipe (v/4L) is half that of an open pipe (v/2L).

ex.q: A string 0.5 m long carries waves at 200 m s⁻¹. Find the fundamental and the next two harmonics.

topics.rl: The bansuri (bamboo flute) behaves like a pipe open at both ends; covering holes changes its effective length and so its notes.

topics.t: Resonance tube and harmonic numericals
topics.h: In the CBSE physics lab, you lower a glass tube in water while a tuning fork hums above it. Suddenly it booms: resonance!
p: Resonance tube: an air column closed at the bottom by water. With a fork of frequency ν, resonance occurs when L = λ/4, 3λ/4, 5λ/4, …
Successive resonance lengths differ by λ/2: L₂ − L₁ = λ/2, so v = 2ν(L₂ − L₁). This removes the error of the end correction.
Harmonic numericals: for strings ν = nv/(2L) with v = √(T/μ); for closed pipes ν = (2n − 1)v/(4L); for open pipes ν = nv/(2L).
Check which harmonics are allowed before answering (e.g. a closed pipe can't give 2ν₁).

ex.q: With a 500 Hz fork, resonances occur at 16.5 cm and 50.5 cm. Find the speed of sound.
st: L₂ − L₁ = 34 cm = λ/2, so λ = 68 cm = 0.68 m.

topics.rl: Resonance-tube experiments in Indian school labs routinely give the speed of sound within a few percent of 340 m s⁻¹. Lab safety: strike the tuning fork only on a rubber pad (never on the glass tube or the bench), and handle the glass tube gently to avoid breakage.

topics.t: Beats
topics.h: When two harmonium reeds are slightly out of tune, you hear a 'wah-wah-wah' throbbing. Those are beats.
p: Beats: periodic rise and fall (waxing and waning) of loudness heard when two sound waves of slightly different frequencies superpose.
Beat frequency = number of beats per second = |ν₁ − ν₂|.
Musicians tune instruments by sounding a note with a standard and adjusting until the beats disappear.

Unknown fork: if fork B gives n beats with a known fork A (ν_A), then ν_B = ν_A ± n. Loading B with wax lowers ν_B; filing its prongs raises ν_B. Watch whether beats increase or decrease to choose the sign.
Mixed numericals: read wave equations, standing waves on strings, organ pipes and beats.

ex.q: A 512 Hz fork A gives 5 beats s⁻¹ with fork B. When B is loaded with a little wax, the beats fall to 3 s⁻¹. Find ν_B.
st: Wax lowers ν_B. If ν_B = 517, it moves towards 512 and beats decrease ✓. If 507, beats would increase ✗.

topics.rl: Sitar players tuning to a tanpura listen for beats; when the throbbing stops, the strings are in unison.

qa.q: Measurement of a physical quantity basically involves
qa.a: Comparing it with an accepted reference standard called a unit
qa.e: A measurement compares the quantity with a chosen standard (the unit) and reports how many times the unit it contains.

qa.q: Which of the following is a derived quantity?
qa.a: Pressure
qa.e: Pressure is force per unit area, so it is built from mass, length and time. The others are SI base quantities.

qa.q: The unit of force, newton, written in base SI units is
qa.a: kg m s⁻²
qa.e: F = ma, so 1 N = 1 kg × 1 m s⁻² = 1 kg m s⁻².

qa.q: In the CGS system, the unit of mass is the
qa.a: gram
qa.e: CGS stands for centimetre–gram–second, so mass is measured in grams.

qa.q: A complete set of base units together with all derived units is called
qa.a: A system of units
qa.e: Base units plus the derived units built from them form a system of units, such as CGS, FPS, MKS or SI.

qa.q: Why was a single international system (SI) adopted?
qa.a: Different countries used different unit systems, which made exchange of scientific data confusing
qa.e: Many local systems (CGS, FPS, MKS) existed, so data had to be converted constantly. One agreed system removes that confusion.

qa.q: A train moves 54 km in 1 hour. Its speed in m s⁻¹ is
qa.e: Convert km to m and hours to seconds before dividing.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Velocity is a derived quantity.
Reason (R): Its unit, m s⁻¹, is obtained from the base units of length and time.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Velocity = displacement/time, so its unit is made from the base units metre and second. R explains A.

qa.q: How many base quantities does the SI system have?
qa.e: Length, mass, time, electric current, thermodynamic temperature, amount of substance and luminous intensity: seven.

qa.q: The SI unit of luminous intensity is the
qa.a: candela
qa.e: Luminous intensity is a base quantity with base unit candela (cd). Lumen and lux are derived units.

qa.q: Which fundamental constant is fixed to define the kilogram?
qa.a: Planck constant h
qa.e: The 2019 redefinition fixes h, and the kilogram follows from it (together with the definitions of the metre and second).

qa.q: The second is defined using the radiation of
qa.a: Caesium-133 atoms
qa.e: The unperturbed ground-state hyperfine transition frequency of caesium-133 is fixed at 9 192 631 770 Hz.

qa.q: Which pair is correctly matched?
qa.a: Amount of substance — mole
qa.e: The SI base unit of amount of substance is the mole. Temperature is in kelvin, current in ampere and mass in kilogram.

qa.q: The ampere is now defined by fixing the value of
qa.a: The elementary charge e
qa.e: e is fixed at 1.602 176 634 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, and the ampere follows (with the second).

qa.q: Which of these is NOT an SI base unit?
qa.a: newton
qa.e: The newton (kg m s⁻²) is derived from base units; kelvin, mole and candela are base units.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The kelvin is defined by fixing the numerical value of the Boltzmann constant.
Reason (R): The kelvin is one of the seven SI base units.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both statements are true, but being a base unit says nothing about how the kelvin is defined; the definition comes from fixing k.

qa.q: An arc of length 6 cm subtends an angle at the centre of a circle of radius 3 cm. The angle in radians is
qa.e: θ = arc/radius = 6/3 = 2 rad.

qa.q: A full sphere subtends a solid angle of nπ steradian at its centre. What is n?
qa.e: Ω = A/r² = 4πr²/r² = 4π sr.

qa.q: The unit of solid angle is the
qa.a: steradian
qa.e: Solid angle dΩ = dA/r² is measured in steradians (sr).

qa.q: Which prefix stands for 10⁻⁶?
qa.a: micro
qa.e: micro (µ) = 10⁻⁶; milli = 10⁻³; nano = 10⁻⁹; mega = 10⁶.

qa.q: Which way of writing a mass follows the SI rules for unit symbols?
qa.a: 25 kg, with a lowercase symbol, no plural 's' and no full stop
qa.e: The kilogram symbol is lowercase 'kg', is never pluralised, and is not an abbreviation needing a full stop.

qa.q: A wavelength of 600 nm expressed in metres is 600 × 10⁻ⁿ m. What is n?
qa.e: nano means 10⁻⁹, so 600 nm = 600 × 10⁻⁹ m = 6 × 10⁻⁷ m.

qa.q: Why is the radian called a dimensionless unit?
qa.a: It is a ratio of two lengths (arc/radius)
qa.e: θ = s/r divides one length by another, so the dimensions cancel.

qa.q: The symbol of the newton is a capital N, but the unit is written 'newton' in full. Which rule explains this?
qa.a: Symbols of units named after people start with a capital letter; the full name is written in lowercase
qa.e: Units named after scientists (N, Pa, J, K) get a capital symbol, while the full unit name stays lowercase.

qa.q: How many cm² are there in 2.5 m²?
qa.e: 1 m = 100 cm, so 1 m² = 10⁴ cm².

qa.q: The density of mercury is 13.6 g cm⁻³. In kg m⁻³ it is
qa.e: 1 g cm⁻³ = 1000 kg m⁻³, so 13.6 g cm⁻³ = 13600 kg m⁻³.

qa.q: 1 J equals 10ⁿ erg. What is n?
qa.e: 1 J = 1 kg m² s⁻² = (10³ g)(10⁴ cm²) s⁻² = 10⁷ g cm² s⁻² = 10⁷ erg.

qa.q: A 1.5 L bottle has a volume of how many cm³?
Which of these is a unit of distance, not of time?
qa.a: Light year
qa.e: A light year is the distance light travels in one year, about 9.46 × 10¹⁵ m.

qa.q: Energy of 5 eV in units of 10⁻¹⁹ J is
qa.e: 1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, so 5 eV = 8 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.

qa.q: The size of an atom is about 1 Å. How many ångströms make 1 nm?
qa.e: 1 nm = 10⁻⁹ m and 1 Å = 10⁻¹⁰ m, so 1 nm = 10 Å.

qa.q: The astronomical unit (AU) is
qa.a: The mean distance between the Earth and the Sun
qa.e: 1 AU ≈ 1.496 × 10¹¹ m is the average Earth–Sun distance.

qa.q: The number of significant figures in 0.06900 is
qa.e: Leading zeros are not significant. 6, 9 and the two trailing zeros after the decimal point are significant.

qa.q: How many significant figures does 20.07 have?
qa.e: Both zeros lie between non-zero digits (2 and 7), so all four digits count.

qa.q: Which number has exactly three significant figures?
qa.e: In 0.000340 the leading zeros do not count; 3, 4 and the trailing zero after the decimal do, giving 3.

qa.q: Why is it unclear how many significant figures 5600 has?
qa.a: Trailing zeros in a number without a decimal point may only be place holders
qa.e: Without a decimal point or scientific notation, we cannot tell whether the trailing zeros were measured.

qa.q: The number of significant figures in 6.320 × 10⁻⁴ is
qa.e: Only the digits in 6.320 count: 6, 3, 2 and the trailing 0. The power of ten is not counted.

qa.q: Significant figures in a measured value indicate its
qa.a: Precision
qa.e: The number of reliable digits plus one uncertain digit shows how finely the value was measured: its precision.

qa.q: A metre scale has a least count of 1 mm. A length reading recorded correctly is
qa.e: With a 1 mm least count you can read to 0.1 cm, so 12.3 cm shows the reliable digits plus one uncertain digit.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): 0.00250 has three significant figures.
Reason (R): Leading zeros in a number less than one are not significant, but trailing zeros after the decimal point are.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: The leading zeros are dropped and 2, 5 and the final 0 are counted. R gives exactly that rule.

qa.q: The radius of a hydrogen atom is about 0.53 Å = 5.3 × 10⁻¹¹ m. By the NCERT rule its order of magnitude (power of ten) is
qa.e: a = 5.3 > 5, so we round up: order = −11 + 1 = −10.

qa.q: The order of magnitude of 3.2 × 10⁵ m is
qa.e: a = 3.2 ≤ 5, so the order is the exponent itself, 5.

qa.q: The length 2.540 cm is expressed as 0.02540 m. The number of significant figures is now
qa.e: Changing units only shifts the decimal point; the leading zeros added are not significant. Still 4.

qa.q: In the expression for kinetic energy ½mv², the number ½ has
qa.a: Unlimited significant figures
qa.e: ½ is an exact pure number, so it never limits the precision of the result.

qa.q: Which form correctly shows that 3800 m was measured to 3 significant figures?
qa.e: 3.80 × 10³ has exactly three significant digits and uses 1 ≤ a < 10.

qa.q: A student counted 25 oscillations of a pendulum. The number 25 has
qa.a: Unlimited significant figures since it is an exact count
qa.e: Counted numbers are exact; they do not limit the significant figures of a calculation.

qa.q: The mass of the Earth is 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg. Its order of magnitude by the NCERT rule is

Assertion (A): The number 4500, written without a decimal point, definitely has four significant figures.
Reason (R): Trailing zeros in a number without a decimal point are ambiguous.
qa.a: A is false but R is true
qa.e: A is false: the trailing zeros may only be place holders, so 4500 could have 2, 3 or 4 significant figures. R is true.

qa.q: The result of 3.0 × 4.123, with correct significant figures, is
qa.e: 3.0 has 2 significant figures, so the product (12.369) is rounded to 2: 12.

qa.q: 2.5 m + 0.236 m + 1.03 m, reported correctly, is
qa.e: The sum is 3.766 m. The least number of decimal places is 1 (in 2.5), so we round to 3.8 m.

qa.q: A mass of 5.74 g occupies 1.2 cm³. Its density in g cm⁻³, correctly reported, is
qa.e: 5.74/1.2 = 4.783…; 1.2 has 2 significant figures, so the result is 4.8.

qa.q: The side of a cube is 1.2 cm. Its volume, with correct significant figures, in cm³ is
qa.e: 1.2³ = 1.728 cm³; the side has 2 significant figures, so V = 1.7 cm³.

qa.q: Subtract: 12.4 s − 3.25 s. Correctly reported, the result (in s) is
qa.e: 12.4 − 3.25 = 9.15 s. Keep 1 decimal place (as in 12.4). The dropped digit is 5 and the preceding 1 is odd, so 9.15 becomes 9.2.

qa.q: For the volume of a sphere V = (4/3)πr³ with r = 2.0 cm, how many significant figures should V have?
qa.e: 4/3 and π are exact or can be taken to any precision; r has 2 significant figures, so V has 2.

qa.q: A student finds the area of a sheet 2.1 m × 3.5 m as 7.35 m². The best criticism is
qa.a: The answer should be 7.4 m² because each length has only 2 significant figures
qa.e: Product of two 2-significant-figure values must be given to 2 significant figures: 7.35 → 7.4 m².

qa.q:
Assertion (A): 436.32 g + 227.2 g + 0.301 g should be reported as 663.8 g.
Reason (R): In addition, the result keeps as many decimal places as the term with the fewest decimal places.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: 227.2 has one decimal place, so the exact sum 663.821 g is reported as 663.8 g. R gives the rule.

qa.q: Rounded to three significant figures, 4.0635 becomes
qa.e: Keep 4.06; the dropped digits 35 are less than 50, so the 6 is unchanged.

qa.q: Following the NCERT rule, 6.375 rounded to three significant figures is
qa.e: The dropped digit is exactly 5 and the preceding digit 7 is odd, so it is raised to 8.

qa.q: Following the NCERT rule, 3.465 rounded to three significant figures is
qa.e: The dropped digit is exactly 5 and the preceding digit 6 is even, so it stays: 3.46.

qa.q: Length l = 20.0 ± 0.2 cm. Its percentage error is
qa.e: Percentage error = (0.2/20.0) × 100 = 1%.

qa.q: For A = l × b with 2% error in l and 3% error in b, the percentage error in A is
qa.e: For a product, percentage errors add: 2% + 3% = 5%.

qa.q: Why should intermediate results carry one extra digit?
qa.a: To avoid building up rounding errors before the final answer
qa.e: Rounding at every step adds small errors that pile up. Keep one extra digit and round only at the end.

qa.q: The side of a square is measured with 1% error. The percentage error in its area is
qa.e: A = a × a, so the relative error is 1% + 1% = 2%.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): 2.745 rounded to three significant figures is 2.74.
Reason (R): When the digit dropped is exactly 5, the preceding digit is left unchanged if it is even.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: The preceding digit 4 is even, so it stays: 2.74. R states the rule used.

qa.q: The dimensions of velocity are
qa.a: [M⁰ L T⁻¹]
qa.e: Velocity = displacement/time = [L]/[T] = [L T⁻¹], with no mass dependence.

qa.q: Force has dimension in time equal to
qa.e: [F] = [M L T⁻²], so the power of T is −2.

qa.q: Which of these quantities has dimensions [L³]?
qa.a: Volume
qa.e: Volume is length × length × length = [L³].

qa.q: The symbol for the dimension of thermodynamic temperature is
qa.e: NCERT uses [K] for temperature; [T] is time and [A] is current.

qa.q: The power of [L] in the dimensions of acceleration is
qa.e: [a] = [L T⁻²]: power 1 for length, −2 for time.

qa.q: A distance of 5 km and a distance of 5000 m have
qa.a: The same dimensions [L]
qa.e: Dimensions describe the nature of a quantity, not its unit or size.

qa.q: Which pair has the same dimensions?
qa.a: Speed and velocity
qa.e: Speed and velocity are both [L T⁻¹]. Force [M L T⁻²] ≠ momentum [M L T⁻¹]; weight is a force.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Dimensions of a physical quantity do not change when it is expressed in a different system of units.
Reason (R): Dimensions show the nature of a quantity in terms of base quantities, not its unit.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: A length is [L] in cm, m or feet. R explains why.

qa.q: The dimensional formula of work is
qa.a: [M L² T⁻²]
qa.e: Work = force × displacement = [M L T⁻²][L] = [M L² T⁻²].

qa.q: The dimensional formula of power is
qa.a: [M L² T⁻³]
qa.e: Power = work/time = [M L² T⁻²]/[T] = [M L² T⁻³].

qa.q: Which physical quantity has the same dimensions as pressure?
qa.a: Stress
qa.e: Stress = force/area, just like pressure, so both are [M L⁻¹ T⁻²].

qa.q: Momentum has the dimensional formula
qa.a: [M L T⁻¹]
qa.e: p = mv = [M][L T⁻¹] = [M L T⁻¹].

qa.q: Which of these is dimensionless?
qa.a: Refractive index
qa.e: Refractive index = speed of light in vacuum/speed in medium, a ratio of like quantities.

qa.q: What is the power of [L] in the dimensional formula of density?
qa.e: ρ = m/V = [M]/[L³] = [M L⁻³].

qa.q: The dimensional equation for force is written as
qa.a: [F] = [M L T⁻²]
qa.e: A dimensional equation sets the quantity in brackets equal to its dimensional formula.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Relative density is a dimensionless quantity.
Reason (R): Relative density has the SI unit kg m⁻³.
qa.a: A is true but R is false
qa.e: A is true: it is a ratio of two densities. R is false: being a ratio, it has no unit.

qa.q: According to the principle of homogeneity, two quantities can be added only if they
qa.a: Have the same dimensions
qa.e: Addition and subtraction make sense only for like quantities, i.e. same dimensions.

qa.q: Which equation is dimensionally incorrect? (s distance, u, v velocities, a acceleration, t time)
qa.a: s = ut + at³
qa.e: [at³] = [L T⁻²][T³] = [L T], not [L], so s = ut + at³ fails.

qa.q: In y = A sin(kx − ωt), where x is a length, the dimensions of k are
qa.a: [L⁻¹]
qa.e: kx must be dimensionless, so [k] = 1/[L] = [L⁻¹].

qa.q: In y = A sin(kx − ωt), the dimensions of ω are
qa.a: [T⁻¹]
qa.e: ωt is dimensionless, so [ω] = [T⁻¹].

qa.q: x = x₀ + v₀t + ½at² passes the dimensional test. This proves that
qa.a: Each term has dimensions of length, but the factor ½ is not confirmed
qa.e: Dimensional analysis shows consistency only; it cannot check dimensionless factors like ½.

qa.q: A student writes the formula for the period of a pendulum as T = 2π√(g/l). Using dimensions, this is
qa.a: Wrong, because √(g/l) has dimensions [T⁻¹]
qa.e: [g/l] = [L T⁻²]/[L] = [T⁻²], so √(g/l) = [T⁻¹], not [T]. The correct formula is T = 2π√(l/g).

qa.q: In the expression e^(−αt), where t is time, the dimension of α is
qa.a: [T⁻¹]
qa.e: The exponent αt must be dimensionless, so [α] = [T⁻¹].

qa.q:
Assertion (A): A dimensionally correct equation may not be a correct physical relation.
Reason (R): Dimensionless constants such as ½ or 2π cannot be found or checked by dimensional analysis.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Because pure numbers carry no dimensions, an equation with a wrong numerical factor still passes. R explains A.

qa.q: Which expression has the dimensions of energy?
qa.a: mgh
qa.e: [m][g][h] = [M][L T⁻²][L] = [M L² T⁻²], the dimensions of energy.

qa.q: In v = at + b/(t + c), the dimensions of c are
qa.e: c is added to t, so it must have the dimensions of time.

qa.q: In v = at + b/(t + c), the dimensions of b are
qa.e: b/(t + c) must be a velocity, so [b] = [L T⁻¹][T] = [L].

qa.q: In v = at + b/(t + c), the dimensions of a are
qa.a: [L T⁻²]
qa.e: at must be a velocity, so [a] = [L T⁻¹]/[T] = [L T⁻²].

qa.q: Which formula for the kinetic energy K of a body of mass m and speed v could be correct on dimensional grounds?
qa.a: K = m²v³/(2m v)
qa.e: m²v³/(2mv) simplifies to mv²/2, which is [M L² T⁻²]. The others give [M L T⁻¹], [M² L² T⁻²] or [M L³ T⁻³].

qa.q: In the van der Waals form (P + a/V²)(V − b) = RT, the dimensions of b are those of
qa.a: Volume
qa.e: b is subtracted from V, so it has the dimensions of volume, [L³].

qa.q: In (P + a/V²)(V − b) = RT, the constant a has the dimensions of
qa.a: Pressure × volume²
qa.e: a/V² is added to P, so [a] = [P][V²] = [M L⁻¹ T⁻²][L⁶] = [M L⁵ T⁻²].

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Both ½mv² and mgh are dimensionally correct expressions for energy.
Reason (R): Each has dimensions [M L² T⁻²].
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: [M][L T⁻¹]² and [M][L T⁻²][L] both give [M L² T⁻²]. R explains A.

qa.q: By dimensional analysis, the time period of a simple pendulum is proportional to l raised to the power
qa.e: Equating powers gives a = ½ and b = −½, so T ∝ √(l/g).

qa.q: Using dimensions, 1 N equals 10ⁿ dyne. What is n?
A pendulum's length is made 4 times larger. Its period becomes how many times the original?
qa.e: T ∝ √l, so the period becomes √4 = 2 times.

qa.q: Which of these can dimensional analysis NOT do?
qa.a: Find the value of a dimensionless constant like 2π
qa.e: Pure numbers have no dimensions, so their values cannot be obtained.

qa.q: The speed v of a wave on a string depends on tension F [M L T⁻²] and mass per unit length μ [M L⁻¹]. Dimensional analysis gives v ∝
qa.e: Fᵃμᵇ: M: a + b = 0; L: a − b = 1; T: −2a = −1 → a = ½, b = −½. So v ∝ √(F/μ).

qa.q: Pressure is 10⁵ Pa. In CGS units (dyne cm⁻²) this is 10ⁿ. What is n?
qa.e: [P] = [M L⁻¹ T⁻²]: n₂ = n₁ (10³)¹(10²)⁻¹ = 10 n₁. So 10⁵ Pa = 10⁶ dyne cm⁻².

qa.q: Why can dimensional analysis not derive a relation in which a quantity depends on four variables in mechanics?
qa.a: There are only three equations (from M, L and T) to fix four unknown powers
qa.e: Matching powers of M, L and T gives only three equations, which cannot fix four exponents.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Dimensional analysis can give the value of the constant 2π in T = 2π√(l/g).
Reason (R): Dimensional analysis works by equating the powers of M, L and T on both sides of a relation.
qa.a: A is false but R is true
qa.e: A is false: pure numbers like 2π have no dimensions, so they cannot be found. R correctly describes the method.

qa.q: A car moves from x = +40 m to x = −20 m. Its displacement in metres is
qa.e: Δx = x₂ − x₁ = −20 − 40 = −60 m. The minus sign shows motion in the −x direction.

qa.q: A person walks 60 m east and then 20 m west along the same straight road in 40 s. The average speed in m s⁻¹ is
qa.e: Average speed = path length/time = (60 + 20)/40 = 2 m s⁻¹.

qa.q: For the same walk (60 m east, then 20 m west in 40 s), the magnitude of average velocity in m s⁻¹ is
qa.e: Displacement = 60 − 20 = 40 m east, so average velocity = 40/40 = 1 m s⁻¹.

qa.q: An athlete completes exactly one round of a 400 m circular track in 50 s. The average velocity is
qa.a: Zero
qa.e: The athlete returns to the start, so displacement and hence average velocity are zero. (Average speed is 8 m s⁻¹.)

qa.q: In which case can the object be treated as a point object?
qa.a: The Earth revolving around the Sun
qa.e: The Earth's size is tiny compared with its orbit, so for orbital motion it can be treated as a point.

qa.q: Kinematics is the study of
qa.a: Motion without considering its causes
qa.e: Kinematics describes how things move; dynamics explains why.

qa.q: If the origin is shifted, which quantity remains unchanged for a given motion?
qa.a: Displacement
qa.e: Displacement Δx = x₂ − x₁ is a difference, so shifting the origin changes both x values equally and Δx stays the same.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The average speed of a body can be greater than the magnitude of its average velocity.
Reason (R): Path length is always greater than or equal to the magnitude of displacement.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Average speed uses path length and average velocity uses displacement over the same time, so R explains A.

qa.q: Instantaneous velocity is defined as
qa.a: The limit of Δx/Δt as Δt → 0
qa.e: v = lim(Δt→0) Δx/Δt = dx/dt.

qa.q: On a position–time graph, the instantaneous velocity at a point is given by
qa.a: The slope of the tangent at that point
qa.e: The tangent's slope is the limit of chord slopes as the interval shrinks.

qa.q: For x = 0.1t³ (SI units), the average velocity from t = 2 s to t = 3 s in m s⁻¹ is
For x = 0.1t³ (SI units), the instantaneous velocity at t = 3 s in m s⁻¹ is
The x–t graph of a body is a straight line sloping upward. Its instantaneous velocity
qa.a: Is constant and positive
qa.e: A straight line has the same slope everywhere, so v is constant; an upward slope means v > 0.

qa.q: At the highest point of an x–t graph shaped like a hill, the velocity is
qa.a: Zero
qa.e: The tangent at the peak is horizontal, so the slope (velocity) is zero.

qa.q: A car's speedometer reading is its
qa.a: Instantaneous speed
qa.e: The speedometer shows the speed at that instant.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): At any instant, speed is the magnitude of velocity.
Reason (R): Over any time interval, average speed equals the magnitude of average velocity.
qa.a: A is true but R is false
qa.e: A is true for instantaneous values. R is false: if the body turns back, path length exceeds |displacement|, so average speed is larger.

qa.q: The position of a particle is x = 3t² − 2t + 5 (SI units). Its velocity at t = 3 s in m s⁻¹ is
For x = 3t² − 2t + 5 (SI units), the acceleration in m s⁻² is
qa.e: a = dv/dt = d(6t − 2)/dt = 6 m s⁻².

qa.q: x = t³ − 6t² (SI units). At what time t (in s, t > 0) is the particle momentarily at rest?
qa.e: v = 3t² − 12t = 3t(t − 4) = 0 gives t = 4 s (t > 0).

qa.q: For x = t³ − 6t² (SI units), the acceleration is zero at t (in s) =
qa.e: a = dv/dt = 6t − 12 = 0 gives t = 2 s.

qa.q: Acceleration at an instant equals
qa.a: The slope of the v–t graph at that instant
qa.e: a = dv/dt is the slope of the tangent to the v–t curve.

qa.q: For x = a + bt², which statement is correct?
qa.a: The acceleration is constant and equal to 2b
qa.e: v = 2bt and a = 2b, a constant.

qa.q: The velocity of a particle is v = 4t + 3t² (SI units). Its acceleration at t = 2 s in m s⁻² is

Assertion (A): For x = 5 + 4t (SI units), the acceleration of the particle is zero.
Reason (R): The particle starts from x = 5 m at t = 0.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true, but the starting position does not explain zero acceleration; the constant velocity dx/dt = 4 m s⁻¹ does.

qa.q: A bus's velocity changes from 20 m s⁻¹ to 8 m s⁻¹ in 4 s (same direction, taken as +x). Its average acceleration in m s⁻² is
qa.e: a = (8 − 20)/4 = −3 m s⁻². The negative sign means acceleration is opposite to the motion (the bus slows).

qa.q: A car moving in the −x direction is slowing down. Its acceleration is
qa.a: Positive
qa.e: Velocity is negative and its magnitude is decreasing, so v is becoming less negative; Δv > 0 and a > 0.

qa.q: An object moves on a circle at constant speed. Its acceleration is
qa.a: Non-zero, because the direction of velocity changes
qa.e: Velocity is a vector; a change of direction alone means acceleration.

qa.q: An x–t graph that curves upward (like a U opening upward) indicates
qa.a: Positive acceleration
qa.e: Its slope (velocity) increases with time, so a > 0.

qa.q: A straight-line x–t graph with negative slope represents
qa.a: Constant negative velocity and zero acceleration
qa.e: A straight line has constant slope: constant velocity (negative here), so a = 0.

qa.q: Velocity changes from −10 m s⁻¹ to +10 m s⁻¹ in 5 s. The average acceleration in m s⁻² is
The SI unit of acceleration is
qa.a: m s⁻²
qa.e: Acceleration = velocity/time = (m s⁻¹)/s = m s⁻².

qa.q:
Assertion (A): A negative acceleration always means the body is slowing down.
Reason (R): The sign of acceleration depends on the choice of positive direction.
qa.a: A is false but R is true
qa.e: A is false: a body moving in −x and speeding up has negative a. R is true.

qa.q: A body starts from rest and accelerates uniformly to 12 m s⁻¹ in 6 s. The area under its v–t graph, in m, is
qa.e: Area of triangle = ½ × 6 × 12 = 36 m = displacement.

qa.q: A body accelerates uniformly from rest to 12 m s⁻¹ in 6 s. Its acceleration in m s⁻² is
qa.e: Slope = 12/6 = 2 m s⁻².

qa.q: A v–t graph is a straight line from v = +10 m s⁻¹ at t = 0 to v = −10 m s⁻¹ at t = 4 s. The displacement in 4 s, in m, is
qa.e: Area above the axis (½ × 2 × 10 = 10 m) cancels area below (−10 m).

qa.q: For the same graph (+10 to −10 m s⁻¹ in 4 s), the distance travelled, in m, is
qa.e: Distance = 10 m + 10 m = 20 m (both areas as magnitudes).

qa.q: A v–t graph is a straight line from +10 m s⁻¹ at t = 0 to −10 m s⁻¹ at t = 4 s. The body reverses its direction at t (in s) =
qa.e: v becomes zero midway at t = 2 s and then turns negative.

qa.q: Which graph cannot represent a real one-dimensional motion?
qa.a: An x–t graph that shows two different positions at the same time
qa.e: A body cannot be at two places at one instant.

qa.q: A car moves at 15 m s⁻¹ for 4 s and then brakes uniformly to rest in 3 s. The total distance, in m, is
qa.e: 60 m (rectangle) + ½ × 3 × 15 = 22.5 m (triangle) = 82.5 m.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The x–t graph of a real body cannot have a sharp kink.
Reason (R): A kink would need the velocity to change instantly, i.e. infinite acceleration.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Velocity changes continuously in real motion, so x–t graphs are smooth. R explains A.

qa.q: A train starts from rest with acceleration 0.5 m s⁻². Its velocity after 40 s, in m s⁻¹, is
The same train (from rest, a = 0.5 m s⁻²) covers how many metres in 40 s?
A car accelerates from 10 m s⁻¹ to 30 m s⁻¹ over 100 m. Its acceleration in m s⁻² is
A body moving with uniform acceleration has initial velocity 6 m s⁻¹ and final velocity 14 m s⁻¹ after 4 s. Its displacement, in m, is
Which equation is obtained by eliminating time from the other two?
qa.a: v² = v₀² + 2ax
qa.e: Using t = (v − v₀)/a in x = (v + v₀)t/2 gives v² = v₀² + 2ax.

qa.q: In deriving x = v₀t + ½at² from the v–t graph, the term ½at² is the area of the
qa.a: Triangle above the rectangle
qa.e: The triangle has base t and height (v − v₀) = at, so its area is ½at².

qa.q: For uniformly accelerated motion, average velocity equals (v₀ + v)/2 because
qa.a: Velocity changes linearly with time
qa.e: With constant a, v rises linearly, so the time-average is the simple mean of the end values.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): v² = v₀² + 2ax does not contain time.
Reason (R): It is obtained by eliminating t between v = v₀ + at and x = (v₀ + v)t/2.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Eliminating t is exactly how the third equation is derived. R explains A.

qa.q: A particle starts at x₀ = −4 m with v₀ = 6 m s⁻¹ and a = −2 m s⁻². Its position at t = 2 s, in m, is
Which relation remains valid even when acceleration is not constant?
qa.a: v = dx/dt
qa.e: dx/dt is the definition of velocity and applies always; the others assume constant a.

qa.q: A ball is thrown vertically upward. At its highest point
qa.a: Velocity is zero but acceleration is g downward
qa.e: The ball is momentarily at rest, but gravity still accelerates it downward at g.

qa.q: A body has v = −5 m s⁻¹ and a = −2 m s⁻². It is
qa.a: Speeding up
qa.e: a and v have the same sign, so the speed increases.

qa.q: For a = 6t (variable), a student uses v = v₀ + at to find v. The mistake is
qa.a: The equation needs constant acceleration; here v = v₀ + 3t² by integration
qa.e: Integrating a = 6t gives v = v₀ + 3t²; v = v₀ + at is only for constant a.

qa.q: A car at x₀ = 10 m moves with v₀ = 4 m s⁻¹ and a = 2 m s⁻². Its velocity when it reaches x = 22 m, in m s⁻¹, is
The equation v² = v₀² + 2a(x − x₀) can be derived by calculus using
qa.a: a = v dv/dx
qa.e: a = dv/dt = (dv/dx)(dx/dt) = v dv/dx; integrating v dv = a dx gives the result.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): A body can have zero velocity and non-zero acceleration at the same instant.
Reason (R): At the topmost point of vertical motion under gravity, v = 0 while a = g downward.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: The top of a throw is a classic example of A, so R explains A.

qa.q: A stone is dropped from rest. Taking g = 9.8 m s⁻², its speed after 2 s in m s⁻¹ is
A ball is thrown vertically upward at 19.6 m s⁻¹ (g = 9.8 m s⁻²). The maximum height reached, in m, is
qa.e: At the top v = 0: h = v₀²/2g = 19.6²/19.6 = 19.6 m.

qa.q: A ball is thrown vertically upward at 19.6 m s⁻¹ (g = 9.8 m s⁻²). The time to reach the top in s is
A ball is thrown up at 20 m s⁻¹ from the top of a 25 m tower (g = 10 m s⁻²). Taking up as positive, the equation for the time t to hit the ground is
qa.e: With origin at the top and up positive, the ground is at y = −25 m and a = −10 m s⁻².

qa.q: A ball thrown up at 20 m s⁻¹ from a 25 m tower (g = 10 m s⁻²) lands when −25 = 20t − 5t². The time to hit the ground in s is
A body falls from rest. The distances covered in the 1st, 2nd and 3rd seconds are in the ratio
qa.e: Total distances go as 1 : 4 : 9 (t²), so distances in successive seconds are 1 : 3 : 5.

qa.q: With g = 10 m s⁻², the distance a body falling from rest covers during the 3rd second, in m, is
qa.e: Distance in 3 s = 45 m, in 2 s = 20 m, so during the 3rd second = 25 m.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): In free fall, a body moving upward has an upward acceleration.
Reason (R): Near the Earth's surface, gravity gives every freely moving body an acceleration g directed downward.
qa.a: A is false but R is true
qa.e: A is false: the acceleration is g downward even while the body rises (it is slowing down). R is true.

qa.q: A car moving at 72 km h⁻¹ brakes with a uniform retardation of 4 m s⁻². Its stopping distance in m is
If the car's initial speed is tripled (same retardation), its stopping distance becomes how many times larger?
qa.e: d ∝ v₀², so tripling v₀ multiplies d by 9.

qa.q: A ruler is caught after falling 44.1 cm (g = 9.8 m s⁻²). The reaction time in s is
A train at 20 m s⁻¹ applies brakes and stops in 10 s with uniform retardation. The distance covered while braking, in m, is
qa.e: Average velocity = (20 + 0)/2 = 10 m s⁻¹, distance = 10 × 10 = 100 m.

qa.q: A stone is dropped from a 44.1 m high cliff (g = 9.8 m s⁻²). The time to reach the ground in s is
The stone dropped from 44.1 m hits the ground with speed (m s⁻¹)
A bike accelerates from rest at 2 m s⁻² for 5 s, then moves at constant velocity for 10 s. The total distance in m is
qa.e: First phase: ½ × 2 × 25 = 25 m, reaching 10 m s⁻¹. Second: 10 × 10 = 100 m. Total 125 m.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Stopping distance of a vehicle is proportional to the square of its initial speed (constant retardation).
Reason (R): Stopping distance does not depend on the braking retardation.
qa.a: A is true but R is false
qa.e: A is true since d = v₀²/(2a). R is false: a larger retardation a gives a smaller d.

qa.q: Which of these is a vector quantity?
qa.a: Momentum
qa.e: Momentum p = mv has the direction of velocity. Energy, temperature and mass have no direction.

qa.q: Which of these is a scalar quantity?
qa.a: Work
qa.e: Work is a scalar, even though it is calculated from force and displacement.

qa.q: Two forces of 6 N and 8 N act on a body. Which value (in N) can the magnitude of their resultant NOT have?
qa.e: The resultant lies between 8 − 6 = 2 N and 8 + 6 = 14 N, so 15 N is impossible.

qa.q: Why do we need vectors to describe motion in a plane?
qa.a: Position, velocity and acceleration need both magnitude and direction in two dimensions
qa.e: In 1D a sign is enough; in 2D or 3D direction can be any angle, so we need vectors.

qa.q: The notation |A| represents
qa.a: The magnitude of vector A
qa.e: |A| is the size of A, a non-negative scalar.

qa.q: A student adds 3 kg and 4 kg to get 7 kg, and 3 m east and 4 m north to get 7 m. What is wrong?
qa.a: Displacements are vectors; the resultant is 5 m, not 7 m
qa.e: Masses are scalars (7 kg is right). Perpendicular displacements combine to √(3² + 4²) = 5 m.

qa.q: Which pair contains one scalar and one vector?
qa.a: Speed and velocity
qa.e: Speed is a scalar; velocity is a vector.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Temperature is a scalar quantity.
Reason (R): Temperature can have negative values on the Celsius scale.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Temperature has no direction, so it is a scalar (A true). R is also true, but a negative sign does not decide whether something is a vector, so R does not explain A.

qa.q: A vector of magnitude 5 units is multiplied by −3. The new vector has
qa.a: Magnitude 15 units, opposite direction
qa.e: |−3| × 5 = 15 and the negative sign reverses the direction.

qa.q: A man walks 4 m east and then 3 m north. The magnitude of his displacement in m is
qa.e: Displacement joins start and end: √(4² + 3²) = 5 m.

qa.q: Two vectors A and B are equal when
qa.a: They have the same magnitude and the same direction
qa.e: Equality needs both magnitude and direction to match; the starting point does not matter.

qa.q: Which statement about displacement is correct?
qa.a: It depends only on the initial and final positions
qa.e: Displacement is r_final − r_initial, independent of the path.

qa.q: The position vector of a point is the vector
qa.a: From the origin to the point
qa.e: It starts at the origin O and ends at the point.

qa.q: A particle moves along a semicircle of radius 7 m from one end of a diameter to the other. Its displacement magnitude in m is
qa.e: Displacement is the diameter: 2 × 7 = 14 m. (The path length is π × 7 ≈ 22 m.)

qa.q: Vector A is 6 m s⁻¹ west. The vector −A/2 is
qa.a: 3 m s⁻¹ east
qa.e: Dividing by 2 halves the magnitude; the minus sign reverses west to east.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): A vector can be moved parallel to itself without changing it.
Reason (R): A vector is fully specified by its magnitude and direction.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Since only magnitude and direction define the vector, a parallel shift keeps it the same. R explains A.

qa.q: In the triangle method, the resultant of A + B is drawn from
qa.a: The tail of A to the head of B
qa.e: Place B's tail at A's head; the resultant joins the free tail (of A) to the free head (of B).

qa.q: In the parallelogram method, A + B is represented by
qa.a: The diagonal from the common tail of A and B
qa.e: With A and B drawn from a common point, the diagonal through that point is A + B. The other diagonal is A − B (or B − A).

qa.q: Vector addition being commutative means
qa.a: A + B = B + A
qa.e: Commutative means the order does not matter.

qa.q: Multiplying a velocity vector by a time interval gives
qa.a: A displacement vector
qa.e: v (m s⁻¹) × t (s) gives a vector in metres: a displacement.

qa.q: A + (−A) equals
qa.a: The null vector
qa.e: A vector plus its negative gives the zero (null) vector, which is still a vector.

qa.q: A boy walks 6 m east, then 8 m north, then 6 m west. The magnitude of his net displacement in m is
qa.e: East and west cancel, leaving 8 m north.

qa.q: Which property of the null vector is correct?
qa.a: λ0 = 0 for any real λ
qa.e: Scaling the null vector by any number still gives the null vector.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The resultant of three vectors forming a closed triangle taken in order is zero.
Reason (R): When vectors are placed head to tail and the last head meets the first tail, the resultant is the null vector.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Head-to-tail addition that returns to the start gives no net arrow. R explains A.

qa.q: Two vectors of magnitude 3 and 4 are perpendicular. The magnitude of their difference is
Rain falls vertically at 12 m s⁻¹ and wind blows horizontally at 5 m s⁻¹. The speed of the rain relative to the ground in m s⁻¹ is
qa.e: Resultant = √(12² + 5²) = √169 = 13 m s⁻¹.

qa.q: Rain falls vertically at 12 m s⁻¹ and a wind blows towards the east at 5 m s⁻¹. To keep dry, a person standing still should tilt the umbrella
qa.a: Towards the west, at tan⁻¹(5/12) from the vertical
qa.e: The rain moves east and down, so it comes from the west. Tilt into it at θ with tan θ = 5/12.

qa.q: A − B can be found by
qa.a: Adding −B to A

qa.q: Two equal vectors of magnitude 10 have an angle of 60° between them. The magnitude of their difference is
A velocity changes from 4 m s⁻¹ east to 3 m s⁻¹ north. The magnitude of the change in velocity in m s⁻¹ is
qa.e: Δv = v₂ − v₁ = 3 north + 4 west, magnitude √(9 + 16) = 5 m s⁻¹.

qa.q: Which is true for any two vectors A and B?
qa.a: A − B = −(B − A)
qa.e: B − A is the negative of A − B.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): When wind blows, rain falling vertically appears slanted to a person standing still.
Reason (R): The rain's velocity becomes the vector sum of its vertical velocity and the wind's horizontal velocity.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: The horizontal push of the wind adds a component, so the resultant is slanted. R explains A.

qa.q: The magnitude of the vector 6î − 8ĵ is
A vector of magnitude 20 units makes 60° with the x-axis. Its y-component (sin 60° = 0.866) is
A unit vector has
qa.a: Magnitude 1 and no dimensions
qa.e: Unit vectors only give direction; they are pure numbers of size 1.

qa.q: A = 3î + 4ĵ. The angle θ it makes with the x-axis satisfies tan θ =
qa.e: tan θ = A_y/Aₓ = 4/3.

qa.q: For A = 2î + 3ĵ + 6k̂, the direction cosine with the z-axis is
The sum of the squares of the direction cosines of any vector is
qa.e: cos²α + cos²β + cos²γ = (Aₓ² + A_y² + A_z²)/A² = 1.

qa.q: A force of 50 N acts at 37° to the horizontal (cos 37° = 0.8). Its horizontal component in N is

Assertion (A): A vector can be resolved along any two non-collinear directions in its plane.
Reason (R): Any two non-collinear vectors can be scaled and added to give any vector in that plane.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Using the parallelogram law with two non-parallel directions, any planar vector can be built. R explains A.

qa.q: A = 3î + 2ĵ and B = î − 5ĵ. The magnitude of A + B is
qa.e: A + B = 4î − 3ĵ, magnitude √(16 + 9) = 5.

qa.q: Two forces of 5 N each act at 120° to each other. The resultant in N is
Two forces of 3 N and 5 N act at 60°. The resultant in N (cos 60° = 0.5) is
The resultant of two vectors has the greatest magnitude when the angle between them is
qa.e: cos θ is largest (= 1) at θ = 0°, giving R = A + B.

qa.q: Two vectors of magnitudes A and B add up to a resultant perpendicular to A. Then
qa.a: A + B cos θ = 0
qa.e: tan α = B sin θ/(A + B cos θ); for α = 90° the denominator must be zero.

qa.q: A boat heads due north at 4 m s⁻¹ across a river flowing east at 3 m s⁻¹. Its resultant speed in m s⁻¹ is
In the law of sines for vector addition, R/sin θ equals
qa.a: A/sin β = B/sin α
qa.e: In the triangle of A, B and R, each side divided by the sine of the opposite angle is the same.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Two vectors of magnitudes 4 and 7 can give a resultant of magnitude 2.
Reason (R): The resultant of two vectors always lies between |A − B| and A + B.
qa.a: A is false but R is true
qa.e: A is false: the resultant must lie between 3 and 11. R is true.

qa.q: A particle moves from (1 m, 2 m) to (4 m, 6 m) in 2 s. The magnitude of its average velocity in m s⁻¹ is
For r = 4t î + 3t ĵ (SI units), the speed in m s⁻¹ is
For r = 2t² î + 5t ĵ (SI units), vₓ at t = 2 s in m s⁻¹ is
qa.e: vₓ = dx/dt = 4t = 8 m s⁻¹.

qa.q: The direction of the instantaneous velocity of a particle moving on a curved path is
qa.a: Along the tangent to the path at that point
qa.e: v = dr/dt is the limit of chords, which becomes the tangent.

qa.q: For r = 3t î + 2t² ĵ (SI units), the velocity at t = 2 s is
qa.a: 3î + 8ĵ m s⁻¹
qa.e: v = 3î + 4tĵ; at t = 2 s, v = 3î + 8ĵ m s⁻¹.

qa.q: Average velocity over an interval is directed along
qa.a: The displacement Δr
qa.e: v̄ = Δr/Δt has the direction of Δr.

qa.q: A particle has vₓ = 6 m s⁻¹ and v_y = 8 m s⁻¹. Its speed in m s⁻¹ is

Assertion (A): In uniform circular motion, the velocity at each point is along the tangent to the circle.
Reason (R): Instantaneous velocity is always along the tangent to the path of motion.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: R is the general rule; the circle is one case. R explains A.

qa.q: r = (2t²) î + (3t) ĵ (SI units). The acceleration is
qa.a: 4 î m s⁻²
qa.e: v = 4t î + 3 ĵ; a = 4 î m s⁻², constant and along x.

qa.q: v = 3t î + 4t ĵ (SI units). The magnitude of acceleration in m s⁻² is
qa.e: a = 3 î + 4 ĵ, magnitude 5 m s⁻².

qa.q: Velocity changes from 6î m s⁻¹ to 8ĵ m s⁻¹ in 2 s. The magnitude of average acceleration in m s⁻² is
For a body in uniform circular motion, the angle between v and a is
qa.e: v is tangential and a points to the centre, so they are perpendicular.

qa.q: In two-dimensional motion, the angle between velocity and acceleration
qa.a: Can be anything from 0° to 180°
qa.e: Acceleration points the way the velocity changes, which can be at any angle.

qa.q: r = t² î + t² ĵ (SI units). The direction of acceleration makes what angle with the x-axis?
qa.e: a = 2î + 2ĵ; equal components give 45°.

qa.q: For r = (t³) î + (2t²) ĵ (SI units), aₓ at t = 1 s in m s⁻² is
qa.e: vₓ = 3t², aₓ = 6t = 6 m s⁻².

qa.q:
Assertion (A): A body can have acceleration perpendicular to its velocity.
Reason (R): In uniform circular motion, acceleration is towards the centre while velocity is tangential.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Uniform circular motion is the standard example, so R explains A.

qa.q: A particle starts from rest at the origin with a = 3î + 4ĵ m s⁻². Its distance from the origin after 2 s, in m, is
A particle has v₀ = 5 î m s⁻¹ and a = 2 ĵ m s⁻² (constant), starting at the origin. Its y-coordinate when x = 10 m, in m, is
For the same particle (v₀ = 5î m s⁻¹, a = 2ĵ m s⁻²), its speed at t = 2 s in m s⁻¹ is (√41 ≈ 6.40)
A particle has v₀ = 10ĵ m s⁻¹ and a = 2î m s⁻². Its velocity at t = 5 s is
qa.a: 10î + 10ĵ m s⁻¹
qa.e: v = v₀ + at = 10ĵ + 10î.

qa.q: Why can 2D constant-acceleration motion be treated as two 1D motions?
qa.a: The x and y components of the vector equations are independent
qa.e: Each component equation contains only its own components, linked only by t.

qa.q: A particle starts at r₀ = 2î m with v₀ = 3ĵ m s⁻¹ and a = 0. Its position at t = 4 s is
qa.a: 2î + 12ĵ m
qa.e: r = r₀ + v₀t = 2î + 12ĵ m.

qa.q: A particle starts from rest at the origin with a = 6î + 8ĵ m s⁻². Its speed after 3 s in m s⁻¹ is
qa.e: |a| = 10 m s⁻², v = at = 30 m s⁻¹ (from rest, along a).

qa.q:
Assertion (A): A body with v₀ = 4î m s⁻¹ and constant a = 2ĵ m s⁻² keeps vₓ = 4 m s⁻¹ throughout.
Reason (R): The magnitude of its acceleration is 2 m s⁻².
qa.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true, but the size of the acceleration is not the reason; vₓ stays fixed because the acceleration has no x-component.

qa.q: At the highest point of a projectile's path, the velocity is
qa.a: Horizontal, equal to v₀ cos θ₀
qa.e: v_y = 0 at the top, but vₓ = v₀ cos θ₀ remains.

qa.q: A projectile is launched at 40 m s⁻¹ at 60° (cos 60° = 0.5). Its horizontal velocity after 2 s, in m s⁻¹, is
qa.e: vₓ = v₀ cos θ₀ = 20 m s⁻¹ and never changes.

qa.q: The acceleration of a projectile at the top of its path is
qa.a: g downward
qa.e: Gravity acts all the time, so a = g downward everywhere.

qa.q: The trajectory y = x tan θ₀ − gx²/(2v₀² cos²θ₀) shows that the path is a
qa.a: Parabola
qa.e: y = ax − bx² is the equation of a parabola.

qa.q: A ball is thrown at 20 m s⁻¹ at 30° (g = 10 m s⁻²). Its vertical velocity after 0.5 s in m s⁻¹ is
qa.e: v_y = v₀ sin θ₀ − gt = 10 − 5 = 5 m s⁻¹.

qa.q: For the same ball (20 m s⁻¹ at 30°, g = 10 m s⁻²), the height after 1 s in m is
qa.e: y = (v₀ sin θ₀)t − ½gt² = 10 − 5 = 5 m.

qa.q: Which assumption is made in simple projectile motion?
qa.a: Air resistance is negligible and g is constant
qa.e: Ignoring air drag and taking g constant gives the clean parabolic equations.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The horizontal and vertical motions of a projectile are independent.
Reason (R): Gravity acts only vertically, so it changes v_y but not vₓ.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Since the only force is vertical, the horizontal motion is unaffected. R explains A.

qa.q: A ball is projected at 30 m s⁻¹ at 45° (g = 10 m s⁻²). Its range in m is
A projectile is launched at 50 m s⁻¹ at 30° (g = 10 m s⁻²). The time of flight in s is
For the same projectile (50 m s⁻¹ at 30°, g = 10 m s⁻²), the maximum height in m is
Two projectiles are launched with the same speed at 25° and 65°. Their ranges are
qa.a: Equal
qa.e: 25° and 65° are complementary, so sin 2θ is the same (sin 50° = sin 130°).

qa.q: At what angle of projection are the horizontal range and the maximum height equal?
qa.a: tan⁻¹ 4
qa.e: v₀² sin 2θ/g = v₀² sin²θ/(2g) → 2 sin θ cos θ = sin²θ/2 → tan θ = 4.

qa.q: The maximum range of a gun is 2 km. The shell's launch speed in m s⁻¹ (g = 10 m s⁻²) is about
When air resistance is included, the range of a long throw
qa.a: Decreases, and the best angle is a little less than 45°
qa.e: Drag removes energy and momentum, cutting range; the optimum angle drops below 45°.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): For a given launch speed, the horizontal range is maximum at 45°.
Reason (R): At 45° the time of flight is maximum.
qa.a: A is true but R is false
qa.e: A is true (sin 2θ₀ = 1). R is false: the time of flight 2v₀ sin θ₀/g is greatest at 90°.

qa.q: A ball rolls off a 20 m high table-top cliff at 5 m s⁻¹ (g = 10 m s⁻²). The time to reach the ground in s is
qa.e: t = √(2h/g) = √(40/10) = 2 s; the horizontal speed does not matter.

qa.q: A ball rolls off the edge of a 20 m high cliff at 5 m s⁻¹ (g = 10 m s⁻²). The horizontal distance it covers before landing in m is
A plane flying horizontally at 100 m s⁻¹ at a height of 500 m drops a packet (g = 10 m s⁻²). How far ahead of the target (horizontally) should it be released, in m?
qa.e: t = √(2 × 500/10) = 10 s; horizontal distance = 100 × 10 = 1000 m.

qa.q: A bullet is fired horizontally at 200 m s⁻¹ at a target 100 m away at the same height (g = 9.8 m s⁻²). By how much (in m) does it fall below the aim point?
A bullet fired at 30° lands 3 km away. The maximum range with the same speed (sin 60° = 0.866) is about (in km)
qa.e: R = R_max sin 60° → R_max = 3/0.866 ≈ 3.46 km.

qa.q: A gun's shell fired at 30° lands 3 km away. Can the same gun, with the same muzzle speed, hit a target 5 km away by changing only the angle?
qa.a: No, because 5 km exceeds the maximum range of about 3.46 km
qa.e: No angle gives more than R_max ≈ 3.46 km.

qa.q: A stone thrown horizontally at 15 m s⁻¹ hits the ground after 2 s (g = 10 m s⁻²). Its landing speed in m s⁻¹ is
qa.e: v_y = gt = 20 m s⁻¹; speed = √(15² + 20²) = 25 m s⁻¹.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Two stones thrown horizontally with different speeds from the same height land at the same time.
Reason (R): The time of fall depends only on the height and g, not on the horizontal velocity.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: t = √(2h/g) for both. R explains A.

qa.q: A particle moves on a circle of radius 3 m with angular speed 2 rad s⁻¹. Its linear speed in m s⁻¹ is
qa.e: v = Rω = 3 × 2 = 6 m s⁻¹.

qa.q: A wheel makes 10 revolutions in 5 s. Its frequency in Hz is
qa.e: ν = revolutions/time = 10/5 = 2 Hz.

qa.q: A body moves on a circle of radius 2 m at 4 m s⁻¹. Its centripetal acceleration in m s⁻² is
qa.e: a_c = v²/R = 16/2 = 8 m s⁻².

qa.q: A stone in a circular groove of radius 0.25 m completes one round every 2 s. Its angular speed in units of π rad s⁻¹ is
qa.e: ω = 2π/T = 2π/2 = π rad s⁻¹.

qa.q: For a particle in uniform circular motion, which quantity is constant?
qa.a: Speed
qa.e: Only the magnitude of velocity (speed) is constant; directions keep changing.

qa.q: ω = 10 rad s⁻¹ and R = 0.2 m. The centripetal acceleration in m s⁻² is
The period of a body in UCM is 0.2 s. Its frequency in Hz is

Assertion (A): In uniform circular motion, the velocity of the body changes continuously.
Reason (R): The direction of motion changes at every point even though the speed is constant.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Velocity is a vector; its direction changes along the circle. R explains A.

qa.q: The centripetal acceleration of a body in uniform circular motion is directed
qa.a: Towards the centre of the circle
qa.e: Δv points inward in the limit, so a is towards the centre.

qa.q: If the speed of a body in UCM is doubled (same radius), its centripetal acceleration becomes how many times the original?
qa.e: a = v²/R, so doubling v gives 4 times a.

qa.q: Which statement about centripetal acceleration in UCM is correct?
qa.a: Its magnitude is constant but its direction changes
qa.e: Magnitude v²/R is fixed, but it always points to the centre, a changing direction.

qa.q: A car goes round a circular track of radius 100 m at 20 m s⁻¹. Its centripetal acceleration in m s⁻² is
A particle moves on a circle with increasing speed. Its acceleration is
qa.a: Neither purely radial nor purely tangential
qa.e: It has a centripetal (radial) part v²/R and a tangential part dv/dt.

qa.q: In the derivation of a = v²/R, the key step uses
qa.a: Similar triangles formed by position and velocity vectors
qa.e: The angle between r and r′ equals that between v and v′, so the triangles are similar.

qa.q: A centrifuge has R = 0.05 m and ω = 200 rad s⁻¹. The centripetal acceleration in m s⁻² is

Assertion (A): The centripetal acceleration in uniform circular motion is not a constant vector.
Reason (R): Its magnitude v²/R keeps changing during the motion.
qa.a: A is true but R is false
qa.e: A is true because its direction changes. R is false: in uniform circular motion the magnitude v²/R is constant.

qa.q: The branch of mechanics that studies the causes of motion is
qa.a: Dynamics
qa.e: Dynamics links forces to changes in motion; kinematics only describes motion.

qa.q: According to Aristotle, a body moving uniformly
qa.a: Needs a continuous external force
qa.e: Aristotle thought force was needed to maintain motion; this is called Aristotle's fallacy.

qa.q: Aristotle's view is wrong mainly because he ignored
qa.a: Friction and air resistance
qa.e: Everyday bodies stop because of friction and drag. An applied force only cancels them.

qa.q: A force is needed to
qa.a: Change the velocity of a body
qa.e: Force changes velocity (speed and/or direction); uniform motion needs no net force.

qa.q: Galileo observed that a ball rolling UP an inclined plane
qa.a: Slows down
qa.e: Gravity's component acts against the motion going up, so the ball decelerates.

qa.q: From his incline experiments, Galileo concluded that on a frictionless horizontal plane a ball would
qa.a: Move with constant velocity
qa.e: Down speeds up, up slows down, so horizontal should mean no change.

qa.q: Which of these is an example of a force acting at a distance?
qa.a: The Earth pulling a falling apple
qa.e: Gravity acts without contact. The others are contact forces.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): A cyclist must keep pedalling to move at constant speed on a level road.
Reason (R): A net force is needed to keep a body moving with constant velocity.
qa.a: A is true but R is false
qa.e: A is true because pedalling balances friction and air drag. R is false: at constant velocity the net force is zero.

qa.q: Newton's first law is also called the law of
qa.a: Inertia
qa.e: It describes the tendency of bodies to keep their state: inertia.

qa.q: The measure of the inertia of a body is its
qa.a: Mass
qa.e: More mass means more resistance to change in motion.

qa.q: Galileo's double-incline experiment led to the idea that
qa.a: A body keeps moving with constant velocity if no force acts
qa.e: With friction removed, nothing stops the ball on a horizontal plane.

qa.q: Which state needs no net external force?
qa.a: Both rest and uniform straight-line motion
qa.e: Rest and uniform straight-line motion are equivalent; neither needs a net force.

qa.q: A coin on a card placed over a glass falls into the glass when the card is flicked quickly. This shows
qa.a: Inertia of rest
qa.e: The coin tends to stay at rest while the card is pulled away.

qa.q: Bhaskara II's idea of 'tatkaliki gati' is related to
qa.a: Instantaneous motion (velocity)
qa.e: It anticipated the modern notion of instantaneous velocity.

qa.q: Why is it harder to stop a loaded truck than an empty one moving at the same speed?
qa.a: The loaded truck has more mass, so more inertia
qa.e: Greater mass means greater inertia (and momentum), so more force or time is needed to stop it.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): A body moving with uniform velocity continues to do so unless a net external force acts on it.
Reason (R): A body has an inherent tendency to resist any change in its state of motion.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: That tendency is inertia, which is exactly what Newton's first law describes. R explains A.

qa.q: A book rests on a table. The net force on it is zero because
qa.a: Its weight is balanced by the normal force from the table
qa.e: Two equal and opposite forces act on the book, so a = 0.

qa.q: An astronaut detaches from a spaceship accelerating at 50 m s⁻² in deep space. His acceleration just after leaving, in m s⁻², is
qa.e: Once outside, no force acts on him, so by the first law a = 0.

qa.q: When a bus brakes suddenly, standing passengers fall forward because
qa.a: Their bodies tend to continue moving forward
qa.e: The bus slows, but the passengers' upper bodies keep moving by inertia.

qa.q: A 0.5 kg ball moves at 8 m s⁻¹. Its momentum in kg m s⁻¹ is
qa.e: p = mv = 0.5 × 8 = 4 kg m s⁻¹.

qa.q: Momentum is
qa.a: A vector in the direction of velocity
qa.e: p = mv is a positive scalar (mass) times the velocity vector.

qa.q: A spaceship far from all stars and planets switches off its engines. It will
qa.a: Continue with constant velocity
qa.e: No net force means no acceleration: uniform motion continues.

qa.q: A cricket ball (0.16 kg) and a tennis ball (0.06 kg) both move at 30 m s⁻¹. The ratio of their momenta (cricket : tennis) is
qa.e: p ∝ m at equal speeds: 0.16/0.06 = 8/3.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): If the net external force on a body is zero, its acceleration must be zero.
Reason (R): Newton's first law states that a body keeps its state of rest or uniform motion unless a net external force acts.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Zero net force means no change in velocity, i.e. a = 0. R explains A.

qa.q: A force of 15 N acts on a 3 kg body. Its acceleration in m s⁻² is
The momentum of a body changes from 10 kg m s⁻¹ to 30 kg m s⁻¹ in 4 s. The average force in N is
One newton is the force that gives
qa.a: A 1 kg mass an acceleration of 1 m s⁻²
qa.e: 1 N = 1 kg × 1 m s⁻². The CGS option describes a dyne.

qa.q: A ball moves horizontally and gravity acts vertically on it. Gravity changes
qa.a: Only the vertical component of its velocity
qa.e: By the component form, a force affects only the velocity component along it.

qa.q: A stone is released from a moving train. The instant after release, its horizontal acceleration is
qa.a: Zero (ignoring air resistance)
qa.e: The second law is local: once released, no horizontal force acts, so aₓ = 0.

qa.q: Forces Fₓ = 6 N and F_y = 8 N act on a 2 kg body. The magnitude of its acceleration in m s⁻² is
Which statement shows that the second law contains the first law?
qa.a: If F = 0, then a = 0
qa.e: With zero force, the second law gives zero acceleration: the first law.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): A force perpendicular to the velocity of a body changes only its direction of motion.
Reason (R): A force changes only the component of velocity along the force.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: The force has no component along v, so speed does not change; only direction does. R explains A.

qa.q: A 0.01 kg bullet moving at 200 m s⁻¹ stops after penetrating 0.1 m into a wooden block. The average retarding force in N is
A 0.2 kg ball hits a wall at 10 m s⁻¹ and rebounds at 10 m s⁻¹ along the same line. The magnitude of the impulse in N s is
A force of 50 N acts on a body for 0.2 s. The change in momentum in kg m s⁻¹ is
qa.e: Δp = FΔt = 50 × 0.2 = 10 kg m s⁻¹.

qa.q: A particle of mass 2 kg moves with y = 5t + ½(3)t² and x = 4t (SI units). The force on it in N is
qa.a: 6 along y
qa.e: aₓ = 0 and a_y = 3 m s⁻², so F = ma = 6 N along y.

qa.q: Why does a cricketer move his hands backward while catching a fast ball?
qa.a: To increase the time of impact and reduce the force
qa.e: F = Δp/Δt: same Δp over more time gives less force.

qa.q: A 0.15 kg ball moving at 12 m s⁻¹ is stopped by a fielder in 0.06 s. The average force in N is
For applying F = ma to a system of particles, F means
qa.a: The net external force on the system
qa.e: Internal forces cancel in action–reaction pairs; only external forces accelerate the system.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): A large force acting for a short time can produce the same change in momentum as a small force acting for a long time.
Reason (R): Change in momentum equals the impulse F × Δt.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Equal F × Δt gives equal Δp, whatever the split. R explains A.

qa.q: Action and reaction forces do not cancel each other because they
qa.a: Act on different bodies
qa.e: To cancel, forces must act on the same body. Action and reaction never do.

qa.q: The Earth pulls a 2 kg ball with 19.6 N. The force with which the ball pulls the Earth, in N, is
qa.e: By the third law, it is 19.6 N upward on the Earth; the Earth's acceleration is tiny because its mass is huge.

qa.q: Which pair is an action–reaction pair?
qa.a: Force of the Earth on the Moon and force of the Moon on the Earth
qa.e: Third-law pairs are between two bodies, acting on each other.

qa.q: A truck collides with a small car. During the collision, the force on the car by the truck is
qa.a: Equal in magnitude to the force on the truck by the car
qa.e: Third law: forces are equal and opposite, whatever the masses. The car's acceleration is larger.

qa.q: Two billiard balls collide head-on. Their impulses on each other are
qa.a: Equal in magnitude and opposite in direction
qa.e: Equal and opposite forces act for the same contact time.

qa.q: For a system of two blocks pushed together, the force between the blocks
qa.a: Is internal and cancels when considering the system as a whole
qa.e: For the whole system it cancels, but for each block separately it must be included.

qa.q: Which statement about action and reaction is correct?
qa.a: Either force can be called the action
qa.e: There is no cause–effect order; they arise together, and gravity pairs exist too.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): When a bird flies, it pushes air downward and the air pushes the bird upward.
Reason (R): Forces always occur in equal and opposite pairs acting on different bodies.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: The wing–air interaction is a third-law pair. R explains A.

qa.q: A 5 kg rifle fires a 0.05 kg bullet at 300 m s⁻¹. The recoil speed of the rifle in m s⁻¹ is
A 3 kg shell at rest explodes into two pieces. A 1 kg piece flies off at 40 m s⁻¹. The speed of the other piece in m s⁻¹ is
qa.e: 0 = 1 × 40 + 2 × v → v = −20 m s⁻¹, so its speed is 20 m s⁻¹ in the opposite direction.

qa.q: Momentum of a system is conserved when
qa.a: The net external force on it is zero
qa.e: Internal forces cancel in pairs; only external forces can change total momentum.

qa.q: A rocket moves forward in empty space because
qa.a: It pushes exhaust gas backward and the gas pushes it forward
qa.e: Third law and momentum conservation: no air is needed.

qa.q: A shell moving horizontally at 10 m s⁻¹ explodes into two equal halves. One half falls straight down with zero horizontal speed just after the explosion. The other half's horizontal speed in m s⁻¹ is
qa.e: Horizontal momentum: m × 10 = (m/2)(0) + (m/2)v → v = 20 m s⁻¹.

qa.q: When we walk, the force that pushes us forward is
qa.a: The ground's frictional push on our feet
qa.e: Our feet push the ground backward; the ground's reaction (static friction) pushes us forward.

qa.q: Two skaters at rest push each other apart. Skater A (40 kg) moves at 3 m s⁻¹. Skater B (60 kg) moves at (in m s⁻¹)
qa.e: 40 × 3 = 60 × v → v = 2 m s⁻¹, opposite to A.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The total momentum of a shell is unchanged just after it explodes in flight.
Reason (R): The forces of the explosion are internal to the shell–fragments system.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Internal forces cancel in pairs and gravity acts only negligibly during the brief explosion, so total momentum is conserved. R explains A.

qa.q: Which set of three forces CANNOT keep a particle in equilibrium?
qa.e: Three forces can balance only if each is ≤ the sum of the other two. 7 > 2 + 3, so no closed triangle.

qa.q: A 10 kg mass hangs at rest from a rope (g = 9.8 m s⁻²). The tension in the rope in N is
qa.e: Equilibrium: T = mg = 10 × 9.8 = 98 N.

qa.q: A 20 kg mass hangs from two strings, each making 60° with the vertical (g = 10 m s⁻², cos 60° = 0.5). The tension in each string in N is
A 6 kg mass hangs from a string and is pulled aside by a horizontal force till the string makes 45° with the vertical (g = 10 m s⁻²). The horizontal force in N is
qa.e: tan 45° = F/mg → F = mg = 60 N.

qa.q: The conditions for equilibrium of a particle in component form are
qa.a: ΣFₓ = 0, ΣF_y = 0, ΣF_z = 0
qa.e: Every component of the net force must vanish.

qa.q: Two forces acting on a particle keep it in equilibrium. They must be
qa.a: Equal in magnitude, opposite in direction and along the same line
qa.e: Only then is their sum zero.

qa.q: Forces of 3 N east and 4 N north act on a particle. The third force needed for equilibrium has magnitude (in N)
qa.e: It must cancel the resultant √(9 + 16) = 5 N, pointing south-west.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): A lamp hanging from two wires is in equilibrium.
Reason (R): The vector sum of the two tensions and the weight is zero.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Zero net force is the meaning of equilibrium, and R gives it. R explains A.

qa.q: A spring with k = 400 N m⁻¹ is compressed by 0.05 m. The magnitude of the spring force in N is
The negative sign in F = −kx shows that the spring force
qa.a: Is opposite to the displacement from natural length
qa.e: It is a restoring force, always pointing back towards the natural length.

qa.q: A 5 kg block rests on a horizontal table (g = 10 m s⁻²). The normal force on it in N is
qa.e: Vertical equilibrium: N = mg = 50 N.

qa.q: Contact forces like normal force and friction ultimately arise from
qa.a: Electrical forces between charged constituents of matter
qa.e: Electrons and nuclei of the two surfaces interact electrically.

qa.q: In a massless string passing over a frictionless pulley, the tension is
qa.a: The same throughout the string
qa.e: A massless string needs no net force, so the tension is uniform.

qa.q: The normal force on a block on a surface is
qa.a: Perpendicular to the surface of contact
qa.e: It is perpendicular to the surface; on an incline N = mg cos θ, not mg.

qa.q: A 2 kg block hangs from a spring of k = 196 N m⁻¹ and is at rest (g = 9.8 m s⁻²). The extension in m is

Assertion (A): Friction and normal reaction are both components of the contact force between two surfaces.
Reason (R): Friction always acts in the direction of motion of a body.
qa.a: A is true but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false: friction opposes relative motion (or impending motion) between the surfaces.

qa.q: A 20 kg crate is on a floor with μ_s = 0.4 (g = 10 m s⁻²). The minimum horizontal force needed to just start it moving, in N, is
The same crate (20 kg) is pushed with 50 N and does not move. The friction force on it in N is
qa.e: Static friction self-adjusts to match the 50 N push.

qa.q: A block just begins to slide on an incline at 30°. The coefficient of static friction is (tan 30° = 0.577)
qa.e: At the angle of repose, μ_s = tan θ = 0.577.

qa.q: A 5 kg block slides on a floor with μ_k = 0.2 (g = 10 m s⁻²). The kinetic friction in N is
Limiting friction between two surfaces is
qa.a: Proportional to the normal reaction and independent of area of contact
qa.e: These are the empirical laws of friction.
