qa.q: Why is it easier to keep a box sliding than to start it moving?
qa.a: μ_k is less than μ_s
qa.e: Kinetic friction is smaller than limiting static friction.

qa.q: A box slides with kinetic friction 40 N. Its speed doubles. The kinetic friction becomes approximately (in N)
qa.e: Kinetic friction is roughly independent of speed.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Ball bearings reduce friction in machines.
Reason (R): Ball bearings are usually made of hardened steel.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true, but the material is not the reason; bearings work because rolling friction is much smaller than sliding friction.

qa.q: A box lies on a truck floor with μ_s = 0.2 (g = 9.8 m s⁻²). The maximum acceleration of the truck for the box not to slip, in m s⁻², is
qa.e: Static friction μ_s mg is the only horizontal force: a_max = μ_s g = 0.2 × 9.8 = 1.96 m s⁻².

qa.q: Masses 5 kg and 3 kg hang over a frictionless pulley (Atwood machine, g = 10 m s⁻²). The acceleration in m s⁻² is
For the same Atwood machine (5 kg and 3 kg, g = 10 m s⁻²), the tension in N is
A 70 kg man stands in a lift accelerating upward at 2 m s⁻² (g = 10 m s⁻²). The floor pushes him with (in N)
The same man in a lift moving down at constant speed has an apparent weight (in N) of
qa.e: Constant velocity means a = 0, so N = mg = 700 N.

qa.q: A 4 kg block on a frictionless table is tied over a pulley to a hanging 1 kg block (g = 10 m s⁻²). The acceleration in m s⁻² is
qa.e: a = m₂g/(m₁ + m₂) = 10/5 = 2 m s⁻².

qa.q: What force actually makes a car accelerate forward on a road?
qa.a: Static friction from the road on the tyres
qa.e: The tyres push the road backward; the road's static friction pushes the car forward.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): A person in a freely falling lift feels weightless.
Reason (R): In free fall, gravity stops acting on the person.
qa.a: A is true but R is false
qa.e: A is true because the floor's normal force becomes zero. R is false: gravity still acts; that is why the person falls.

qa.q: A 0.5 kg stone is whirled in a horizontal circle of radius 1 m at 4 m s⁻¹. The tension (centripetal force) in N is
A cyclist goes round a level curve of radius 3 m at 5 m s⁻¹ with μ_s = 0.1 (g = 9.8 m s⁻²). Will he slip?
qa.a: Yes, because v² = 25 exceeds μ_s R g = 2.94
qa.e: Safe only if v² ≤ μ_s R g; 25 > 2.94, so friction cannot supply mv²/R.

qa.q: The maximum safe speed on a level curve does not depend on
qa.a: The mass of the vehicle
qa.e: v_max = √(μ_s R g); mass cancels.

qa.q: For a car on a level road with μ_s = 0.6 and R = 60 m (g = 10 m s⁻²), v_max in m s⁻¹ is
Centripetal force is best described as
qa.a: The net force towards the centre, provided by real forces such as tension or friction
qa.e: It is a role played by existing forces, not a separate force.

qa.q: A car of mass 1000 kg moves on a level circular road of radius 50 m at 10 m s⁻¹. The friction force needed in N is
If the speed of a car on a curve is doubled, the friction force needed to keep it on the same curve becomes how many times the original?
qa.e: f = mv²/R ∝ v².

qa.q:
Assertion (A): A car can take a level curve at any speed if its tyres are new.
Reason (R): The static friction available cannot exceed μ_s mg.
qa.a: A is false but R is true
qa.e: A is false: v_max = √(μ_s R g) limits the speed whatever the tyres. R is true.

qa.q: A road of radius 40 m is banked at 45° (g = 10 m s⁻²). The optimum speed in m s⁻¹ is
At the optimum speed on a banked road, the centripetal force is provided by
qa.a: The horizontal component of the normal force
qa.e: With no friction, N sin θ = mv²/R.

qa.q: A track of radius 100 m is banked with tan θ = 0.1 (g = 10 m s⁻²). The optimum speed in m s⁻¹ is
On a banked road with friction, which expression gives v_max?
qa.a: √[Rg(μ_s + tan θ)/(1 − μ_s tan θ)]
qa.e: Friction acts down the slope at v_max, giving the plus sign in the numerator.

qa.q: Radius 90 m, tan θ = 0.25, μ_s = 0.6 (g = 10 m s⁻²). Note (0.6 + 0.25)/(1 − 0.15) = 1. The maximum safe speed in m s⁻¹ is
For the same road (R = 90 m, tan θ = 0.25, g = 10 m s⁻²), the optimum speed in m s⁻¹ is
Why are railway tracks on curves built with the outer rail higher than the inner rail?
qa.a: So that a component of the normal force supplies the centripetal force, reducing wear and the risk of derailing
qa.e: Banking (cant) makes N sin θ help provide mv²/R, so the rails' sideways push on the wheel flanges is reduced.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The optimum speed on a banked road is independent of the mass of the vehicle.
Reason (R): v₀ = √(Rg tan θ) contains no mass term.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Mass cancels when dividing N sin θ = mv²/R by N cos θ = mg. R explains A.

qa.q: In a free-body diagram of a body, we show
qa.a: All external forces acting on that body
qa.e: An FBD isolates one body and shows only the forces acting ON it.

qa.q: A 2 kg block rests on top of a 6 kg block on the floor (g = 10 m s⁻²). The normal force from the floor on the lower block in N is
qa.e: Floor supports both: (2 + 6) × 10 = 80 N.

qa.q: A 2 kg block rests on top of a 6 kg block on the floor (g = 10 m s⁻²). The upward force (in N) exerted by the lower block on the upper block is
qa.e: The upper block is in equilibrium: normal from below = its weight = 20 N upward.

qa.q: Two blocks of 4 kg and 6 kg in contact on a frictionless floor are pushed by 20 N applied to the 4 kg block. The acceleration in m s⁻² is
qa.e: Treat both as one system: a = 20/10 = 2 m s⁻².

qa.q: In the same set-up (20 N on 4 kg block pushing a 6 kg block), the contact force between the blocks in N is
qa.e: FBD of the 6 kg block: F_contact = 6 × 2 = 12 N.

qa.q: When applying the second law to the whole stack of two blocks, the forces between the blocks
qa.a: Cancel as internal forces
qa.e: They are an action–reaction pair inside the system and cancel.

qa.q: A horse pulls a cart forward. Which force makes the horse–cart system accelerate?
qa.a: The ground's friction on the horse's hooves (minus friction on the cart)
qa.e: Horse–cart forces are internal. The ground's forces are external.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): To find the tension in a rope joining two blocks, we draw the free-body diagram of one block.
Reason (R): Tension is internal to the two-block system and does not appear when the system is treated as a whole.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Isolating one block makes the tension external to it, so it appears in that FBD. R explains why we must isolate.

qa.q: If A = 3î + 4ĵ and B = 2î − ĵ, then A·B equals
The scalar product of two vectors is
qa.a: A scalar
qa.e: A·B = AB cos θ is a number with no direction.

qa.q: î·k̂ equals
qa.e: î and k̂ are perpendicular, so cos 90° = 0.

qa.q: Two vectors of magnitudes 4 and 5 have an angle of 60° between them. Their dot product is
Which property does the scalar product have?
qa.a: A·B = B·A
qa.e: Since cos θ is the same either way, the dot product is commutative.

qa.q: A·(B + C) equals
qa.a: A·B + A·C
qa.e: The scalar product is distributive over addition.

qa.q: If A·B = 0 for two non-zero vectors, then
qa.a: A is perpendicular to B
qa.e: AB cos θ = 0 with A, B ≠ 0 means cos θ = 0, θ = 90°.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): A·A = A².
Reason (R): The scalar product is commutative.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true, but commutativity does not explain A·A = A²; that follows from cos 0° = 1.

qa.q: Riya says she did a lot of 'work' by reading notes for two hours at her desk. In physics, work is done on a body only when
qa.a: A force acts on it and its point of application moves with a component of displacement along the force
qa.e: In physics, work W = F·d needs a force and a displacement with a component along it. Everyday 'work' (reading, effort, tiredness) is not physics work.

qa.q: A force of 10 N moves a body 5 m in the direction of the force. The work done in J is
A force of 20 N pulls a box 4 m along the floor at 60° to the horizontal. The work done in J is
F = (3î + 4ĵ) N acts on a body displaced by d = (2î + 3ĵ) m. The work done in J is
A = 3î + 4ĵ and B = 4î + 3ĵ. The cosine of the angle between them is
A man holds a 20 kg suitcase and walks 10 m on a level platform. The work done by him on the suitcase against gravity is
qa.a: Zero
qa.e: His upward force is perpendicular to the horizontal displacement, so W = 0.

qa.q: Gravity does no work on a satellite in a circular orbit because
qa.a: Gravity is perpendicular to the satellite's velocity at every point
qa.e: Gravity points to the centre, velocity is tangential: θ = 90°.

qa.q: F = 6î N acts on a body that moves through d = 3î + 4ĵ m. The component of F along d in N is

Assertion (A): No work is done when you push hard against a fixed wall.
Reason (R): Work requires a displacement of the point of application of the force.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: The wall does not move, so d = 0 and W = 0. R explains A.

qa.q: A cyclist skids to a stop over 10 m. The road's friction force on the cycle is 200 N. The work done by the road on the cycle in J is
qa.e: Friction opposes the displacement: W = 200 × 10 × cos 180° = −2000 J.

qa.q: When a ball is thrown upward, the work done by gravity during the upward motion is
qa.a: Negative
qa.e: Gravity (down) opposes the displacement (up), θ = 180°.

qa.q: How many joules are there in 2 kWh?
An electron gains 100 eV of energy. In units of 10⁻¹⁹ J this is
A force does negative work on a body when the angle between force and displacement is
qa.a: Greater than 90°
qa.e: cos θ < 0 for 90° < θ ≤ 180°.

qa.q: A 60 N push moves a crate 3 m while 40 N of friction acts. The net work done on the crate in J is
1 erg equals 10ⁿ J. What is n?
qa.e: 1 J = 10⁷ erg, so 1 erg = 10⁻⁷ J.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Kinetic friction always does negative work on a body sliding over a fixed surface.
Reason (R): Kinetic friction acts opposite to the velocity of the body relative to the surface.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Force opposite to displacement means θ = 180°, so W < 0. R explains A.

qa.q: A 4 kg block moving at 5 m s⁻¹ has kinetic energy (in J)
If the speed of a car is tripled, its kinetic energy becomes how many times the original?
qa.e: K ∝ v², so 3² = 9.

qa.q: A 2 kg body is accelerated from 3 m s⁻¹ to 7 m s⁻¹. The net work done on it in J is
The work–energy theorem states that
qa.a: Net work done on a body equals the change in its kinetic energy
qa.e: W_net = K_f − K_i.

qa.q: A 1 g raindrop falls from 1 km and lands at 50 m s⁻¹ (g = 10 m s⁻²). The work done by air resistance in J is
A body has kinetic energy 100 J and momentum 20 kg m s⁻¹. Its mass in kg is
Kinetic energy can never be negative because
qa.a: Mass is positive and v² is never negative
qa.e: K = ½mv² with m > 0 and v² ≥ 0.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): If the net work done on a body is zero, its velocity must stay constant.
Reason (R): The net work done on a body equals the change in its kinetic energy.
qa.a: A is false but R is true
qa.e: A is false: only the speed stays constant; the direction can change (as in uniform circular motion). R is true.

qa.q: Which of these has kinetic energy closest to 10⁵–10⁶ J?
qa.a: A car moving on a highway
qa.e: A car of about 1000 kg at 20–30 m s⁻¹ has K = ½mv² ≈ 2–5 × 10⁵ J. A raindrop has ~10⁻³ J, a walking person ~10² J and a gently tossed ball only a few joules.

qa.q: A force rises linearly from 0 to 20 N as a body moves from x = 0 to x = 4 m. The work done in J is
qa.e: Area of triangle = ½ × 4 × 20 = 40 J.

qa.q: Work done by a variable force F(x) from x₁ to x₂ is
qa.a: ∫ F(x) dx from x₁ to x₂
qa.e: Work is the integral of force over displacement.

qa.q: F = 3x² N (x in m). The work done from x = 0 to x = 2 m in J is
qa.e: W = ∫₀² 3x² dx = [x³]₀² = 8 J.

qa.q: On an F–x graph, F = 10 N from x = 0 to 3 m, then F = −5 N from 3 to 5 m. The net work in J is
A trunk is pushed with 80 N for 6 m, then with a force decreasing linearly from 80 N to 0 over the next 4 m. Total work in J is
qa.e: 480 J (rectangle) + ½ × 4 × 80 = 160 J (triangle) = 640 J.

qa.q: Friction on the same trunk is a constant 50 N over the whole 10 m. The work done by friction in J is
qa.e: W = −50 × 10 = −500 J; friction opposes motion.

qa.q: The work done by a spring force F = −kx when it is stretched from 0 to x is found by
qa.a: The area of the triangle under the F–x line: −½kx²
qa.e: Integrating −kx gives −½kx².

qa.q:
Assertion (A): For a variable force, work is the area under the force–displacement graph.
Reason (R): Work is the sum of small products F Δx, which in the limit equals the area under the curve.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: The area is exactly ∫F dx. R explains A.

qa.q: A 50 g bullet moving at 200 m s⁻¹ passes through a plank and emerges with 10% of its initial kinetic energy. Its emergent speed in m s⁻¹ is about
A 1 kg block with 10 J of kinetic energy enters a 2 m rough region where friction rises linearly from 0 to 6 N. Its kinetic energy on leaving, in J, is
The work–energy theorem is
qa.a: A scalar form of Newton's second law, integrated over displacement
qa.e: Integrating F = m dv/dt along the path gives ΔK = W, a scalar equation.

qa.q: A 0.01 kg bullet at 400 m s⁻¹ stops inside a block. The work done by the block on the bullet in J is
In the proof of the theorem for a variable force, the key substitution is
qa.a: F = m dv/dt and v = dx/dt, giving dK = F dx
qa.e: dK/dt = mv dv/dt = Fv = F dx/dt.

qa.q: A 2 kg block slides 5 m on a rough floor and its speed falls from 6 m s⁻¹ to 4 m s⁻¹. The average friction force in N is
A bullet emerges from a plank with half its initial speed. The fraction of initial kinetic energy lost is
qa.e: K ∝ v²: (1/2)² = 1/4 remains, so 3/4 is lost.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): We can find the kinetic energy lost by a bullet in a plank without knowing how the resistive force varies.
Reason (R): The work–energy theorem relates the change in kinetic energy only to the total work done.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: ΔK depends only on initial and final speeds, which equals the total work. R explains A.

qa.q: A 5 kg body is lifted 4 m (g = 10 m s⁻²). Its gain in gravitational potential energy in J is
A force is conservative if the work done by it
qa.a: Depends only on the initial and final positions
qa.e: Path-independence (and zero work round a closed path) defines a conservative force.

qa.q: Which force is non-conservative?
qa.a: Kinetic friction
qa.e: Friction's work depends on path and converts energy to heat.

qa.q: V(x) = 3x² J (x in m). The force on the particle at x = 2 m in N is
A ball is carried from the ground to a shelf 2 m high by two different routes. The work done by gravity is
qa.a: The same for both routes
qa.e: Gravity is conservative: W = −mgh, path-independent.

qa.q: The SI unit of potential energy is
qa.a: joule
qa.e: Like all energy, PE is in joules.

qa.q: A block is dragged around a closed path on a rough floor and returned to its start. The total work done by friction is
qa.a: Negative and non-zero
qa.e: Friction opposes motion everywhere along the path; the works add up negatively.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Potential energy cannot be defined for kinetic friction.
Reason (R): The work done by friction depends on the path followed.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: PE requires work to depend only on end points; friction fails this. R explains A.

qa.q: A 2 kg ball is dropped from 45 m (g = 10 m s⁻², no air resistance). Its speed just before hitting the ground in m s⁻¹ is
For the same ball (2 kg from 45 m), its kinetic energy at a height of 25 m in J is
Mechanical energy is conserved when
qa.a: Only conservative forces do work
qa.e: Non-conservative forces like friction change mechanical energy into heat.

qa.q: At what height above the ground is the KE of a falling ball equal to its PE, if dropped from 40 m?
qa.e: K = V means mgh = mg(40 − h) → h = 20 m.

qa.q: The derivation of energy conservation uses
qa.a: ΔK = W (work–energy theorem) and W = −ΔV (conservative force)
qa.e: Combining the two gives Δ(K + V) = 0.

qa.q: A pendulum bob is released from 0.45 m above its lowest point (g = 10 m s⁻²). Its speed at the lowest point in m s⁻¹ is
A ball thrown up at 20 m s⁻¹ (g = 10 m s⁻²) reaches a maximum height (in m) of
qa.e: At the top K = 0: ½mv² = mgh → h = v²/(2g) = 400/20 = 20 m.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): A ball dropped from a height reaches the ground with the same speed whatever its mass (ignoring air).
Reason (R): A heavier ball experiences a larger gravitational force.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true, but R alone doesn't explain A; the larger force is balanced by larger inertia, so mass cancels in mgh = ½mv².

qa.q: A stone on a 0.9 m string just completes a vertical circle (g = 10 m s⁻²). Its speed at the top in m s⁻¹ is
qa.e: v_top = √(gL) = √9 = 3 m s⁻¹.

qa.q: For the same stone (L = 0.9 m), the minimum speed at the bottom in m s⁻¹ is (√45 ≈ 6.71)
A 0.5 kg bob moves in a vertical circle with the minimum speed needed. The tension at the bottom (g = 10 m s⁻²) in N is
Why can't the bob on a string have zero speed at the top of the circle?
qa.a: The string would go slack because gravity needs a speed of at least √(gL) to keep it moving in the circle
qa.e: Tension cannot be negative; at the top mg ≤ mv²/L must hold.

qa.q: A particle has total energy E = 5 J. Its potential energy is V = 8 J at x = 2 m. At x = 2 m, the particle
qa.a: Can never be found
qa.e: K = E − V = −3 J, impossible. That region is forbidden.

qa.q: On a PE graph, a particle with energy E turns back at points where
qa.a: V(x) = E
qa.e: At turning points K = 0, so V = E.

qa.q: A bob on a 2 m string has speed √(5gL) at the bottom (g = 10 m s⁻²). Its speed at the side (height L) in m s⁻¹ is (√60 ≈ 7.75)
qa.e: v² = 5gL − 2gL = 3gL = 60, so v ≈ 7.75 m s⁻¹.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): For a bob just completing a vertical circle on a string, the tension at the top is zero.
Reason (R): At the top, the weight alone can provide the required centripetal force mv²/L.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: With v_top = √(gL), mg = mv²/L exactly, so T = 0. R explains A.

qa.q: A spring with k = 500 N m⁻¹ is compressed by 4 cm. The potential energy stored in J is
The spring constant k of a spring that stores 2 J when stretched by 0.1 m is (in N m⁻¹)
A 1000 kg car hits a spring buffer of k = 25000 N m⁻¹ at 5 m s⁻¹. The maximum compression in m is
qa.e: ½mv² = 12500 J = ½kx² → x² = 1 → x = 1 m.

qa.q: Same car (1000 kg, 4 m s⁻¹) hits a spring of k = 44000 N m⁻¹ on a road with μ = 0.5 (g = 10 m s⁻²). The maximum compression (solve 22000x² + 5000x − 8000 = 0) in m is
A 0.5 kg block on a spring (k = 200 N m⁻¹) oscillates with amplitude 0.1 m on a frictionless floor. Its maximum speed in m s⁻¹ is
The spring force is conservative because
qa.a: The work it does depends only on the initial and final extensions
qa.e: W = −(½kx_f² − ½kx_i²), independent of the path.

qa.q: A block attached to a spring moves fastest
qa.a: At the equilibrium position x = 0
qa.e: There all the energy is kinetic (V = 0).

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The work done in stretching a spring by x from its natural length is ½kx².
Reason (R): The spring force increases linearly from 0 to kx, so the work is the area of a triangle.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Area = ½ × x × kx = ½kx². R explains A.

qa.q: A boy of mass 50 kg climbs 6 m of stairs in 10 s (g = 10 m s⁻²). His average power in W is
A car engine exerts 2000 N while the car moves at 25 m s⁻¹. The power in kW is
The kilowatt hour is a unit of
qa.a: Energy
qa.e: kW × h = (J/s) × s = J, so it measures energy.

qa.q: A 1.5 kW geyser runs for 40 minutes a day. The energy used in kWh per day is
A 1800 kg elevator carries a load upward at 2 m s⁻¹ against 4000 N friction (g = 10 m s⁻²). The minimum power in kW is
Instantaneous power delivered by a force F to a body moving with velocity v is
qa.a: F·v
qa.e: P = dW/dt = F·dr/dt = F·v.

qa.q: A motor of 1 hp runs for 1 hour. The energy used in kWh is (1 hp = 746 W)

Assertion (A): Two cranes lifting identical loads to the same height do equal work, but the faster one has more power.
Reason (R): Power is the total work done by a machine.
qa.a: A is true but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false: power is the rate of doing work, not the total work.

qa.q: A 3 kg ball at 4 m s⁻¹ collides with and sticks to a 1 kg ball at rest. The common velocity in m s⁻¹ is
For the same collision (3 kg at 4 m s⁻¹ sticking to 1 kg at rest), the kinetic energy lost in J is
qa.e: K_i = 24 J; K_f = ½ × 4 × 9 = 18 J; loss = 6 J.

qa.q: Which quantity is conserved in all collisions of an isolated system?
qa.a: Total linear momentum
qa.e: With no external impulse, momentum is always conserved.

qa.q: A 0.01 kg bullet at 500 m s⁻¹ embeds in a 0.99 kg block at rest. The block's speed after impact in m s⁻¹ is
In an elastic collision
qa.a: Both momentum and kinetic energy are conserved
qa.e: That is the definition of an elastic collision.

qa.q: Two bodies of 1 kg each move towards each other at 2 m s⁻¹ each and stick. The KE lost in J is
qa.e: Total momentum = 0, so they stop; all 4 J of KE is lost.

qa.q: In a perfectly inelastic collision, the kinetic energy lost is greatest when
qa.a: The final common velocity is zero (total momentum zero)
qa.e: If total momentum is zero, the bodies stop and all KE is lost.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): In an inelastic collision, total momentum is conserved but total kinetic energy is not.
Reason (R): Some kinetic energy is converted into heat, sound or deformation, while no external impulse acts.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: R explains both parts of A: no external impulse (momentum) and conversion of KE.

qa.q: A 1 kg ball at 3 m s⁻¹ hits an identical ball at rest elastically. The speed of the second ball afterwards in m s⁻¹ is
qa.e: Equal masses exchange velocities: v₂ = 3 m s⁻¹, v₁ = 0.

qa.q: A 4 kg body at 5 m s⁻¹ collides elastically with a 1 kg body at rest. The velocity of the 4 kg body after collision in m s⁻¹ is
For the same collision (4 kg at 5 m s⁻¹, 1 kg at rest), the velocity of the 1 kg body in m s⁻¹ is
A ping-pong ball hits a stationary bowling ball elastically. The ping-pong ball
qa.a: Bounces back with nearly the same speed
qa.e: m₁ ≪ m₂: v₁ ≈ −u₁, v₂ ≈ 0.

qa.q: A neutron collides head-on elastically with a deuteron (mass 2m) at rest. The fraction of its kinetic energy it loses is
qa.e: It keeps [(m − 2m)/(m + 2m)]² = 1/9, so loses 8/9.

qa.q: Why are light nuclei (like hydrogen or deuterium) good moderators?
qa.a: Neutrons transfer most of their KE to nuclei of similar mass
qa.e: Energy transfer is greatest when masses are nearly equal.

qa.q: A 1 kg ball at 6 m s⁻¹ hits a 2 kg ball at rest elastically. The velocity of the 1 kg ball after collision in m s⁻¹ is
qa.e: v₁ = (1 − 2) × 6/3 = −2 m s⁻¹: it bounces back.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): In a head-on elastic collision of two equal masses with one at rest, the moving body stops.
Reason (R): With m₁ = m₂, v₁ = (m₁ − m₂)u₁/(m₁ + m₂) = 0.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: The formula gives v₁ = 0 and v₂ = u₁. R explains A.

qa.q: A ball hits an identical ball at rest elastically and moves off at 37° to its original direction. The other ball moves off at
qa.e: θ₁ + θ₂ = 90°, so θ₂ = 53°.

qa.q: A 2 kg ball moving at 5 m s⁻¹ along x collides with a ball at rest. Afterwards, the total momentum along x in kg m s⁻¹ is
qa.e: Momentum along x is conserved: 2 × 5 = 10 kg m s⁻¹.

qa.q: A ball moving along the x-axis strikes a ball at rest, and both fly off at angles to the x-axis. The total momentum along y after the collision is
qa.e: Initially there was no y-momentum, so the y-components cancel afterwards.

qa.q: In a 2D elastic collision, why is one extra piece of information (like an angle) needed?
qa.a: There are only three equations for four unknowns
qa.e: Two momentum components and one energy equation cannot fix four unknowns.

qa.q: A 1 kg ball at 4 m s⁻¹ (along x) hits an identical ball at rest. After an elastic collision, the first moves at 2 m s⁻¹ at 60° to x. The x-component of the second ball's velocity in m s⁻¹ is
qa.e: x-momentum: 4 = 2 cos 60° + vₓ → vₓ = 4 − 1 = 3 m s⁻¹.

qa.q: A 2 kg ball moving along x hits a 1 kg ball at rest. Afterwards the 1 kg ball moves along +y at 2 m s⁻¹. The y-component of the 2 kg ball's momentum in kg m s⁻¹ is
qa.e: Total y-momentum stays zero: p_y + 1 × 2 = 0, so p_y = −2 kg m s⁻¹.

qa.q: Momentum in a 2D collision is conserved
qa.a: As a vector, so along each axis separately
qa.e: Momentum is a vector; each component is conserved independently.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Two identical balls, one at rest, separate at right angles after an elastic glancing collision.
Reason (R): Momentum and kinetic energy conservation for equal masses give v₁·v₂ = 0.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: u₁ = v₁ + v₂ and u₁² = v₁² + v₂² together give v₁·v₂ = 0. R explains A.

qa.q: A rigid body is one in which
qa.a: The distance between any two particles remains constant
qa.e: Rigidity means fixed inter-particle distances.

qa.q: Which is an example of pure rotation about a fixed axis?
qa.a: A ceiling fan spinning
qa.e: The fan's axis is fixed; every point moves in a circle.

qa.q: In pure translational motion of a rigid body
qa.a: All particles have the same velocity at every instant
qa.e: Translation means every point moves identically.

qa.q: In rotation about a fixed axis, a particle of the body moves
qa.a: In a circle in a plane perpendicular to the axis
qa.e: Each point traces a circle centred on the axis.

qa.q: A spinning top whose axis sweeps out a cone about the vertical is an example of
qa.a: Rotation about a fixed point
qa.e: The tip stays fixed, but the axis itself moves (precession).

qa.q: The motion of a wheel of a moving bicycle is best described as
qa.a: Translation plus rotation
qa.e: The hub translates while the wheel rotates about it.

qa.q: The body of a car moving along a straight road (ignoring its wheels) is in
qa.a: Pure translation
qa.e: Every point of the car body moves with the same velocity, so it translates.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): A block sliding down a smooth incline is in pure translation.
Reason (R): All particles of the block have the same velocity at every instant.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Identical velocities for all particles is what pure translation means. R explains A.

qa.q: A 2 kg mass at x = 0 and a 6 kg mass at x = 4 m. The centre of mass is at x (in m) =
Three equal masses are at (0, 0), (3, 0) and (0, 3) (in m). The y-coordinate of their CM in m is
The centre of mass of a uniform ring is
qa.a: At its centre, where there is no mass
qa.e: By symmetry it is at the centre, even though no material is there.

qa.q: An L-shaped lamina is made of three identical unit squares placed at (0–1, 0–1), (1–2, 0–1) and (0–1, 1–2) (in m). The x-coordinate of its CM in m is
Masses 1 kg, 2 kg and 3 kg are at x = 1 m, 2 m and 3 m. The CM is at x (in m) =
The centre of mass of a uniform triangular lamina lies at
qa.a: The centroid, where the medians meet
qa.e: Dividing the lamina into strips parallel to each side puts the CM on every median.

qa.q: The centre of mass of two particles lies
qa.a: On the line joining them, closer to the heavier one
qa.e: m₁d₁ = m₂d₂: the larger mass has the smaller distance.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The centre of mass of a body may lie outside the body.
Reason (R): The centre of mass is a mass-weighted average position, not necessarily a material point.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: For a ring or a boomerang, the average position is in empty space. R explains A.

qa.q: A shell explodes in mid-air into many fragments. Just after the explosion, the centre of mass
qa.a: Continues on the original parabolic path
qa.e: Explosion forces are internal; gravity alone acts on the CM.

qa.q: A projectile has range 100 m. At its highest point it splits into two equal parts; one falls vertically. The other lands at (in m from the launch point)
qa.e: The CM lands at 100 m; one half at 50 m, so the other at 150 m.

qa.q: The acceleration of the CM of a system depends on
qa.a: Only the net external force
qa.e: MA = F_ext.

qa.q: Two skaters on frictionless ice pull each other with a rope. Their CM
qa.a: Stays where it was (if initially at rest)
qa.e: The rope forces are internal; with no external horizontal force the CM stays at rest.

qa.q: Masses 2 kg and 3 kg have velocities 5 m s⁻¹ and 0. The velocity of their CM in m s⁻¹ is
A 4 kg and a 6 kg body are acted on by external forces of 10 N and 20 N in the same direction. The CM acceleration in m s⁻² is
qa.e: A = F_ext/M = 30/10 = 3 m s⁻².

qa.q: The translational motion of a system of particles is described by
qa.a: The motion of its centre of mass
qa.e: The CM carries the 'overall' translation of the system.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): When a man walks on a boat floating on still water, the boat moves backward.
Reason (R): With no external horizontal force, the CM of the man–boat system does not move.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: To keep the CM fixed, the boat must move opposite to the man. R explains A.

qa.q: A nucleus at rest splits into two fragments of masses in the ratio 1 : 3. The ratio of their speeds (lighter : heavier) is
qa.e: Equal and opposite momenta: m₁v₁ = m₂v₂ → v₁/v₂ = m₂/m₁ = 3.

qa.q: For a system with no external force, which must be constant?
qa.a: Velocity of the centre of mass
qa.e: dP/dt = 0 → MV constant.

qa.q: Total momentum of a system equals
qa.a: Total mass × velocity of the CM
qa.e: P = MV.

qa.q: A 200 u nucleus at rest emits a 4 u particle at 2 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹. The recoil speed of the remaining 196 u nucleus, in units of 10⁵ m s⁻¹, is about
Two stars of a binary system attract each other gravitationally. With no other forces, their CM
qa.a: Moves with constant velocity
qa.e: Mutual gravity is internal.

qa.q: dP/dt for a system of particles equals
qa.a: The net external force
qa.e: Internal forces sum to zero.

qa.q: A 3 kg body at 4 m s⁻¹ and a 1 kg body at −4 m s⁻¹ (along x). The total momentum in kg m s⁻¹ is
qa.e: P = 12 − 4 = 8 kg m s⁻¹.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The products of a decay of a nucleus at rest fly off in opposite directions.
Reason (R): The total linear momentum of the isolated system must remain zero.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Zero initial momentum must stay zero, which requires opposite momenta. R explains A.

qa.q: The cross product î × k̂ equals
qa.a: −ĵ
qa.e: k̂ × î = ĵ, so î × k̂ = −ĵ.

qa.q: Two vectors of magnitudes 3 and 4 make 30° with each other. The magnitude of their cross product is
If a × b = 0 for non-zero vectors a and b, then
qa.a: a is parallel or antiparallel to b
qa.e: sin θ = 0 means θ = 0° or 180°.

qa.q: For a = 2î and b = 3ĵ, a × b equals
For a = î + ĵ and b = ĵ + k̂, a × b equals
qa.a: î − ĵ + k̂

qa.q: The cross product is
qa.a: Anticommutative and distributive
qa.e: a × b = −b × a and a × (b + c) = a × b + a × c.

qa.q: The magnitude of a × b equals
qa.a: The area of the parallelogram with sides a and b
qa.e: ab sin θ is base × height of the parallelogram.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The vector product of a vector with itself is the null vector.
Reason (R): The angle between a vector and itself is zero and sin 0° = 0.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: |a × a| = a² sin 0° = 0. R explains A.

qa.q: A wheel rotates at 20 rad s⁻¹. The linear speed of a point 0.3 m from the axis in m s⁻¹ is
The direction of the angular velocity of a wheel rotating anticlockwise (as seen from above) is
qa.a: Vertically upward along the axis
qa.e: Right-hand rule: curl fingers anticlockwise, thumb points up.

qa.q: Two points A and B on a rotating disc are at distances 2 cm and 6 cm from the axis. The ratio v_A : v_B is
qa.e: Same ω, so v ∝ r: 2/6 = 1/3.

qa.q: The angular velocity of a fan increases from 10 rad s⁻¹ to 30 rad s⁻¹ in 4 s. Its average angular acceleration in rad s⁻² is
qa.e: α = Δω/Δt = 20/4 = 5 rad s⁻².

qa.q: Which quantity is the same for all particles of a rigid body rotating about a fixed axis?
qa.a: Angular velocity
qa.e: Every particle turns through the same angle in the same time.

qa.q: ω = 2k̂ rad s⁻¹ and r = 3î m. The velocity v = ω × r is
qa.a: 6ĵ m s⁻¹
qa.e: k̂ × î = ĵ, so v = 6ĵ m s⁻¹.

qa.q: The Earth rotates once in 24 h (86400 s). Its angular speed in units of 10⁻⁵ rad s⁻¹ is about

Assertion (A): Points on the rim of a rotating wheel move faster than points near the hub.
Reason (R): Points on the rim have a larger angular velocity than points near the hub.
qa.a: A is true but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false: all points of a rigid wheel share the same ω; the rim is faster because v = ωr⊥.

qa.q: A force of 50 N is applied perpendicular to a spanner at 0.2 m from the nut. The torque in N m is
A force of 40 N acts at 0.5 m from a hinge, at 30° to the door. The torque in N m is
Torque is zero when the force
qa.a: Passes through the axis of rotation
qa.e: Then r⊥ = 0 (or θ = 0°).

qa.q: r = 2î m and F = 5ĵ N. The torque τ = r × F in N m is
A 2 kg particle moves at 3 m s⁻¹ along a line 4 m from the origin (perpendicular distance). Its angular momentum about the origin in kg m² s⁻¹ is
qa.e: l = r⊥ mv = 4 × 2 × 3 = 24 kg m² s⁻¹.

qa.q: The relation dl/dt = τ is the rotational analogue of
qa.a: F = dp/dt
qa.e: Torque changes angular momentum as force changes linear momentum.

qa.q: Why are door handles placed far from the hinges?
qa.a: A larger moment arm gives more torque for the same force
qa.e: τ = F × r⊥: bigger r⊥, bigger torque.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Torque and work have different dimensions.
Reason (R): Torque is a vector quantity while work is a scalar.
qa.a: A is false but R is true
qa.e: A is false: both have dimensions [M L² T⁻²]. R is true, but being a vector does not change dimensions.

qa.q: The total angular momentum of a system is conserved when
qa.a: The net external torque is zero
qa.e: dL/dt = τ_ext.

qa.q: Internal torques in a system cancel because
qa.a: Internal forces are equal, opposite and act along the line joining the particles
qa.e: Equal and opposite forces along the same line produce equal and opposite torques.

qa.q: A 2 kg particle moves at 5 m s⁻¹ along the line y = 4 m (parallel to x). Its angular momentum about the origin has magnitude (kg m² s⁻¹)
qa.e: l = r⊥ mv = 4 × 2 × 5 = 40, constant along the line.

qa.q: A comet goes around the Sun in an elliptical orbit. Its angular momentum about the Sun
qa.a: Stays constant
qa.e: Gravity is central, so τ = 0 about the Sun.

qa.q: A particle moves along a straight line passing through the origin. Its angular momentum about the origin is
qa.a: Zero
qa.e: r is parallel to p, so r × p = 0.

qa.q: dL/dt = τ_ext for a system is the rotational analogue of
qa.a: dP/dt = F_ext
qa.e: Torque is to angular momentum what force is to momentum.

qa.q: A satellite's momentum wheel spins faster clockwise. The satellite body
qa.a: Turns anticlockwise to keep the total angular momentum constant
qa.e: With no external torque, any change in the wheel's L must be balanced by the body.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The angular momentum of a particle moving with constant velocity is constant about any fixed point.
Reason (R): Its perpendicular distance from the point and its momentum stay the same.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: l = r⊥ p, and both factors are fixed. R explains A.

qa.q: A rigid body is in mechanical equilibrium when
qa.a: Net force and net torque on it are both zero
qa.e: Both translational and rotational equilibrium are needed.

qa.q: A couple produces
qa.a: Rotation without translation
qa.e: Net force is zero (no translation) but net torque is not.

qa.q: Two equal and opposite forces of 15 N act on a rod with lines of action 0.4 m apart. The torque of the couple in N m is
In 3D, the number of independent conditions for equilibrium of a rigid body is
qa.e: Three force components and three torque components.

qa.q: A lever has an effort arm of 1.5 m and a load arm of 0.25 m. Its mechanical advantage is
qa.e: MA = effort arm/load arm = 1.5/0.25 = 6.

qa.q: A light 1 m rod pivoted at its centre has 4 N hung 20 cm from one end. The force (in N) needed at the other end to balance it is
qa.e: 4 N is 30 cm from the pivot: 4 × 0.3 = F × 0.5 → F = 2.4 N.

qa.q: The torque of a couple about any point is
qa.a: The same, equal to F × d
qa.e: A couple's moment is independent of the reference point.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): A body can be in translational equilibrium but not in rotational equilibrium.
Reason (R): A couple has zero net force but a non-zero net torque.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Under a couple, ΣF = 0 but Στ ≠ 0, so it rotates without translating. R explains A.

qa.q: A uniform metre stick (100 g) balances at 50 cm. A 50 g mass is placed at the 20 cm mark. The new balance point is at (in cm)
A 5 m ladder (weight 200 N, CG at the middle) leans on a smooth wall with its foot 3 m from the wall. The wall's push on the ladder in N is
qa.e: Height = 4 m. Torque about the foot: F × 4 = 200 × 1.5 → F = 75 N.

qa.q: A 5 m ladder of weight 200 N leans against a smooth wall with its foot 3 m from the wall. The friction force at the floor in N is
qa.e: Horizontal balance: friction = wall's push = 75 N.

qa.q: A 1200 kg car has wheelbase 2.5 m and its CM 1 m behind the front axle (g = 10 m s⁻²). The total force on the rear wheels in N is
qa.e: Moments about the front axle: R_rear × 2.5 = 12000 × 1 → R_rear = 4800 N.

qa.q: A 1200 kg car has wheelbase 2.5 m and its CM 1 m behind the front axle (g = 10 m s⁻²). The force on EACH front wheel in N is
qa.e: Front total = 12000 − 4800 = 7200 N, shared by two wheels: 3600 N each.

qa.q: A uniform 2 m plank of 10 kg rests on supports at 0.5 m from each end (g = 10 m s⁻²). Each support pushes up with (in N)
qa.e: By symmetry, each support carries half of 100 N.

qa.q: The centre of gravity is the point where
qa.a: The total torque of gravity on the body is zero
qa.e: Gravity's torques about the CG cancel.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): A body suspended freely from a point comes to rest with its CG directly below that point.
Reason (R): Only then does the weight produce zero torque about the point of suspension.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Any other position leaves a torque that swings it back. R explains A.

qa.q: Two 1 kg point masses are fixed at the ends of a light rod 2 m long. I about a ⊥ axis through the centre in kg m² is
qa.e: Each is 1 m away: I = 1 × 1² + 1 × 1² = 2 kg m².

qa.q: The moment of inertia of a uniform disc of mass 2 kg and radius 0.3 m about its axis in kg m² is
A thin rod of mass 3 kg and length 2 m rotates about a ⊥ axis through its centre. I in kg m² is
Moment of inertia of a body depends on
qa.a: Its mass, the distribution of mass and the axis of rotation
qa.e: I = Σmr² depends on where mass is relative to the axis.

qa.q: A ring and a disc have equal mass and radius. About their central axes
qa.a: The ring has the larger moment of inertia
qa.e: All the ring's mass is at R (MR²); the disc's is spread inside (MR²/2).

qa.q: The radius of gyration of a disc of radius R about its central axis is
qa.e: MR²/2 = Mk² → k = R/√2.

qa.q: A flywheel with I = 4 kg m² spins at 5 rad s⁻¹. Its rotational KE in J is

Assertion (A): Moment of inertia is the rotational analogue of mass.
Reason (R): It measures a body's resistance to a change in its rotational motion, and K = ½Iω² mirrors K = ½mv².
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: I plays the role of m in rotational equations. R explains A.

qa.q: A motor wheel's angular speed rises from 20 rad s⁻¹ to 40 rad s⁻¹ in 10 s. Its angular acceleration in rad s⁻² is
A motor wheel speeds up uniformly from 20 rad s⁻¹ to 40 rad s⁻¹ in 10 s. The angle it turns through in rad is
qa.e: θ = ω₀t + ½αt² = 200 + 100 = 300 rad (or average ω 30 × 10).

qa.q: A fan at 30 rad s⁻¹ is switched off and stops in 10 s with uniform deceleration. The angle turned while stopping in rad is
A wheel starts from rest and turns through 100 rad in 10 s with constant α. Its α in rad s⁻² is
The main purpose of a flywheel in an engine is to
qa.a: Keep the angular speed steady because of its large moment of inertia
qa.e: Large I resists changes in ω, smoothing out uneven torque.

qa.q: A disc speeds up from rest to 6 rad s⁻¹ with α = 3 rad s⁻². The angle turned in rad is
qa.e: ω² = 2αθ → θ = 36/6 = 6 rad.

qa.q: Convert 120 rpm to rad s⁻¹ (take π = 3.14).
qa.e: 120 rev/min = 2 rev/s = 2 × 2π = 4π ≈ 12.56 rad s⁻¹.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The equation ω² = ω₀² + 2α(θ − θ₀) is valid only for constant angular acceleration.
Reason (R): Angular acceleration is measured in rad s⁻².
qa.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true, but the unit of α does not explain why the equation needs constant α.

qa.q: A torque of 12 N m acts on a wheel of I = 3 kg m². Its angular acceleration in rad s⁻² is
qa.e: α = τ/I = 12/3 = 4 rad s⁻².

qa.q: A motor delivers 50 N m of torque at 40 rad s⁻¹. Its power in W is
A constant torque of 8 N m turns a wheel through 5 revolutions (take 2π = 6.28). The work done in J is
A 20 N force is applied tangentially to the rim of a 4 kg ring of radius 0.5 m pivoted at its centre. α in rad s⁻² is
qa.e: I = MR² = 1 kg m²; τ = 20 × 0.5 = 10 N m; α = 10 rad s⁻².

qa.q: For a body rotating about a fixed axis, which torque components affect its rotation?
qa.a: Only components along the axis
qa.e: Perpendicular components would tilt the axis; the bearings supply forces to cancel them.

qa.q: A cord is pulled 3 m off a flywheel with a steady 15 N force (from rest, no friction). The flywheel's rotational KE in J becomes
qa.e: Work done = F × length = 15 × 3 = 45 J, all into ½Iω².

qa.q: The rotational analogue of F = ma is
qa.a: τ = Iα
qa.e: Torque equals moment of inertia times angular acceleration.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): A larger torque is needed to give the same angular acceleration to a body with larger moment of inertia.
Reason (R): Torque, moment of inertia and angular acceleration are related by τ = Iα.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: For fixed α, τ ∝ I. R explains A.

qa.q: A man on a rotating stool has I = 8 kg m² and ω = 3 rad s⁻¹. He pulls in his arms, making I = 4 kg m². The new ω in rad s⁻¹ is
qa.e: I₁ω₁ = I₂ω₂ → 24 = 4ω₂ → ω₂ = 6 rad s⁻¹.

qa.q: A man on a rotating stool (I = 8 kg m², ω = 3 rad s⁻¹) pulls in his arms so that I = 4 kg m². The ratio of his final to initial rotational KE is
qa.e: K = L²/(2I); L fixed, I halves, so K doubles.

qa.q: A turntable spins at 40 rpm. A child on it folds his hands, reducing I to 2/5 of the original. The new speed in rpm is
qa.e: ω₂ = ω₁ × I₁/I₂ = 40 × 5/2 = 100 rpm.

qa.q: A diver tucks in during a dive. His angular momentum (ignoring air)
qa.a: Stays the same while his ω increases
qa.e: No external torque about his CM, so L = Iω is constant.

qa.q: A disc (I = 0.5 kg m²) is spun up from rest by a 2 N m torque for 5 s. Its final angular momentum in kg m² s⁻¹ is
qa.e: ΔL = τΔt = 2 × 5 = 10 kg m² s⁻¹.

qa.q: For the same disc (I = 0.5 kg m², L = 10 kg m² s⁻¹), its rotational KE in J is
When a skater pulls in her arms, the extra rotational kinetic energy comes from
qa.a: Work done by her muscles
qa.e: Pulling in the arms against their tendency to fly out needs work.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): A skater spins faster when she pulls her arms in.
Reason (R): When she pulls her arms in, the ice exerts a large torque on her.
qa.a: A is true but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false: there is negligible external torque; Iω stays constant, so smaller I gives larger ω.

qa.q: According to Kepler's first law, the Sun is located
qa.a: At one focus of the elliptical orbit
qa.e: The orbit is an ellipse with the Sun at one focus; the other focus is empty.

qa.q: The point of a planet's orbit closest to the Sun is called
qa.a: Perihelion
qa.e: Peri = near; aphelion is the farthest point. (Apogee/perigee are for orbits around the Earth.)

qa.q: Who analysed Tycho Brahe's observations to discover the laws of planetary motion?
qa.a: Johannes Kepler
qa.e: Kepler worked with Brahe's data to find his three laws.

qa.q: The geocentric model placed
qa.a: The Earth at the centre with heavenly bodies moving around it
qa.e: Geo = Earth; Ptolemy's model put the Earth at the centre.

qa.q: A planet's perihelion and aphelion distances are 2 AU and 4 AU. Its semi-major axis in AU is
Galileo's key contribution to the study of gravity was showing that
qa.a: All bodies fall towards the Earth with the same acceleration (ignoring air)
qa.e: He showed that the acceleration of falling bodies does not depend on their mass.

qa.q: Which ancient Indian astronomer described the Earth rotating on its own axis?
qa.a: Aryabhata
qa.e: Aryabhata (5th century CE) described the daily rotation of the Earth.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): A planet's distance from the Sun keeps changing during its orbit.
Reason (R): The Sun lies at the centre of each planet's elliptical orbit.
qa.a: A is true but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false: the Sun is at one focus, not the centre.

qa.q: A planet is 4 times as far from the Sun (semi-major axis) as the Earth. Its period in years is
qa.e: T² ∝ a³: T = 4^(3/2) = 8 years.

qa.q: A comet is at 0.5 AU at perihelion and 10 AU at aphelion. The ratio of its speeds v_p/v_a is
qa.e: v_p r_p = v_a r_a → v_p/v_a = r_a/r_p = 20.

qa.q: Kepler's second law is a consequence of the conservation of
qa.a: Angular momentum
qa.e: Gravity is central, so τ = 0 and L is constant; dA/dt = L/2m.

qa.q: According to the law of areas, a planet moves
qa.a: Fastest at perihelion and slowest at aphelion
qa.e: Equal areas in equal times means larger speed when closer to the Sun.

qa.q: Two satellites of a planet have orbital radii in the ratio 1 : 4. The ratio of their periods is
The areal velocity of a planet equals
qa.e: dA/dt = ½ r²(dθ/dt) = L/(2m).

qa.q: Which quantity is nearly the same for all the planets of the solar system?
qa.a: T²/a³
qa.e: The third law says T² ∝ a³ with the same constant for all.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): A planet's line to the Sun sweeps equal areas in equal times.
Reason (R): The gravitational force on the planet is directed towards the Sun, so its torque about the Sun is zero.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Zero torque means constant L, and areal velocity = L/2m is constant. R explains A.

qa.q: The gravitational force between two masses is F. If the distance between them is tripled, the force becomes how many times F?
Two 1 kg masses are 1 m apart. In units of 10⁻¹¹ N, the force between them is (G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²)
Two masses m and 4m are 3 m apart. The force between them is F. If m is replaced by 2m, the force becomes how many times F?
qa.e: F ∝ m₁m₂: doubling one mass doubles F.

qa.q: Three equal masses m are at the vertices of an equilateral triangle. The net gravitational force on a mass M at the centroid is
qa.a: Zero
qa.e: Three equal forces at 120° to each other add to zero.

qa.q: Masses m, m and 2m are at the vertices of an equilateral triangle. The net gravitational force on a mass M at the centroid (r = distance from centroid to a vertex) is
qa.a: GmM/r² towards the 2m mass
qa.e: The three equal parts still cancel; the extra m gives GmM/r² towards that vertex.

qa.q: Gravitational force is called a central force because it
qa.a: Acts along the line joining the centres of the two bodies
qa.e: Central means directed along the line of centres.

qa.q: The minus sign in the vector form F₂₁ = −(Gm₁m₂/r²) r̂₁₂ indicates that the force
qa.a: Is attractive, pointing from m₂ towards m₁
qa.e: r̂₁₂ points from m₁ to m₂; the force on m₂ points the opposite way, towards m₁.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): We do not notice gravitational attraction between everyday objects.
Reason (R): G is extremely small, about 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻².
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: With small masses, Gm₁m₂/r² is tiny. R explains A.

qa.q: The gravitational force on a point mass placed inside a uniform spherical shell is
qa.a: Zero
qa.e: All parts of the shell pull in different directions and cancel exactly.

qa.q: The Moon is about 60 Earth radii from the Earth's centre. By the inverse-square law, its acceleration towards the Earth is g divided by
The value of G is approximately (in units of 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²)
qa.e: G ≈ 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻².

qa.q: Cavendish's apparatus for measuring G was a
qa.a: Torsion balance
qa.e: The tiny gravitational force twisted a fine wire.

qa.q: Why could Newton treat the Earth as a point mass when finding its pull on the Moon?
qa.a: A uniform sphere attracts outside bodies as if all its mass were at its centre
qa.e: By the shell theorem, each shell acts as a point mass at the centre.

qa.q: SI unit of G is
qa.a: N m² kg⁻²
qa.e: From F = Gm₁m₂/r²: G = Fr²/(m₁m₂).

qa.q: A mass is inside a hollow spherical shell, off-centre. The net gravitational force on it due to the shell is
qa.a: Zero everywhere inside
qa.e: The cancellation holds at every point inside, not just the centre.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The value of G was found only long after Newton stated his law.
Reason (R): Measuring G needs detecting the extremely small force between laboratory masses.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Cavendish's sensitive torsion balance (1798) was needed. R explains A.

qa.q: The expression for g at the Earth's surface is
qa.a: GM_E/R_E²
qa.e: Equating mg with GM_E m/R_E² gives g = GM_E/R_E².

qa.q: A planet has the same radius as the Earth but 3 times its mass. g there is how many times the Earth's g?
qa.e: g ∝ M for the same R.

qa.q: A planet has the same mass as the Earth but half its radius. g there is how many times the Earth's g?
A body of mass 10 kg is taken to the Moon, where g is about 1/6 of the Earth's. Its mass on the Moon in kg is
qa.e: Mass is an intrinsic property; it does not change.

qa.q: With g = 9.8 m s⁻², R = 6.4 × 10⁶ m and G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹, the Earth's mass M = gR²/G comes out (in units of 10²⁴ kg) about
Why do a heavy and a light ball dropped together (no air) hit the ground at the same time?
qa.a: g = GM_E/R_E² is independent of the falling body's mass
qa.e: The force mg grows with m, but so does inertia, giving the same a = g.

qa.q: A 60 kg person's weight on the Earth (g = 9.8 m s⁻²) is (in N)

Assertion (A): All bodies near the Earth's surface fall with the same acceleration in the absence of air.
Reason (R): The acceleration due to gravity g = GM_E/R_E² does not involve the mass of the falling body.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Since g has no m, every body gets the same acceleration. R explains A.

qa.q: At a height equal to the Earth's radius, g becomes
A body weighs 90 N on the surface. Its weight at a depth of R/3 in N is
A body weighs 90 N on the surface. Its weight at a height of R/2 in N is
For small heights, at what height (in km) does g decrease by 1%? (R = 6400 km)
At what depth (in km) does g decrease by 1%? (R = 6400 km)
The value of g at the centre of the Earth is
qa.a: Zero
qa.e: g(d) = g(1 − d/R) = 0 at d = R.

qa.q: At what height above the surface does g become g/9? (in terms of R)
qa.a: 2R

qa.q:
Assertion (A): g decreases as we go down into a mine.
Reason (R): In a mine, only the mass of the inner sphere below us attracts us; the outer shell exerts no net force.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: g(d) = GM(R − d)/R³ = g(1 − d/R) falls with depth. R explains A.

qa.q: The gravitational PE of a mass m at distance r from the Earth's centre (zero at infinity) is
qa.a: −GMm/r
qa.e: W(r) = −GMm/r; the minus sign reflects attraction.

qa.q: A 2 kg stone is lifted from 3 m to 8 m above the ground (g = 10 m s⁻²). The increase in PE in J is
The work needed to take a mass m from the Earth's surface to infinity is
qa.a: GMm/R
qa.e: Work = 0 − (−GMm/R) = GMm/R.

qa.q: When a body moves farther from the Earth, its gravitational potential energy
qa.a: Increases (becomes less negative)
qa.e: −GMm/r rises towards zero as r grows.

qa.q: Raising 1 kg from the surface to height R needs GMm/(2R) of work. With g = 10 m s⁻² and R = 6.4 × 10⁶ m, this is (in units of 10⁶ J)
Why can't we use mgh for raising a satellite to 20000 km?
qa.a: g decreases significantly with height, so mgh overestimates the work
qa.e: mgh assumes constant g, valid only for h ≪ R.

qa.q: Gravitational force is conservative. This means the work done by it
qa.a: Depends only on the initial and final positions
qa.e: Path independence defines a conservative force and lets us define PE.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Gravitational potential energy of a body near the Earth is negative.
Reason (R): Its zero is chosen at infinity, and gravity is attractive, so energy must be supplied to take the body to infinity.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Starting from a lower value and needing positive work to reach zero means the value is negative. R explains A.

qa.q: The gravitational potential at a distance r from a point mass M is
qa.a: −GM/r
qa.e: Potential = PE per unit mass = −GM/r.

qa.q: The number of terms (pairs) in the PE of a system of 4 particles is
qa.e: Pairs = 4C2 = 6.

qa.q: Four equal masses m at the corners of a square of side l. The PE of the system is
qa.e: 4 sides give −4Gm²/l; 2 diagonals give −2Gm²/(l√2) = −√2 Gm²/l.

qa.q: Four equal masses m are placed at the corners of a square of side l. The gravitational potential at the centre of the square is
qa.e: Each mass is at l/√2: V = 4 × (−Gm√2/l) = −4√2 Gm/l.

qa.q: The gravitational field (force) at the centre of the square of four equal masses is
qa.a: Zero
qa.e: Forces from opposite corners cancel by symmetry, although the potential does not.

qa.q: The SI unit of gravitational potential is
qa.a: J kg⁻¹
qa.e: Potential = energy per unit mass.

qa.q: Two masses of 2 kg and 3 kg are 1 m apart. Their mutual PE in units of G (J) is

Assertion (A): Gravitational potentials due to several masses must be added as vectors.
Reason (R): Gravitational potential is a scalar quantity.
qa.a: A is false but R is true
qa.e: A is false: potentials add algebraically because they are scalars. R is true.

qa.q: The escape speed from the Earth's surface is
qa.e: From ½mv² = GMm/R and GM = gR².

qa.q: A planet has the same radius as the Earth but 4 times its mass. Its escape speed in km s⁻¹ is (Earth: 11.2)
A planet has twice the Earth's mass and twice its radius. Its escape speed in km s⁻¹ is (Earth: 11.2)
Escape speed from the Earth for a 1 kg body is v_e. For a 100 kg body it is
qa.a: v_e
qa.e: Mass cancels in ½mv² = GMm/R.

qa.q: Why does the Moon have no atmosphere?
qa.a: Its escape speed (about 2.3 km s⁻¹) is so low that gas molecules escape over time
qa.e: Low escape speed lets gas molecules leak away into space.

qa.q: A body is projected from the Earth with speed √(2gR)/2 (half the escape speed). It will
qa.a: Rise to a finite height and fall back
qa.e: Its total energy is negative, so it is bound.

qa.q: Two spheres of masses M and 4M are held with centres 6R apart. The point between them where the net gravitational force is zero is at a distance from the centre of M of
qa.a: 2R
qa.e: GM/x² = 4GM/(6R − x)² → 6R − x = 2x → x = 2R.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Escape speed from the Earth does not depend on the angle of projection (ignoring air).
Reason (R): Escape depends only on the kinetic energy at launch being at least GMm/R.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Energy is a scalar, so direction doesn't matter. R explains A.

qa.q: The orbital speed of a satellite close to the Earth's surface is about (in km s⁻¹)
If the orbital radius of a satellite is made 4 times larger, its orbital speed becomes how many times the original?
Satellite A orbits at radius r and B at 4r. The ratio T_B/T_A is
For a satellite just above the Earth's surface, T = 2π√(R/g). With R = 6.4 × 10⁶ m and g = 9.8 m s⁻² (π = 3.1416), T in minutes is about
The ratio of escape speed to orbital speed near the Earth's surface is (√2 ≈ 1.41)
Mars's moon Phobos has orbital radius r and period T. Mars's mass is given by
qa.a: 4π²r³/(GT²)
qa.e: From GMm/r² = m(4π²/T²)r.

qa.q: The orbital speed of a satellite does NOT depend on
qa.a: The satellite's own mass
qa.e: v = √(GM/r): the satellite's mass cancels.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Satellites in higher orbits move more slowly.
Reason (R): The period of a satellite increases with the radius of its orbit.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true, but a longer period could also come from a longer path; the slower speed follows from v = √(GM/r).

qa.q: Which of these is a natural satellite of the Earth?
qa.a: The Moon
qa.e: The Moon is the Earth's only natural satellite. Cartosat, INSAT and the ISS are artificial satellites placed in orbit by humans.

qa.q: The total energy of a satellite of mass m in a circular orbit of radius r is
qa.a: −GMm/(2r)
qa.e: E = K + U = GMm/2r − GMm/r = −GMm/2r.

qa.q: For a satellite, the ratio K : |U| is
qa.e: K = GMm/2r and |U| = GMm/r.

qa.q: A satellite's total energy is −4 × 10⁹ J. Its kinetic energy in units of 10⁹ J is
For the same satellite (E = −4 × 10⁹ J), its potential energy in units of 10⁹ J is
When a satellite is moved to a higher circular orbit, its
qa.a: Total energy increases, kinetic energy decreases
qa.e: E = −GMm/2r rises towards zero; K = GMm/2r falls.

qa.q: Energy needed to move a satellite from orbit radius r to 2r is (in terms of GMm/r)
Which statement is correct?
qa.a: No material can shield a body from gravitational force
qa.e: Gravitational attraction acts through all matter.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): A satellite orbiting the Earth is bound to it.
Reason (R): Its total mechanical energy −GMm/(2r) is negative.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Negative total energy means it cannot escape to infinity. R explains A.

qa.q: The property of a body by which it regains its original shape after the deforming force is removed is
qa.a: Elasticity
qa.e: That is the definition of elasticity.

qa.q: Which of these is nearly a perfectly plastic material?
qa.a: Putty
qa.e: Putty stays in whatever shape it is pressed into.

qa.q: A rigid body is
qa.a: An idealisation; real bodies always deform a little
qa.e: No real body is perfectly rigid.

qa.q: Plasticity means a body
qa.a: Gets permanently deformed when the force is removed
qa.e: Plastic deformation is permanent.

qa.q: Why is elasticity important in designing a bridge?
qa.a: So that loads cause only small, recoverable deformation and no permanent bending or failure
qa.e: Designers keep stresses well within the elastic range.

qa.q: When a rubber band is stretched within its limit and released, it
qa.a: Returns to its original length
qa.e: Within limits, rubber behaves elastically.

qa.q: Which behaves almost elastically for small loads?
qa.a: A steel wire
qa.e: Steel recovers fully for small deformations.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): A lump of wet clay remains deformed after being pressed.
Reason (R): Clay is a plastic material.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Plastic materials undergo permanent deformation. R explains A.

qa.q: A wire of cross-sectional area 10⁻⁶ m² carries a load of 50 N. The stress in units of 10⁷ Pa is
qa.e: Stress = 50/10⁻⁶ = 5 × 10⁷ Pa.

qa.q: The SI unit of stress is
qa.a: N m⁻² (pascal)
qa.e: Stress is force per unit area.

qa.q: A force applied parallel to a surface produces
qa.a: Shearing stress
qa.e: Tangential force per unit area is shearing stress.

qa.q: A body immersed deep in water experiences mainly
qa.a: Hydraulic stress
qa.e: Water presses equally from all sides.

qa.q: Stress in a stretched wire is
qa.a: Tensile stress
qa.e: Stretching pulls the cross-section apart.

qa.q: Two wires of the same material carry the same load. Wire A has twice the cross-sectional area of B. Stress in A : stress in B is
qa.e: Stress ∝ 1/A for the same force.

qa.q: Hydraulic stress is equal in magnitude to
qa.a: The pressure acting on the body
qa.e: It is the force per unit area acting normally from all sides.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Stress and pressure have the same SI unit.
Reason (R): Both are defined as force per unit area.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are measured in N m⁻² (Pa). R explains A.

qa.q: A 5 m wire elongates by 2.5 mm. The longitudinal strain in units of 10⁻⁴ is
Strain has
qa.a: No units and no dimensions
qa.e: It is a ratio of two like quantities.

qa.q: Hooke's law states that within the elastic limit
qa.a: Stress is proportional to strain
qa.e: Stress = modulus × strain.

qa.q: The top face of a block 10 cm high shifts sideways by 0.2 mm. The shearing strain in units of 10⁻³ is
Hooke's law is valid
qa.a: Only within the elastic limit (small deformations)
qa.e: It is an empirical law for small strains.

qa.q: The modulus of elasticity is
qa.a: Stress divided by strain
qa.e: It is the constant in stress = modulus × strain.

qa.q: A cube's volume decreases from 1000 cm³ to 999 cm³ under pressure. The volume strain (magnitude) in units of 10⁻³ is

Assertion (A): Longitudinal strain has the unit metre.
Reason (R): Strain is the ratio of a change in dimension to the original dimension.
qa.a: A is false but R is true
qa.e: A is false: a ratio of lengths has no unit. R is true.

qa.q: The maximum stress a material can withstand before breaking is its
qa.a: Ultimate tensile strength
qa.e: σ_u is the peak of the stress–strain curve.

qa.q: The region of the curve where Hooke's law is obeyed is
qa.a: From the origin up to the proportional limit
qa.e: Stress ∝ strain only in the initial straight part.

qa.q: The stress at the yield point is called the
qa.a: Yield strength
qa.e: σ_y marks the end of elastic behaviour.

qa.q: A wire loaded into the plastic region and then unloaded
qa.a: Remains permanently elongated (permanent set)
qa.e: Plastic deformation leaves a permanent set.

qa.q: Between the proportional limit and the yield point, the material
qa.a: Is still elastic but stress is not proportional to strain
qa.e: It recovers on unloading, but the curve is no longer linear.

qa.q: The point at which the wire finally breaks is the
qa.a: Fracture point
qa.e: Point E is fracture.

qa.q: The 'permanent set' is
qa.a: The strain remaining after unloading from the plastic region
qa.e: It is the leftover deformation.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): A steel wire stretched beyond its yield point does not regain its original length.
Reason (R): Beyond the yield point, deformation is plastic.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Plastic deformation is permanent. R explains A.

qa.q: Which material is ductile?
qa.a: Copper
qa.e: Copper has a large plastic range and can be drawn into wires.

qa.q: A brittle material is one that
qa.a: Breaks soon after reaching its ultimate tensile strength
qa.e: There is little plastic deformation before fracture.

qa.q: Rubber and the tissue of the aorta are examples of
qa.a: Elastomers
qa.e: They stretch hugely and still recover.

qa.q: Which is more elastic in the physics sense?
qa.a: Steel, because it has a larger Young's modulus
qa.e: More elastic means greater opposition to deformation, i.e. larger modulus.

qa.q: Steel (Y = 2 × 10¹¹ Pa) and aluminium (Y = 7 × 10¹⁰ Pa) wires of the same size carry equal loads. The ratio of elongations (Al : steel) is about
The stress–strain curve of an elastomer
qa.a: Has no well-defined linear region, though the material returns to its original length
qa.e: Elastomers are elastic over a large range but not linear.

qa.q: Why can't glass be drawn into wires at room temperature like copper?
qa.a: Glass is brittle: it fractures before any significant plastic flow
qa.e: Wire-drawing needs a large plastic region.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): For the same load, a copper wire stretches more than an identical steel wire.
Reason (R): Copper is a better conductor of electricity than steel.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true, but conductivity is irrelevant; copper stretches more because its Young's modulus is smaller.

qa.q: A copper wire (Y = 1.1 × 10¹¹ Pa), 2.2 m long with area 10⁻⁶ m², carries 50 N. Its elongation in mm is
Young's modulus of a wire depends on
qa.a: The material only
qa.e: Y is a property of the material; ΔL depends on L, A and F.

qa.q: Two wires of the same material and length have radii r and 2r. Under the same load, their elongations are in the ratio
qa.e: ΔL ∝ 1/A ∝ 1/r²: (2)² = 4 (thin : thick).

qa.q: A wire stretches 0.5 mm under a load. A wire of the same material, double the length and double the radius, under the same load stretches (in mm)
A steel wire and a copper wire of equal length and area are joined end to end and carry a load. The tension in them is
qa.a: The same
qa.e: In series, the same force passes through both.

qa.q: In the joined wires, which one has the greater elongation?
qa.a: Copper, since its Young's modulus is smaller
qa.e: Same F, L, A: ΔL ∝ 1/Y.

qa.q: A wire under stress 2 × 10⁸ Pa shows strain 10⁻³. Its Young's modulus in units of 10¹¹ Pa is
qa.e: Y = stress/strain = 2 × 10¹¹ Pa.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): A thicker wire of the same material and length stretches less under the same load.
Reason (R): Elongation ΔL = FL/(AY) is inversely proportional to the area of cross-section.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Larger A means smaller stress and hence smaller strain. R explains A.

qa.q: A 2 × 10⁵ Pa extra pressure acts on a liquid with B = 2 × 10⁹ Pa. The fractional decrease in volume in units of 10⁻⁴ is
qa.e: ΔV/V = p/B = 10⁻⁴.

qa.q: Compressibility is
qa.a: The reciprocal of bulk modulus
qa.e: k = 1/B: easy to compress means small B, large k.

qa.q: Which state of matter has the smallest bulk modulus?
qa.a: Gas
qa.e: Gases are the most compressible.

qa.q: A slab with top face 0.01 m² and height 0.1 m (G = 10⁹ Pa) has a tangential force of 1000 N on top. The shear displacement in units of 10⁻⁵ m is
For most materials, the shear modulus G is about
qa.e: Empirically G ≈ Y/3.

qa.q: The minus sign in B = −p/(ΔV/V) is there because
qa.a: An increase in pressure produces a decrease in volume
qa.e: ΔV is negative when p increases, so the minus makes B positive.

qa.q: A glass slab (B = 3.7 × 10¹⁰ Pa) is put under 3.7 × 10⁷ Pa extra pressure. The fractional volume change in units of 10⁻³ is

Assertion (A): Gases are much more compressible than solids.
Reason (R): The bulk modulus of a gas is larger than that of a solid.
qa.a: A is true but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false: gases have much smaller bulk moduli, which is why they compress easily.

qa.q: A wire of length 1 m and diameter 1 mm is stretched by 1 mm, and its diameter decreases by 0.0003 mm. Poisson's ratio is
qa.e: Lateral strain = 0.0003/1 = 3 × 10⁻⁴; longitudinal = 1/1000 = 10⁻³; ratio = 0.3.

qa.q: Poisson's ratio has
qa.a: No units or dimensions
qa.e: It is a ratio of two strains.

qa.q: The elastic potential energy per unit volume of a stretched wire is
qa.a: ½ × stress × strain
qa.e: u = ½ × stress × strain.

qa.q: A wire stretched by 4 mm under 500 N stores energy (in J)
A wire of volume 10⁻⁶ m³ has stress 2 × 10⁸ Pa and strain 10⁻³. The stored elastic energy in J is
When a wire is stretched, its diameter
qa.a: Decreases
qa.e: Lateral contraction accompanies longitudinal extension.

qa.q: Energy density in a stretched wire can also be written as
qa.a: ½ Y (strain)²
qa.e: u = ½ stress × strain and stress = Y × strain.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Work done in stretching a wire is stored as elastic potential energy.
Reason (R): The restoring force is conservative within the elastic limit, so the work can be recovered.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Within the elastic limit, the wire gives back the energy on release. R explains A.

qa.q: For a beam loaded at its centre, the sag is δ = Wl³/(4bd³Y). If the depth d is doubled, the sag becomes how many times?
Why are girders often given an I-shaped cross-section?
qa.a: It gives large depth for bending resistance with less material and prevents buckling
qa.e: Most bending resistance comes from material far from the centre; the I-shape puts it there.

qa.q: A crane rope must lift 6 × 10⁴ N. If the yield strength is 3 × 10⁸ Pa, the minimum area (no safety factor) in units of 10⁻⁴ m² is
Why is a crane rope made of many thin wires twisted together rather than one thick wire?
qa.a: For flexibility and ease of manufacture, with similar strength
qa.e: Thin strands bend easily while together giving the required area.

qa.q: The maximum height of a mountain on Earth (about 10 km) is limited by
qa.a: The shear (elastic) strength of rock at its base
qa.e: Too tall a mountain would make the base rock flow under stress.

qa.q: Two wires A and B of the same length carry the same load. Y_A = 2Y_B and r_A = 2r_B. Ratio of elongations ΔL_A/ΔL_B is
A steel wire of length 4 m and area 2 × 10⁻⁶ m² stretches 2 mm under a load (Y = 2 × 10¹¹ Pa). The load in N is

Assertion (A): Pillars with distributed (bevelled) ends support more load than pillars with rounded ends.
Reason (R): Distributing the load over a larger contact area reduces stress at the ends.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Smaller stress at the ends lets the pillar carry more load safely. R explains A.

qa.q: A force of 200 N acts normally on an area of 0.04 m². The pressure in Pa is
Pressure is a
qa.a: Scalar quantity
qa.e: At a point in a fluid, pressure acts equally in all directions and has no single direction.

qa.q: Why does a sharp knife cut better than a blunt one?
qa.a: The same force acts on a smaller area, giving larger pressure
qa.e: P = F/A increases as A decreases.

qa.q: The relative density of a substance with density 2700 kg m⁻³ is
qa.e: Relative density = 2700/1000 = 2.7, a pure number.

qa.q: Which statement about fluids is correct?
qa.a: Fluids cannot resist shear stress and flow
qa.e: Fluids flow under any shear force; liquids are nearly incompressible.

qa.q: A 50 kg boy stands on both feet, total area 0.025 m² (g = 10 m s⁻²). The pressure in units of 10⁴ Pa is
Gases differ from liquids mainly in that gases are
qa.a: Highly compressible
qa.e: Gas molecules are far apart, so gases compress easily.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Wide foundations are used for tall buildings.
Reason (R): Spreading the weight over a larger area reduces the pressure on the ground.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: P = F/A: a larger A means lower pressure, so the soil does not sink. R explains A.

qa.q: The gauge pressure at the bottom of a 3 m deep tank of water (ρ = 1000 kg m⁻³, g = 9.8 m s⁻²) in Pa is
A diver goes from 5 m to 15 m depth in sea water (ρ = 1030 kg m⁻³, g = 10 m s⁻²). The increase in pressure in Pa is
Three vessels of different shapes are filled with water to the same height. The pressure at their bases is
qa.a: The same in all
qa.e: Pressure depends only on depth (hydrostatic paradox).

qa.q: Pascal's law states that in a fluid at rest
qa.a: Pressure is the same in all directions at a point, and same at the same level
qa.e: That's the content of Pascal's law.

qa.q: The absolute pressure at depth h in a liquid open to the air is
qa.a: P_a + ρgh
qa.e: Atmospheric pressure acts on the surface and adds to ρgh.

qa.q: At what depth in water (ρ = 1000 kg m⁻³, g = 10 m s⁻²) is the gauge pressure equal to 1.5 × 10⁵ Pa? (in m)
Why are dams built thicker at the bottom?
qa.a: Water pressure increases with depth
qa.e: P = P_a + ρgh grows with h.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The pressure at the bottom of a wide tank is greater than at the bottom of a narrow tube filled with water to the same depth.
Reason (R): Hydrostatic pressure depends only on the depth, the density and g.
qa.a: A is false but R is true
qa.e: A is false (hydrostatic paradox): both pressures are equal. R is true.

qa.q: The height of a water column that balances atmospheric pressure (1.013 × 10⁵ Pa, g = 9.8 m s⁻²) is about (in m)
1 atm equals how many torr?
qa.e: 1 atm = 760 mm Hg = 760 torr.

qa.q: An open-tube mercury manometer shows a level difference of 20 cm. The gauge pressure (ρ = 13.6 × 10³ kg m⁻³, g = 10 m s⁻²) in Pa is
Gauge pressure is
qa.a: The pressure above atmospheric pressure
qa.e: P_gauge = P − P_a.

qa.q: As we go higher in the atmosphere, the pressure
qa.a: Decreases
qa.e: Less air above means less weight pressing down.

qa.q: In a mercury barometer, the space above the mercury column is
qa.a: Nearly a vacuum
qa.e: It is the Torricellian vacuum (only a trace of mercury vapour).

qa.q: A tyre gauge reads 2 × 10⁵ Pa (gauge). If atmospheric pressure is 1 × 10⁵ Pa, the absolute pressure in units of 10⁵ Pa is
qa.e: Absolute = gauge + atmospheric = 3 × 10⁵ Pa.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): A barometer made with water would need a much taller tube than one made with mercury.
Reason (R): Water's density is about 1/13.6 of mercury's, so the column must be about 13.6 times taller.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: P_a = ρgh: smaller ρ needs larger h. R explains A.

qa.q: A hydraulic lift has pistons of areas 0.01 m² and 0.5 m². A force of 100 N on the small piston can lift a load (in N) of
The pistons of a hydraulic press have diameters 2 cm and 20 cm. The force multiplication is
qa.e: Area ratio = (20/2)² = 100.

qa.q: In a hydraulic lift, compared with the large piston, the small piston
qa.a: Moves through a larger distance
qa.e: Volume pushed in = volume pushed up: A₁d₁ = A₂d₂.

qa.q: Hydraulic machines are based on
qa.a: Pascal's law of transmission of pressure
qa.e: Pressure in an enclosed fluid is transmitted undiminished.

qa.q: A 1200 kg car rests on a piston of area 0.4 m². The pressure needed in the oil (g = 10 m s⁻²) in Pa is
The force on a small rectangular area 1 m² of a dam wall at 20 m depth (ρ = 1000 kg m⁻³, g = 10 m s⁻², gauge pressure only) in N is
qa.e: P = ρgh = 2 × 10⁵ Pa; F = P × A = 2 × 10⁵ N.

qa.q: When the brake pedal of a car is pressed, the brake force at the wheels is larger than the pedal force because
qa.a: The wheel pistons have a larger area than the master cylinder piston
qa.e: Same pressure, larger area, larger force.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): A hydraulic lift can multiply force but not energy.
Reason (R): The small piston moves through a correspondingly larger distance, so F₁d₁ = F₂d₂ (ideal).
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Work in equals work out; only force is traded for distance. R explains A.

qa.q: A pipe narrows from radius 4 cm to radius 2 cm. If water enters at 1 m s⁻¹, it leaves the narrow part at (in m s⁻¹)
qa.e: A ∝ r²: area falls by 4, so speed rises by 4.

qa.q: The equation of continuity is a consequence of conservation of
qa.a: Mass
qa.e: Mass entering per second = mass leaving per second.

qa.q: In streamline flow, streamlines
qa.a: Never cross each other
qa.e: If they crossed, a particle at that point would have two velocities.

qa.q: Water flows through a hose of area 2 × 10⁻⁴ m² at 5 m s⁻¹. The volume flow rate in litres per second is
qa.e: Av = 10⁻³ m³ s⁻¹ = 1 L s⁻¹.

qa.q: Turbulent flow begins when
qa.a: The flow speed exceeds a critical value
qa.e: Above the critical speed, flow becomes irregular with eddies.

qa.q: Where streamlines in a flow come closer together, the fluid speed is
qa.a: Higher
qa.e: Closer streamlines mean a narrower flow tube, so v is larger.

qa.q: A river 40 m wide flows at 1.5 m s⁻¹. It enters a gorge 10 m wide with the same depth. The speed in the gorge in m s⁻¹ is
qa.e: Av constant: 40 × 1.5 = 10 × v → v = 6 m s⁻¹.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Water comes out faster when you partly close the mouth of a hose with your thumb.
Reason (R): Water is highly compressible.
qa.a: A is true but R is false
qa.e: A is true (Av = constant). R is false: water is nearly incompressible, which is why the continuity equation applies.

qa.q: Bernoulli's principle is based on the conservation of
qa.a: Energy
qa.e: It comes from the work–energy theorem applied to a fluid.

qa.q: Air flows over a roof at 30 m s⁻¹ while inside air is still (ρ = 1.2 kg m⁻³). The pressure difference in Pa is
Water flows horizontally from a 4 cm² section at 1 m s⁻¹ into a 1 cm² section (ρ = 1000 kg m⁻³). The pressure drop in Pa is
Bernoulli's equation applies strictly to
qa.a: Steady, incompressible, non-viscous flow
qa.e: These are its assumptions.

qa.q: For a liquid at rest, Bernoulli's equation reduces to
qa.a: P₁ − P₂ = ρg(h₂ − h₁)
qa.e: With v = 0, only pressure and height terms remain.

qa.q: The term ½ρv² in Bernoulli's equation represents
qa.a: Kinetic energy per unit volume
qa.e: ½mv² divided by volume gives ½ρv².

qa.q: During a strong storm, roofs are often lifted off because
qa.a: Fast wind above reduces pressure there, while the pressure inside stays higher
qa.e: The pressure difference pushes the roof upward.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Bernoulli's equation does not hold exactly for a real liquid like honey flowing in a pipe.
Reason (R): Bernoulli's equation ignores viscous energy losses.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Honey is very viscous, so energy is lost to internal friction. R explains A.

qa.q: Water flows out of a small hole 3.2 m below the surface of an open tank (g = 10 m s⁻²). The speed of efflux in m s⁻¹ is
Torricelli's law says the speed of efflux equals
qa.a: The speed of a body falling freely through the same height
qa.e: v = √(2gh), same as free fall from h.

qa.q: Air moves over a wing at 60 m s⁻¹ and under it at 50 m s⁻¹ (ρ = 1.2 kg m⁻³). The pressure difference in Pa is
A spinning ball curves in flight. This is called
qa.a: The Magnus effect
qa.e: Spin creates a pressure difference across the ball (dynamic lift).

qa.q: When you blow over the top of a paper strip held below your lips, the strip
qa.a: Rises
qa.e: Faster air above lowers the pressure there; higher pressure below lifts it.

qa.q: The lift on an aircraft wing arises mainly because
qa.a: Air flows faster over the top surface, lowering pressure there
qa.e: Bernoulli: faster flow above means lower pressure above.

qa.q: The pressure difference across a 25 m² wing is 400 Pa. The lift force in N is

Assertion (A): In an atomiser, liquid rises up the tube when air is blown across its top.
Reason (R): Fast-moving air at the top of the tube has lower pressure than the air pressing on the liquid surface below.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: The pressure difference pushes liquid up and into the air stream. R explains A.

qa.q: The SI unit of the coefficient of viscosity is
qa.a: Pa s
qa.e: η = (F/A)/(v/l): (N m⁻²)/(s⁻¹) = Pa s. Poise is the CGS unit.
