qa.q: A plate of area 0.2 m² moves at 0.4 m s⁻¹ over a 2 mm layer of liquid with η = 0.5 Pa s. The viscous force in N is
When a liquid is heated, its viscosity
qa.a: Decreases
qa.e: Molecules move apart and slide more easily.

qa.q: When a gas is heated, its viscosity
qa.a: Increases
qa.e: Faster molecules transfer more momentum between layers.

qa.q: 2 poise in SI units (Pa s) is
qa.e: 1 poise = 0.1 Pa s.

qa.q: In laminar flow of a liquid over a fixed surface, the layer in contact with the surface
qa.a: Is at rest
qa.e: The bottom layer sticks to the surface; speed increases away from it.

qa.q: A plate (area 0.05 m²) is dragged at 0.1 m s⁻¹ over a 0.5 mm oil film by a 1 N force. The viscosity in Pa s is

Assertion (A): Honey flows more easily when warmed.
Reason (R): The viscosity of gases increases with temperature.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true, but the gas rule doesn't explain honey; liquids' viscosity decreases on heating.

qa.q: Stokes' law for the viscous drag on a small sphere is
qa.a: F = 6πηav
qa.e: Drag ∝ η, a and v with factor 6π.

qa.q: Terminal velocity of a falling sphere is proportional to
qa.a: The square of its radius
qa.e: v_t = 2a²(ρ − σ)g/(9η).

qa.q: At terminal velocity, the net force on the falling body is
qa.a: Zero
qa.e: Weight is balanced by buoyancy plus drag, so acceleration is zero.

qa.q: A raindrop of radius 0.2 mm has terminal velocity 4 m s⁻¹. A drop of radius 0.1 mm (same conditions) has terminal velocity (m s⁻¹)
An air bubble in water moves upward because
qa.a: Its density is less than that of water, so (ρ − σ) is negative
qa.e: Buoyancy exceeds its weight; the 'terminal velocity' points upward.

qa.q: A sphere (ρ = 8000 kg m⁻³, a = 1 mm) falls through oil (σ = 800 kg m⁻³, η = 0.8 Pa s), g = 10 m s⁻². Its terminal velocity in cm s⁻¹ is
The viscous drag on a 1 mm radius ball moving at 0.02 m s⁻¹ in oil of η = 0.8 Pa s is (take 6π ≈ 18.85), in units of 10⁻⁴ N

Assertion (A): Big raindrops fall faster than small ones.
Reason (R): Terminal velocity is proportional to the square of the drop's radius.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: v_t ∝ a², so larger drops reach higher terminal speeds. R explains A.

qa.q: A wire frame has a slider of length 5 cm holding a soap film of S = 0.04 N m⁻¹. The force on the slider in units of 10⁻³ N is
The SI unit of surface tension is
qa.a: N m⁻¹
qa.e: Force per unit length.

qa.q: Surface tension of water as temperature rises
qa.a: Decreases
qa.e: Molecular attractions weaken as thermal motion grows.

qa.q: Work done to increase the area of a soap film (S = 0.03 N m⁻¹) from 10 cm² to 40 cm² (each surface) in units of 10⁻⁴ J is
qa.e: ΔA = 30 cm² = 3 × 10⁻³ m² per surface; W = S × 2ΔA = 0.03 × 6 × 10⁻³ = 1.8 × 10⁻⁴ J.

qa.q: Surface energy per unit area of a liquid is numerically equal to its
qa.a: Surface tension
qa.e: S = energy per unit area = force per unit length.

qa.q: A molecule at the surface of a liquid has
qa.a: More energy than a molecule inside
qa.e: It lacks neighbours on the outside, so it is in a higher-energy state.

qa.q: Why do small liquid drops take a spherical shape?
qa.a: A sphere has the smallest surface area for a given volume, minimising surface energy
qa.e: Surface tension tends to minimise the surface area.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): A needle placed gently on water can float even though steel is denser than water.
Reason (R): The surface of water acts like a stretched membrane due to surface tension.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Surface tension forces support the needle's small weight. R explains A.

qa.q: A liquid wets a solid surface when the angle of contact is
qa.a: Less than 90°
qa.e: An acute angle means the liquid spreads.

qa.q: The angle of contact of mercury with glass is
qa.a: Obtuse
qa.e: Mercury does not wet glass; θ ≈ 140°.

qa.q: With S_sa = 0.06, S_sl = 0.03 and S_la = 0.06 (all N m⁻¹), cos θ is
Why do detergents help in washing clothes?
qa.a: They lower the angle of contact so water wets the fabric and grease better
qa.e: Smaller θ means better wetting and penetration into fibres.

qa.q: Water forms beads on a lotus leaf because
qa.a: The angle of contact is obtuse
qa.e: Water does not wet the waxy, rough leaf surface.

qa.q: If S_sl > S_sa, the angle of contact is
qa.a: Obtuse
qa.e: cos θ = (S_sa − S_sl)/S_la < 0.

qa.q: The angle of contact is measured
qa.a: Inside the liquid, between the solid surface and the tangent to the liquid surface
qa.e: That is the standard definition.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Water rises in a clean glass capillary but mercury is depressed.
Reason (R): Water's contact angle with glass is acute, while mercury's is obtuse.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: The sign of cos θ decides rise or fall (h = 2S cos θ/ρgr). R explains A.

qa.q: The excess pressure inside a soap bubble of radius 2 cm (S = 0.03 N m⁻¹) in Pa is
The excess pressure inside an air bubble of radius 0.1 mm in water (S = 0.07 N m⁻¹) in Pa is
qa.e: One surface: ΔP = 2S/r = 0.14/10⁻⁴ = 1400 Pa.

qa.q: Water rises 3 cm in a capillary tube. In a tube of half the radius, it would rise (in cm)
qa.e: h ∝ 1/r: half the radius gives twice the rise.

qa.q: Mercury in a glass capillary
qa.a: Is depressed below the outside level
qa.e: Its contact angle is obtuse, so cos θ < 0 and h is negative.

qa.q: Water (S = 0.072 N m⁻¹, θ = 0°) in a glass tube of radius 0.3 mm (ρ = 1000 kg m⁻³, g = 9.8 m s⁻²) rises by about (in cm)
Two soap bubbles of different sizes are connected by a tube. Air flows
qa.a: From the smaller bubble to the larger one
qa.e: The smaller bubble has larger excess pressure (4S/r), so air moves to the larger one.

qa.q: A soap bubble has two surfaces, so its excess pressure is
qa.a: 4S/r
qa.e: Each surface contributes 2S/r.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Water rises higher in a narrower capillary tube.
Reason (R): Capillary rise is directly proportional to the radius of the tube.
qa.a: A is true but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false: h = 2S cos θ/(ρgr) is inversely proportional to r.

qa.q: Heat is best defined as
qa.a: Energy transferred because of a temperature difference
qa.e: Heat is energy in transit due to a temperature difference.

qa.q: The SI unit of temperature is
qa.a: kelvin
qa.e: The kelvin is the SI base unit of temperature.

qa.q: Two bodies are in thermal equilibrium when they have the same
qa.a: Temperature
qa.e: Equal temperatures mean no net heat flows.

qa.q: A hot iron ball is dropped into cold water. Heat flows
qa.a: From the ball to the water until temperatures equalise
qa.e: Heat goes from higher to lower temperature.

qa.q: A bucket of water at 40 °C and a cup of water at 80 °C. Which statement is correct?
qa.a: The cup is at the higher temperature, though the bucket may hold more internal energy
qa.e: Temperature is intensive; total energy depends on amount.

qa.q: The SI unit of heat is
qa.a: joule
qa.e: Heat is energy, measured in joules (calorie is an older unit).

qa.q: Why do we need to distinguish heat from temperature?
qa.a: Equal heat can produce different temperature rises in different bodies
qa.e: The temperature rise depends on mass and material too.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): When two bodies at different temperatures are in contact, heat flows until their temperatures become equal.
Reason (R): Heat transfer occurs only because of a temperature difference.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Once the difference vanishes, the cause of heat flow vanishes. R explains A.

qa.q: Convert 25 °C to °F.
Convert 104 °F to °C.
At what temperature do the Celsius and Fahrenheit scales give the same reading?
The number of divisions between the ice point and steam point on the Fahrenheit scale is
qa.e: 212 − 32 = 180 divisions.

qa.q: A temperature change of 10 °C equals a change of (in °F)
qa.e: A change of 1 °C equals 9/5 °F, so 10 °C → 18 °F (the 32 does not enter for differences).

qa.q: A thermometer works because
qa.a: Some physical property of a substance changes regularly with temperature
qa.e: Expansion of liquids or gas pressure changes predictably with temperature.

qa.q: A faulty thermometer reads 5° at the ice point and 95° at the steam point. When it reads 50°, the true temperature in °C is

Assertion (A): The relation between Celsius and Fahrenheit temperatures is linear.
Reason (R): Both scales are defined using the same two fixed points with uniform divisions between them.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Uniform scales with common fixed points must be linearly related. R explains A.

qa.q: Absolute zero on the Celsius scale is
qa.e: Extrapolated P = 0 for a constant-volume gas thermometer.

qa.q: A temperature of 47 °C in kelvin (using 273) is
A gas occupies 2 L at 300 K. At constant pressure, its volume at 450 K (in L) is
At constant temperature, the pressure of a gas is doubled. Its volume becomes
qa.a: Half
qa.e: Boyle's law: PV = constant.

qa.q: Number of moles in a gas with P = 8.31 × 10⁵ Pa, V = 0.003 m³ at T = 300 K (R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹) is
The size of one kelvin compared with one Celsius degree is
qa.a: The same
qa.e: T = t + 273.15 just shifts the zero.

qa.q: The standard fixed point of the kelvin scale is the
qa.a: Triple point of water, 273.16 K
qa.e: At the triple point, ice, water and vapour coexist at a unique temperature.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): A constant-volume gas thermometer can be used to define absolute zero.
Reason (R): At low densities, the pressure of any gas at constant volume varies linearly with temperature, extrapolating to zero at the same temperature.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: All gases give the same intercept, −273.15 °C. R explains A.

qa.q: A 2 m aluminium rod (α = 2.5 × 10⁻⁵ K⁻¹) is heated from 20 °C to 120 °C. Its increase in length in mm is
For an isotropic solid with linear expansion coefficient α, the volume expansion coefficient is
qa.a: 3α
qa.e: V = L³ → ΔV/V = 3ΔL/L.

qa.q: A circular hole in a metal plate is heated. The hole's diameter
qa.a: Increases
qa.e: The plate expands uniformly, like a photographic enlargement; the hole grows too.

qa.q: A metal sheet has α = 2 × 10⁻⁵ K⁻¹. Its area expansion coefficient in units of 10⁻⁵ K⁻¹ is
A steel tape calibrated at 20 °C is used at 40 °C to measure a length. Its readings will be
qa.a: Slightly smaller than the true length
qa.e: The tape's markings spread apart when hot, so each 'metre' on it is longer and fewer fit along the object.

qa.q: A copper cube's side increases by 0.1% on heating. Its volume increases by about
The SI unit of the coefficient of linear expansion is
qa.a: K⁻¹
qa.e: α = ΔL/(LΔT): m/(m K) = K⁻¹.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): For an isotropic solid, α_V = 3α.
Reason (R): The coefficient of linear expansion is measured in K⁻¹.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true, but the unit does not explain the factor 3; equal expansion in three directions does.

qa.q: Water has its maximum density at a temperature (in °C) of
qa.e: Between 0 and 4 °C water contracts on heating; above 4 °C it expands.

qa.q: The coefficient of volume expansion of an ideal gas at constant pressure at 0 °C (273 K) is about (in units of 10⁻³ K⁻¹)
When water is heated from 0 °C to 4 °C, its volume
qa.a: Decreases
qa.e: This is the anomalous expansion of water.

qa.q: Fish survive in frozen lakes because
qa.a: Ice forms on top and insulates the water below, which stays near 4 °C
qa.e: Ice is less dense, floats, and is a poor conductor of heat.

qa.q: For an ideal gas at constant pressure, α_V at 300 K compared with 150 K is
qa.a: Half as large
qa.e: α_V = 1/T decreases as T rises.

qa.q: Which expands most for the same rise in temperature?
qa.a: A gas at constant pressure
qa.e: Gases have α_V of order 10⁻³ K⁻¹, much larger than solids and liquids.

qa.q: Water at 2 °C is heated to 3 °C. Its density
qa.a: Increases
qa.e: Volume decreases between 0 °C and 4 °C, so density rises.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): A lake freezes from the top rather than the bottom.
Reason (R): Water has its maximum density at 0 °C.
qa.a: A is true but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false: water is densest at 4 °C; below that it gets lighter and stays on top.

qa.q: A steel rod (Y = 2 × 10¹¹ Pa, α = 1.2 × 10⁻⁵ K⁻¹) is clamped and heated by 40 K. The thermal stress in units of 10⁷ Pa is
Thermal stress in a rod clamped at its ends depends on
qa.a: Y, α and ΔT
qa.e: Stress = YαΔT; the length cancels.

qa.q: A bimetallic strip bends on heating because
qa.a: Its two metals have different coefficients of expansion
qa.e: One metal expands more, so the strip curves towards the other.

qa.q: Gaps are left between sections of railway tracks to
qa.a: Allow for expansion in hot weather
qa.e: Without gaps, thermal stress could buckle the rails.

qa.q: A bimetallic strip of brass and iron is heated. Brass has the larger α. The strip bends with
qa.a: Brass on the outer (convex) side
qa.e: Brass expands more, so it ends up on the longer, outer curve.

qa.q: A rod with Y = 10¹¹ Pa, α = 10⁻⁵ K⁻¹ and area 2 × 10⁻⁴ m² is clamped and heated by 100 K. The force on the clamps in N is
An iron rim is heated before being fitted onto a wooden cart wheel because
qa.a: It expands and slips on easily, then shrinks and grips tightly on cooling
qa.e: Thermal contraction on cooling gives a tight fit.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): A thick glass tumbler may crack when boiling water is poured into it.
Reason (R): The inner surface expands more than the outer surface, producing thermal stress.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Unequal expansion strains the glass, and glass is brittle. R explains A.

qa.q: How much heat is needed to raise 0.5 kg of aluminium (s = 900 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) by 40 K? (in J)
A body absorbs 6000 J and its temperature rises by 15 K. Its heat capacity in J K⁻¹ is
For a gas, C_p is greater than C_v because
qa.a: At constant pressure, part of the heat does work as the gas expands
qa.e: At constant V no work is done, so all heat raises U; at constant P some goes into work.

qa.q: Why is water used as a coolant in car radiators?
qa.a: Its high specific heat lets it absorb much heat with a small temperature rise
qa.e: Large s means lots of heat absorbed per degree.

qa.q: Specific heat capacity depends on
qa.a: The nature of the substance (and slightly on temperature)
qa.e: It is per unit mass, so it is a property of the material.

qa.q: Equal masses of water (s = 4186) and copper (s = 386) receive the same heat. The ratio of temperature rise (copper : water) is about
2 mol of a gas need 498.6 J to rise by 10 K at constant pressure. Its molar specific heat C_p in J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ is

Assertion (A): Coastal areas have milder climates than inland areas.
Reason (R): Water has a high specific heat capacity, so the sea warms and cools slowly.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: The sea acts as a heat reservoir, smoothing temperature swings. R explains A.

qa.q: 0.5 kg of water at 90 °C is mixed with 1 kg of water at 30 °C (no loss). The final temperature in °C is
The principle of calorimetry is
qa.a: Heat lost by hot bodies equals heat gained by cold bodies in an isolated system
qa.e: Energy conservation in an isolated system.

qa.q: A 0.1 kg metal piece at 100 °C is dropped into 0.2 kg of water at 20 °C. The final temperature is 24 °C. The metal's specific heat (s_water = 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, ignore calorimeter) in J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ is
Why is a calorimeter usually made of copper?
qa.a: Copper is a good conductor with low specific heat, so it reaches the mixture's temperature quickly and absorbs little heat
qa.e: Quick equalisation and small heat absorption make measurements accurate.

qa.q: In the method of mixtures, the outer jacket of the calorimeter is used to
qa.a: Minimise heat exchange with the surroundings
qa.e: Insulation keeps the system isolated.

qa.q: A 0.2 kg aluminium sphere (s = 900 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) at 120 °C is dropped into water. It cools to 20 °C. The heat it gives out in J is
When hot and cold water are mixed in a perfectly insulated vessel, the final temperature
qa.a: Lies between the two initial temperatures
qa.e: Heat flows until equilibrium is reached, in between.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The final temperature of a mixture of 1 kg water at 80 °C and 3 kg water at 20 °C is 50 °C.
Reason (R): Heat lost by the hot water equals the heat gained by the cold water.
qa.a: A is false but R is true
qa.e: A is false: 1 × (80 − T) = 3 × (T − 20) gives T = 35 °C (50 °C is the unweighted average). R is true.

qa.q: During the melting of ice at 0 °C, the temperature of the ice–water mixture
qa.a: Remains constant
qa.e: Heat is used to change state, not raise temperature.

qa.q: Food cooks faster in a pressure cooker because
qa.a: The higher pressure raises the boiling point of water
qa.e: Water boils at about 120 °C inside, so food heats more.

qa.q: Water boils at a lower temperature on a mountain because
qa.a: Atmospheric pressure is lower there
qa.e: Lower pressure lowers the boiling point.

qa.q: The process by which a solid changes directly to vapour is
qa.a: Sublimation
qa.e: Dry ice and iodine sublime.

qa.q: A loaded wire passes slowly through a block of ice without cutting it into two. This is called
qa.a: Regelation
qa.e: Pressure under the wire melts the ice; it refreezes above when the pressure is removed.

qa.q: At the triple point of water
qa.a: Ice, liquid water and vapour coexist in equilibrium
qa.e: It occurs at a unique temperature, 273.16 K.

qa.q: The flat portions of the heating curve of water represent
qa.a: Changes of state at constant temperature
qa.e: Melting at 0 °C and boiling at 100 °C.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The melting point of ice decreases when pressure increases.
Reason (R): Ice contracts on melting, so higher pressure favours the denser liquid water.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Since water is denser than ice, pressure helps melting and lowers the melting point. R explains A.

qa.q: Heat needed to melt 0.5 kg of ice at 0 °C (L_f = 3.34 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹), in units of 10⁵ J, is
Steam at 100 °C causes more severe burns than water at 100 °C because
qa.a: Steam releases a large latent heat on condensing
qa.e: The extra 2.26 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹ is released on the skin.

qa.q: Heat to convert 0.2 kg of water at 100 °C to steam (L_v = 22.6 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹), in units of 10⁵ J, is
0.1 kg of ice at 0 °C is added to 0.3 kg of water at 30 °C (s = 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, L_f = 3.36 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹). The heat the water can give in cooling to 0 °C is 37800 J. Will all the ice melt?
qa.a: Yes, since melting needs only 33600 J
qa.e: Melting needs 0.1 × 3.36 × 10⁵ = 33600 J < 37800 J, so all ice melts and the final temperature is above 0 °C.

qa.q: 0.1 kg of ice at 0 °C is dropped into 0.3 kg of water at 30 °C (s = 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, L_f = 3.36 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹, no heat loss). The final temperature of the water in °C is
qa.e: Cooling the 0.3 kg of water to 0 °C would release 37800 J; melting the ice needs 33600 J; the remaining 4200 J warms all 0.4 kg: 0.4 × 4200 × T = 4200 → T = 2.5 °C.

qa.q: The SI unit of latent heat is
qa.a: J kg⁻¹
qa.e: Latent heat is energy per unit mass (no temperature change).

qa.q: Heat needed to warm 1 kg of ice from −10 °C to 0 °C (s_ice = 2100 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) and melt it (L_f = 3.34 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹), in J, is

Assertion (A): Water in a clay matka stays cooler than the surrounding air in summer.
Reason (R): Evaporation from the matka's surface takes away latent heat from the water.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Evaporative cooling removes heat from the remaining water. R explains A.

qa.q: A copper rod (K = 400 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹) of length 0.5 m and area 10⁻⁴ m² has ends at 100 °C and 0 °C. The heat current in W is
The SI unit of thermal conductivity is
qa.a: W m⁻¹ K⁻¹
qa.e: K = HL/(AΔT): W × m/(m² × K) = W m⁻¹ K⁻¹.

qa.q: Rod X (K = 2K₀) and rod Y (K = K₀), same length and area, are joined; free ends at 90 °C (X) and 0 °C (Y). The junction temperature in °C is
Why are cooking pots often given copper bottoms?
qa.a: Copper's high thermal conductivity spreads heat evenly and quickly
qa.e: Good conduction prevents hot spots and speeds cooking.

qa.q: Which mode of heat transfer occurs without bulk movement of matter but needs a medium?
qa.a: Conduction
qa.e: Heat passes by collisions between neighbouring particles.

qa.q: Air is a poor conductor of heat. This is used in
qa.a: Woollen clothes and double-glazed windows that trap air
qa.e: Trapped air reduces heat flow by conduction.

qa.q: A wall (K = 0.5 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹) is 0.2 m thick with area 10 m². Inside is 25 °C and outside 5 °C. The heat loss in W is

Assertion (A): In steady state, the heat current through two rods joined in series is the same.
Reason (R): No heat accumulates at the junction once the temperature there stops changing.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Steady temperature means heat in = heat out at the junction. R explains A.

qa.q: The mode of heat transfer that does not need any medium is
qa.a: Radiation
qa.e: Electromagnetic waves travel through vacuum.

qa.q: A sea breeze blows during the day because
qa.a: Land heats faster, air over it rises and cooler sea air moves in
qa.e: Land's lower specific heat makes it warmer by day.

qa.q: In a thermos flask, the vacuum between the walls reduces heat transfer by
qa.a: Conduction and convection
qa.e: Without matter, there is no conduction or convection; silvering handles radiation.

qa.q: Dark clothes are preferred in winter because
qa.a: They absorb more radiation
qa.e: Dark surfaces are good absorbers.

qa.q: A black body is one that
qa.a: Absorbs all the radiation falling on it
qa.e: An ideal absorber (and the best emitter at any temperature).

qa.q: Forced convection is used in
qa.a: A car radiator with a fan and water pump
qa.e: A pump or fan drives the fluid flow.

qa.q: Heat from the Sun reaches the Earth by
qa.a: Radiation
qa.e: Space between is nearly empty.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): A good absorber of radiation is also a good emitter.
Reason (R): A body in thermal equilibrium must emit as much radiation as it absorbs.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Equilibrium requires equal absorption and emission rates, linking the two abilities. R explains A.

qa.q: If the absolute temperature of a black body is doubled, the power it radiates becomes how many times?
The Sun's radiation peaks near 480 nm. Using b = 2.9 × 10⁻³ m K, the Sun's surface temperature in K is about
According to Wien's law, as a body gets hotter, its wavelength of maximum emission
qa.a: Decreases

qa.q: A black body at 300 K emits radiation with λ_m about (in µm, b = 2.9 × 10⁻³ m K)
Two bodies of the same size and temperature have emissivities 0.8 and 0.2. The ratio of powers radiated is
A body at temperature T sits in surroundings at T_s (T > T_s). Its net rate of radiation loss is
qa.a: eσA(T⁴ − T_s⁴)
qa.e: It emits eσAT⁴ and absorbs eσAT_s⁴.

qa.q: The energy distribution of black-body radiation depends only on
qa.a: The temperature of the body
qa.e: For an ideal black body, only T matters.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): A blue star is hotter than a red star.
Reason (R): Hotter bodies emit most strongly at longer wavelengths.
qa.a: A is true but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false: by Wien's law λ_m T = constant, so hotter bodies peak at shorter wavelengths.

qa.q: According to Newton's law of cooling, the rate of cooling is proportional to
qa.a: The temperature difference between the body and surroundings
qa.e: dT/dt = −k(T − T_s).

qa.q: A pan cools from 94 °C to 86 °C in 2 min in a 20 °C room. Its average cooling rate in °C per min is
qa.e: 8 °C/2 min = 4 °C/min.

qa.q: A pan in a 20 °C room cools at 4 °C/min when its average temperature is 90 °C. By Newton's law of cooling, its cooling rate (°C/min) at an average temperature of 55 °C is
qa.e: Rate ∝ (T_avg − T_s): 4 × (35/70) = 2 °C/min.

qa.q: A body cools from 80 °C to 60 °C in 10 min in a 20 °C room. Using the average-temperature method, the time (in min) to cool from 60 °C to 40 °C is
qa.e: First interval: rate 2 °C/min at average 70 °C (difference 50), so k = 0.04 per min. Second: average 50 °C (difference 30), rate = 1.2 °C/min, time = 20/1.2 ≈ 16.67 min.

qa.q: Newton's law of cooling is accurate when
qa.a: The temperature difference with the surroundings is small
qa.e: For large differences, radiation (T⁴) effects make it inaccurate.

qa.q: In the lab verification, a straight-line graph is obtained by plotting
qa.a: log(T − T_s) against time
qa.e: Exponential decay of (T − T_s) becomes linear on a log plot.

qa.q: Two identical cups of tea at 80 °C and 60 °C are in a 20 °C room. The ratio of their initial cooling rates (hotter : cooler) is

Assertion (A): Hot tea cools rapidly at first and then more slowly.
Reason (R): The rate of cooling is proportional to the temperature difference between the tea and the room.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: As the difference shrinks, the rate falls. R explains A.

qa.q: Thermodynamics mainly deals with
qa.a: Heat, temperature and their interconversion with work for macroscopic systems
qa.e: It is a macroscopic science of energy transfer.

qa.q: A wall that allows no heat flow is called
qa.a: Adiabatic
qa.e: Adiabatic = insulating.

qa.q: Which is a macroscopic variable?
qa.a: Pressure
qa.e: Pressure describes the gas as a whole.

qa.q: Two gases separated by a diathermic wall are in thermal equilibrium when
qa.a: Their temperatures are equal
qa.e: Heat stops flowing when temperatures match.

qa.q: A system is in an equilibrium state when
qa.a: Its macroscopic variables do not change with time
qa.e: Molecules still move, but bulk properties are steady.

qa.q: The part of the universe outside the system is called the
qa.a: Surroundings
qa.e: System + surroundings = universe.

qa.q: A gas in a sealed copper vessel is placed in boiling water. Heat enters because copper is
qa.a: A diathermic wall
qa.e: Copper conducts heat well.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Thermodynamics can be applied without knowing anything about molecules.
Reason (R): Thermodynamics is based on macroscopic variables like P, V and T.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Its laws relate bulk quantities, not molecular details. R explains A.

qa.q: The zeroth law of thermodynamics leads to the concept of
qa.a: Temperature
qa.e: It establishes temperature as the property equal in thermal equilibrium.

qa.q: If A is in thermal equilibrium with C, and B is in thermal equilibrium with C, then
qa.a: A and B are in thermal equilibrium
qa.e: That is the zeroth law.

qa.q: Internal energy of a system is
qa.a: The sum of kinetic and potential energies of its molecules in the CM frame
qa.e: Bulk motion is excluded.

qa.q: A cylinder of gas is carried in a moving train. Its internal energy, compared with when at rest (same temperature), is
qa.a: The same
qa.e: The train's motion adds bulk KE, not internal energy.

qa.q: Internal energy of an ideal gas depends on
qa.a: Its temperature only
qa.e: No intermolecular forces, so U is kinetic and set by T.

qa.q: A thermometer gives the temperature of a body because
qa.a: It reaches thermal equilibrium with the body
qa.e: Zeroth law: in equilibrium, the thermometer's temperature equals the body's.

qa.q: Which is NOT part of a gas's internal energy?
qa.a: Kinetic energy of the gas container moving at 20 m s⁻¹
qa.e: Bulk motion is excluded from U.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Thermometers can compare temperatures of two bodies that never touch each other.
Reason (R): By the zeroth law, two bodies in thermal equilibrium with the same thermometer are in thermal equilibrium with each other.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: The thermometer acts as the third system C. R explains A.

qa.q: A gas is given 800 J of heat and its internal energy increases by 500 J. The work done by the gas in J is
200 J of work is done ON a gas and it gives out 50 J of heat. The change in its internal energy in J is
qa.e: ΔW = −200 J (work on gas), ΔQ = −50 J. ΔU = ΔQ − ΔW = −50 + 200 = 150 J.

qa.q: Which is a state variable?
qa.a: Internal energy
qa.e: U depends only on the state; Q and W depend on the path.

qa.q: The first law of thermodynamics is a statement of
qa.a: Conservation of energy
qa.e: Heat in = increase in U + work out.

qa.q: In the NCERT convention, ΔW is positive when
qa.a: Work is done by the system on its surroundings
qa.e: Expansion work by the gas is positive.

qa.q: Internal energy of a gas can be increased by
qa.a: Heating it or doing work on it
qa.e: Both heat and work transfer energy.

qa.q: A gas goes from state 1 to state 2 by two different paths. Which is the same for both paths?
qa.a: ΔU
qa.e: U is a state function, so ΔU depends only on the end states.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Heat and work are not state variables.
Reason (R): Their values depend on the path taken between two states.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Path dependence is exactly what makes them not state functions. R explains A.

qa.q: A gas expands at constant pressure 2 × 10⁵ Pa from 0.01 m³ to 0.03 m³. The work done by the gas in J is
1 g of water boils at 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa and its volume increases by 1.7 × 10⁻³ m³. The work done against the atmosphere in J is
1 g of water boils at 100 °C (L = 2260 J g⁻¹) and does 170 J of work against the atmosphere. The increase in its internal energy in J is
A gas is compressed at constant pressure 10⁵ Pa from 4 L to 1 L. The work done by the gas in J is
qa.e: ΔV = −3 × 10⁻³ m³, W = −300 J (work is done on the gas).

qa.q: When water boils, most of the latent heat goes into
qa.a: Increasing internal energy (breaking molecular bonds)
qa.e: ΔU ≫ PΔV for boiling water.

qa.q: Work done by a gas at constant pressure equals
qa.a: PΔV
qa.e: Force × distance on the piston = P × A × Δx = PΔV.

qa.q: A gas absorbs 600 J at constant pressure and expands, doing 250 J of work. Its internal energy changes by (in J)

Assertion (A): When water boils at constant atmospheric pressure, the heat supplied is greater than the increase in internal energy.
Reason (R): Part of the heat is used to do work PΔV against the atmosphere as the volume increases.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: ΔQ = ΔU + PΔV with PΔV > 0. R explains A.

qa.q: The molar specific heat of most solids at room temperature is close to
qa.a: 3R
qa.e: Each atom has 3k_BT on average (kinetic + potential in 3 directions).

qa.q: Using C = 3R (R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹), the heat to raise 1 mol of aluminium by 20 K in J is
1 calorie is approximately (in J)
A man's food provides 2400 kcal a day. In units of 10⁶ J this is about
Why is the molar heat capacity of a solid about 3R?
qa.a: Each atom oscillates in 3 directions with both KE and PE, giving 3k_BT per atom
qa.e: 3 directions × (½k_BT KE + ½k_BT PE) = 3k_BT.

qa.q: Heat that raises 500 g of water by 2 °C, in cal, is
qa.e: Q = m × 1 cal g⁻¹ °C⁻¹ × ΔT = 500 × 2 = 1000 cal.

qa.q: Joule's experiments established that
qa.a: Work and heat are equivalent forms of energy transfer, with 4.186 J = 1 cal
qa.e: Mechanical work produced a definite amount of heat.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The molar specific heats of many different solids are nearly equal at room temperature.
Reason (R): Each atom in a solid has on average an energy of 3k_BT, independent of the type of atom.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Molar heat = 3R for all such solids. R explains A.

qa.q: Mayer's relation for an ideal gas is
qa.a: C_p − C_v = R
qa.e: Constant-pressure heating also does work μRΔT.

qa.q: C_p is greater than C_v because at constant pressure
qa.a: The gas expands and does work, needing extra heat
qa.e: Same ΔU for the same ΔT, plus PΔV.

qa.q: For a monatomic ideal gas, γ = C_p/C_v is
1 mol of an ideal gas is heated at constant pressure by 20 K (R = 8.31). The work done by the gas in J is
For a diatomic ideal gas (rigid molecules), C_v is
qa.e: 3 translational + 2 rotational degrees of freedom: 5 × R/2.

qa.q: A gas has C_v = 20.8 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. Its C_p (R = 8.3 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹) in J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ is
In deriving Mayer's relation, ΔU is the same at constant P and constant V for the same ΔT because
qa.a: The internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on temperature
qa.e: U = U(T) for an ideal gas.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): More heat is needed to raise the temperature of a gas by 1 K at constant pressure than at constant volume.
Reason (R): At constant volume, the gas does work on its surroundings.
qa.a: A is true but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false: at constant volume no work is done; at constant pressure the gas does work PΔV.

qa.q: Which of these is an intensive variable?
qa.a: Temperature
qa.e: Temperature does not change when you take part of a system.

qa.q: The equation of state of an ideal gas is
qa.a: PV = μRT
qa.e: It connects P, V and T for any equilibrium state.

qa.q: A quasi-static process is one that
qa.a: Is carried out so slowly that the system stays in equilibrium at every stage
qa.e: Infinitely slow changes keep the system in equilibrium.

qa.q: 2 mol of an ideal gas at 300 K occupy 0.05 m³ (R = 8.31). The pressure in Pa is
If a system is doubled in size at the same state, which variable doubles?
qa.a: Internal energy
qa.e: U is extensive.

qa.q: Why can't we define a single pressure for a gas during a sudden expansion?
qa.a: The gas is not in equilibrium, so pressure varies from place to place
qa.e: Only equilibrium states have well-defined state variables.

qa.q: Density of a gas sample is
qa.a: Intensive
qa.e: Mass/volume does not depend on how much you take.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): State variables are well defined only for equilibrium states.
Reason (R): In non-equilibrium, quantities like pressure and temperature vary across the system.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Without uniformity, a single value cannot describe the system. R explains A.

qa.q: 2 mol of an ideal gas expand isothermally at 400 K to twice the volume (R = 8.31, ln 2 = 0.693). The work done in J is about
In an isothermal expansion of an ideal gas, the heat absorbed
qa.a: Equals the work done by the gas
qa.e: ΔU = 0, so ΔQ = ΔW.

qa.q: 2 mol of a monatomic gas (γ = 5/3) cool adiabatically from 400 K to 300 K (R = 8.31). The work done by the gas in J is
An ideal gas at 1 atm is compressed adiabatically to half its volume (γ = 1.5). The new pressure in atm is about (2^1.5 ≈ 2.83)
qa.e: P₂ = P₁(V₁/V₂)^γ = 2^1.5 ≈ 2.83 atm.

qa.q: For the same gas compressed isothermally to half its volume from 1 atm, the new pressure in atm is
qa.e: PV = constant: P₂ = 2 atm.

qa.q: On a P–V diagram, the slope of an adiabatic curve compared with an isothermal curve at the same point is
qa.a: γ times larger
qa.e: dP/dV: −P/V (isothermal) vs −γP/V (adiabatic).

qa.q: A gas expands adiabatically. Its temperature
qa.a: Falls
qa.e: It does work at the expense of internal energy (ΔQ = 0).

qa.q:
Assertion (A): When a gas expands adiabatically, its temperature rises.
Reason (R): In an adiabatic process, no heat is exchanged with the surroundings.
qa.a: A is false but R is true
qa.e: A is false: the gas does work using its internal energy, so it cools. R is true.

qa.q: In an isochoric process, the work done by the gas is
qa.a: Zero
qa.e: No change in volume means no work.

qa.q: 3 mol of an ideal gas are heated at constant pressure from 300 K to 350 K (R = 8.31). The work done by the gas in J is
In a cyclic process, the change in internal energy is
qa.a: Zero
qa.e: U is a state function and the system returns to its starting state.

qa.q: A gas goes round a cycle and absorbs net 500 J of heat. The net work done by it in J is
qa.e: ΔU = 0 for a cycle, so W = Q.

qa.q: A gas is taken round a triangle on a P–V diagram with vertices (1 L, 1 × 10⁵ Pa), (3 L, 1 × 10⁵ Pa), (1 L, 3 × 10⁵ Pa). The magnitude of net work in J is
2 mol of a monatomic gas (C_v = 3R/2) are heated at constant volume by 20 K (R = 8.31). The heat supplied in J is
On a P–V indicator diagram, a horizontal straight line represents
qa.a: An isobaric process
qa.e: Pressure is constant along it.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The net work done by a gas in a cyclic process equals the area enclosed by the cycle on the P–V diagram.
Reason (R): Work in each step is the area under that part of the P–V curve, and the areas combine with signs around the loop.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Expansion areas count positive, compression negative; the difference is the enclosed area. R explains A.

qa.q: The Kelvin–Planck statement says that
qa.a: No process can have as its sole result the complete conversion of heat into work
qa.e: Some heat must be rejected to a colder body.

qa.q: The Clausius statement says that
qa.a: No process can have as its sole result transfer of heat from a colder body to a hotter body
qa.e: Heat flows cold → hot only with external work.

qa.q: Why can no heat engine be 100% efficient?
qa.a: The second law requires some heat to be rejected to a cold reservoir
qa.e: Even an ideal frictionless engine must reject heat.

qa.q: The need for the second law arises because
qa.a: The first law allows processes that are never observed
qa.e: Conservation of energy alone doesn't forbid heat flowing from cold to hot.

qa.q: An engine absorbs 500 J of heat and does 500 J of work in a cycle, rejecting no heat. This claim violates
qa.a: The second law (Kelvin–Planck)
qa.e: It conserves energy but converts all heat into work.

qa.q: A refrigerator transfers heat from its cold inside to the warmer room. This does not violate the Clausius statement because
qa.a: External work (electrical energy) is supplied
qa.e: Heat transfer is not the sole result; work is consumed.

qa.q: The two statements of the second law are
qa.a: Equivalent
qa.e: Violating either one allows violating the other.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Heat does not flow spontaneously from a cold body to a hot body.
Reason (R): The first law of thermodynamics forbids such a flow.
qa.a: A is true but R is false
qa.e: A is true (second law, Clausius). R is false: the first law would allow it since energy is conserved.

qa.q: A process is reversible if
qa.a: It can be retraced so that both system and surroundings return to their original states
qa.e: Both the system and the surroundings must be restored.

qa.q: Which is an irreversible process?
qa.a: Free expansion of a gas into vacuum
qa.e: Free expansion is sudden and far from equilibrium.

qa.q: A main cause of irreversibility is
qa.a: Dissipative effects like friction and viscosity
qa.e: Dissipation turns organised energy into disordered internal energy.

qa.q: Heat conduction from a hot body to a cold body is
qa.a: Irreversible
qa.e: Heat won't flow back by itself (Clausius).

qa.q: Which condition is necessary (but not sufficient) for reversibility?
qa.a: The process must be quasi-static
qa.e: It must also be free of dissipative effects.

qa.q: Mixing of two different gases in a container is
qa.a: Irreversible
qa.e: The gases will not unmix by themselves.

qa.q: Why are reversible processes called idealisations?
qa.a: Real processes always have some friction or finite differences
qa.e: Nothing real is perfectly slow and frictionless.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): A block sliding to rest on a rough floor is an irreversible process.
Reason (R): Friction converts the block's kinetic energy into internal energy that cannot spontaneously turn back into ordered motion.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Dissipation by friction is the cause of irreversibility. R explains A.

qa.q: A heat engine absorbs 2000 J and does 500 J of work per cycle. Its efficiency is
The same engine (Q₁ = 2000 J, W = 500 J) rejects heat per cycle (in J)
qa.e: Q₂ = Q₁ − W = 1500 J.

qa.q: In which steps of the Carnot cycle is heat exchanged with reservoirs?
qa.a: The two isothermal steps
qa.e: Adiabatic steps have ΔQ = 0.

qa.q: The Carnot cycle consists of
qa.a: Two isothermal and two adiabatic processes
qa.e: Isothermal expansion, adiabatic expansion, isothermal compression, adiabatic compression.

qa.q: During the adiabatic expansion step of a Carnot cycle, the temperature of the working substance
qa.a: Falls from T₁ to T₂
qa.e: The gas does work with no heat input, so it cools.

qa.q: The net work done in one Carnot cycle is represented by
qa.a: The area enclosed by the cycle on the P–V diagram
qa.e: As for any cycle.

qa.q: A Carnot engine is
qa.a: An ideal reversible engine between two temperatures
qa.e: It sets the upper limit for efficiency.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): A heat engine must reject some heat to a cold reservoir.
Reason (R): The first law of thermodynamics forbids complete conversion of heat into work.
qa.a: A is true but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false: it is the second law (Kelvin–Planck), not the first, that forbids it.

qa.q: A Carnot engine works between 227 °C and 27 °C. Its efficiency is
A Carnot engine has η = 0.25 and rejects heat to a sink at 300 K. The source temperature in K is
A Carnot engine takes 600 J from a source at 600 K and rejects heat to a sink at 400 K. The work done per cycle in J is
Carnot's theorem states that
qa.a: No engine between two temperatures can be more efficient than a reversible (Carnot) engine
qa.e: Reversible engines set the maximum.

qa.q: The efficiency of a Carnot engine depends on
qa.a: Only the temperatures of the source and sink
qa.e: η = 1 − T₂/T₁.

qa.q: A Carnot engine works between 500 K and 300 K. Which change raises its efficiency more?
qa.a: Lowering the sink temperature by 50 K
qa.e: Lowering T₂ to 250 K gives η = 0.5; raising T₁ to 550 K gives η ≈ 0.45. Lowering the sink is more effective.

qa.q: For a Carnot engine between 800 K and 400 K that absorbs 1000 J, the heat rejected in J is

Assertion (A): A Carnot engine cannot have an efficiency of 100%.
Reason (R): A Carnot engine works on a reversible cycle.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true, but reversibility does not explain A; η = 1 − T₂/T₁ < 1 because T₂ cannot be 0 K.

qa.q: Avogadro's law states that equal volumes of all gases at the same temperature and pressure contain
qa.a: Equal numbers of molecules
qa.e: Number of molecules, not mass or atoms.

qa.q: Gay-Lussac's law of combining volumes says that gases combine
qa.a: In simple whole-number ratios by volume
qa.e: E.g. 2 volumes H₂ + 1 volume O₂.

qa.q: Kinetic theory explains the pressure of a gas as due to
qa.a: Collisions of molecules with the walls of the container
qa.e: Momentum transferred by molecules hitting the walls produces force.

qa.q: Which ancient Indian thinker proposed that matter is made of tiny indivisible particles?
qa.a: Kanada
qa.e: Kanada is associated with the Vaisheshika atomic view.

qa.q: Dalton's atomic theory was mainly used to explain
qa.a: The laws of chemical combination (definite and multiple proportions)
qa.e: It explained why elements combine in fixed proportions.

qa.q: Under the same conditions, 1 L of oxygen contains N molecules. 3 L of nitrogen contain
qa.a: 3N molecules
qa.e: Avogadro's law: molecules ∝ volume at the same T and P.

qa.q: Kinetic theory relates the macroscopic quantities P and T to
qa.a: The motion of molecules
qa.e: Pressure from momentum transfer; temperature from average kinetic energy.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): At the same temperature and pressure, 2 L of H₂ and 2 L of CO₂ contain the same number of molecules.
Reason (R): Avogadro's law: equal volumes of gases at the same T and P contain equal numbers of molecules.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: R is exactly the reason. R explains A.

qa.q: The Boltzmann constant is related to R and N_A by
qa.a: k_B = R/N_A
qa.e: R per molecule.

qa.q: How many moles are there in 67.2 L of a gas at STP?
A gas at 300 K and 1.38 × 10⁵ Pa occupies 1 m³. The number of molecules (k_B = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹) in units of 10²⁵ is
In a closed bottle of water at constant temperature, the state where evaporation and condensation rates are equal is called
qa.a: Dynamic equilibrium
qa.e: Molecules keep moving between phases at equal rates.

qa.q: Compared with a solid, the typical spacing between gas molecules at room conditions is about
qa.a: 10 times larger
qa.e: Gas molecules are much farther apart.

qa.q: The number of molecules in 2 mol of a gas, in units of 10²³, is
The ideal gas equation can be written as
qa.a: PV = Nk_BT
qa.e: N molecules, each contributing k_BT.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The volume of a gas is much larger than the volume of the same mass of liquid.
Reason (R): Gas molecules are much bigger than liquid molecules.
qa.a: A is true but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false: the molecules are the same; they are just much farther apart in a gas.

qa.q: A mixture contains 2 mol of He and 3 mol of Ar at a total pressure of 10 atm. The partial pressure of He in atm is
Real gases behave most like ideal gases at
qa.a: Low pressure and high temperature
qa.e: Molecules are far apart and fast, so interactions are negligible.

qa.q: 1 mol of gas at 300 K occupies 0.025 m³. Its pressure in Pa (R = 8.31) is
Water vapour at 100 °C has density 0.6 kg m⁻³; liquid water 1000 kg m⁻³. The fraction of the vapour's volume actually occupied by molecules, in units of 10⁻⁴, is about
qa.e: Fraction ≈ ρ_vapour/ρ_liquid = 6 × 10⁻⁴.

qa.q: Dalton's law of partial pressures applies to
qa.a: A mixture of non-reacting ideal gases
qa.e: Each gas exerts pressure independently.

qa.q: A gas at 2 atm occupies 3 L. At constant temperature, its volume at 6 atm in L is
qa.e: Boyle: P₁V₁ = P₂V₂ → V₂ = 6/6 = 1 L.

qa.q: Total pressure in a vessel of 0.1 mol O₂ and 0.4 mol N₂ at 300 K in 0.01 m³ (R = 8.31) in units of 10⁵ Pa is

Assertion (A): Boyle's law and Charles' law are special cases of the ideal gas equation.
Reason (R): PV = μRT reduces to PV = constant when T is fixed and to V ∝ T when P is fixed.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Fixing one variable gives each law. R explains A.

qa.q: According to kinetic theory, the pressure of an ideal gas is
qa.a: (1/3) n m v̄²
qa.e: Momentum transfer averaged over random directions.

qa.q: When a molecule of mass m with velocity vₓ strikes a wall elastically and rebounds, its change in momentum has magnitude
qa.a: 2mvₓ
qa.e: From +mvₓ to −mvₓ: change = 2mvₓ.

qa.q: If the mean square speed of molecules is doubled at constant number density, the pressure becomes how many times?
qa.e: P ∝ v̄².

qa.q: Which is NOT an assumption of the kinetic theory of ideal gases?
qa.a: Molecules attract each other strongly between collisions
qa.e: Intermolecular forces are neglected except during collisions.

qa.q: Why is gas pressure the same in all directions?
qa.a: Molecular motion is random, so all directions are equivalent
qa.e: vₓ² = v_y² = v_z² on average.

qa.q: n = 3 × 10²⁵ m⁻³, m = 5 × 10⁻²⁶ kg, v̄² = 2 × 10⁵ m² s⁻². The pressure in units of 10⁵ Pa is
Kinetic theory explains Dalton's law because
qa.a: Each gas in a mixture contributes its own (1/3)nᵢmᵢv̄ᵢ² to the total pressure
qa.e: Pressures from independent molecules simply add.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Kinetic theory treats collisions of gas molecules with walls as elastic.
Reason (R): In an elastic collision, kinetic energy is conserved, so gas molecules do not lose energy to the walls on average at equilibrium.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Elastic collisions keep the gas's energy steady in equilibrium. R explains A.

qa.q: The average translational kinetic energy of a gas molecule at temperature T is
qa.e: From PV = Nk_BT and P = (1/3)nmv̄².

qa.q: The rms speed of nitrogen (M = 0.028 kg mol⁻¹) at 300 K (R = 8.31) in m s⁻¹ is about
The temperature of a gas is raised from 300 K to 1200 K. Its rms speed becomes how many times?
The ratio of rms speeds of hydrogen (M = 2) to oxygen (M = 32) at the same temperature is
A gas has PV = 2000 J. Its total translational kinetic energy in J is
The ratio of rms speeds of ²³⁵UF₆ (M = 349) to ²³⁸UF₆ (M = 352) is about
qa.e: √(352/349) ≈ 1.0043; the lighter molecule is slightly faster.

qa.q: At what temperature (in K) is the rms speed of a gas double its value at 27 °C?
qa.e: v ∝ √T: T must be 4 × 300 = 1200 K.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): At the same temperature, hydrogen molecules move faster on average than oxygen molecules.
Reason (R): At a given temperature, all gas molecules have the same average kinetic energy, so lighter molecules must be faster.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: ½mv² equal → smaller m, larger v. R explains A.

qa.q: A monatomic gas molecule has how many degrees of freedom?
qa.e: Only translation along x, y and z.

qa.q: A rigid diatomic molecule has how many degrees of freedom?
qa.e: 3 translational + 2 rotational (rotation about the bond axis is negligible).

qa.q: According to the law of equipartition, each quadratic energy term has average energy
qa.a: ½k_BT per molecule
qa.e: That's the statement of the law.

qa.q: A vibrational mode of a diatomic molecule contributes an average energy of
qa.a: k_BT
qa.e: Two terms (kinetic and potential), each ½k_BT.

qa.q: The average energy of a rigid diatomic molecule at 300 K (k_B = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹) in units of 10⁻²¹ J is
Why does a vibrational mode count twice in equipartition?
qa.a: It has both kinetic and potential energy terms
qa.e: Each quadratic term gets ½k_BT.

qa.q: The internal energy of 1 mol of a monatomic ideal gas at temperature T is
qa.e: 3 degrees of freedom × ½RT per mole.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): A monatomic molecule has more energy than a rigid diatomic molecule at the same temperature.
Reason (R): A rigid diatomic molecule has two extra rotational degrees of freedom, each with ½k_BT on average.
qa.a: A is false but R is true
qa.e: A is false: the diatomic molecule has (5/2)k_BT versus (3/2)k_BT. R is true.

qa.q: γ for a monatomic ideal gas is
C_v for a rigid diatomic gas (take R = 8.3 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹) in J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ is
For a diatomic gas with its vibrational mode active, C_v is
qa.e: 5 × ½R + R (vibration) = (7/2)R.

qa.q: For a polyatomic gas with 3 translational, 3 rotational and f vibrational modes, C_v is
For a polyatomic gas with f = 1, γ is
C_p of a monatomic gas (take R = 8.3 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹) in J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ is
qa.e: C_p = (5/2)R = 2.5 × 8.3 = 20.75 (the same number as C_v of a rigid diatomic gas).

qa.q: The measured C_v of helium (about 12.5 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹) agrees with the prediction

Assertion (A): γ for a monatomic gas is greater than γ for a diatomic gas.
Reason (R): A diatomic gas has more degrees of freedom, so C_v is larger and C_p/C_v = 1 + R/C_v is smaller.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Larger C_v means smaller γ. R explains A.

qa.q: The molar specific heat of a solid by the Dulong–Petit law is
qa.a: 3R
qa.e: U = 3RT → C = 3R.

qa.q: Each atom in a solid has average energy 3k_BT because
qa.a: It oscillates in 3 directions, each with KE and PE terms of ½k_BT
qa.e: 3 × (½k_BT + ½k_BT) = 3k_BT.

qa.q: C_v of a mixture of 2 mol He (3R/2) and 2 mol N₂ (5R/2), in units of R, is
The fall in specific heats of solids at very low temperatures is explained by
qa.a: Quantum theory
qa.e: Energy exchanges in discrete amounts freeze out vibrations.

qa.q: Heat needed to raise 2 mol of helium in a rigid cylinder by 10 K (R = 8.31) in J is
Heat needed to raise 1 mol of oxygen (rigid diatomic) at constant pressure by 20 K (R = 8.31) in J is
The Dulong–Petit value 3R in J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ is about (R = 8.31)

Assertion (A): Light, hard solids like diamond have molar specific heats well below 3R at room temperature.
Reason (R): The classical equipartition result needs high enough temperature; at lower effective temperature, quantum effects reduce the specific heat.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Their vibrations are 'stiff', so room temperature is effectively low; quantum effects cut C. R explains A.

qa.q: The mean free path of gas molecules is
qa.a: The average distance travelled between successive collisions
qa.e: That's the definition.

qa.q: If the number density of a gas is doubled, its mean free path becomes
qa.a: Half

qa.q: If the molecular diameter is halved (same n), the mean free path becomes how many times?
The formula for mean free path is
qa.a: 1/(√2 n π d²)
qa.e: Inverse of collision cross-section times density (with √2 for relative motion).

qa.q: A molecule with mean free path 2 × 10⁻⁷ m moves at 400 m s⁻¹. The number of collisions per second, in units of 10⁹, is
qa.e: Frequency = v/l = 400/(2 × 10⁻⁷) = 2 × 10⁹ s⁻¹.

qa.q: At constant temperature, if the pressure of a gas is reduced to one-tenth, the mean free path becomes how many times the original?
qa.e: l ∝ 1/n ∝ 1/P at constant T.

qa.q: Why does a smell spread slowly across a room even though molecules move fast?
qa.a: Molecules collide very frequently and keep changing direction
qa.e: The short mean free path makes the motion a random walk.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The mean free path in a gas decreases when the gas is compressed at constant temperature.
Reason (R): Compression at constant temperature increases the average speed of the molecules.
qa.a: A is true but R is false
qa.e: A is true because n increases. R is false: at constant temperature the average speed is unchanged.

qa.q: Which motion is periodic but not oscillatory?
qa.a: Uniform circular motion
qa.e: It repeats but has no to-and-fro motion about a mean position.

qa.q: Oscillatory motion requires
qa.a: A restoring force directed towards the equilibrium position
qa.e: Without a restoring force there is nothing to pull the body back.

qa.q: Which statement about periodic and oscillatory motion is correct?
qa.a: All oscillatory motions are periodic
qa.e: Oscillation implies regular repetition, but not vice versa.

qa.q: The to-and-fro motion of a body about a mean position is called
qa.a: Oscillatory motion
qa.e: Also called vibratory motion.

qa.q: An example of oscillations in electrical systems is
qa.a: Alternating current in a circuit
qa.e: AC voltage and current oscillate in time.

qa.q: The motion of the hands of a clock is
qa.a: Periodic
qa.e: It repeats every 12 h (hour hand), but does not oscillate.

qa.q: When a pendulum bob is pulled aside and released, it moves back towards the mean position because of
qa.a: The restoring component of gravity
qa.e: mg sin θ acts towards the mean position.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The motion of the Earth around the Sun is periodic but not oscillatory.
Reason (R): The Earth repeats its path regularly but does not move to and fro about an equilibrium position.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Repetition without to-and-fro motion is exactly periodic-but-not-oscillatory. R explains A.

qa.q: A body makes 20 oscillations in 5 s. Its frequency in Hz is
The period of sin²(ωt) is
qa.a: π/ω
qa.e: sin²ωt = ½(1 − cos 2ωt), which repeats after π/ω.

qa.q: Which function is NOT periodic?
qa.a: e^(−ωt)
qa.e: An exponential decay never repeats.

qa.q: In a sound wave, the oscillating 'displacement' variable can be
qa.a: Pressure
qa.e: Sound is a variation of pressure (and air displacement) with time.

qa.q: The period of x(t) = sin ωt + cos 2ωt is
qa.a: 2π/ω
qa.e: The longer of the two periods (2π/ω) is a multiple of the shorter (π/ω).

qa.q: ν = 50 Hz. The period in s is
According to Fourier's idea, any periodic function can be written as
qa.a: A sum of sines and cosines of suitable periods and amplitudes
qa.e: Harmonic functions are the building blocks of periodic motion.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): sin ωt + cos ωt is a periodic function.
Reason (R): The maximum value of sin ωt + cos ωt is √2.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true, but having a maximum value doesn't make a function periodic; it is periodic because it equals √2 sin(ωt + π/4).

qa.q: For x = 0.04 cos(10πt + π/3) m, the amplitude in m is
qa.e: The coefficient of the cosine is A.

qa.q: For x = 0.04 cos(10πt + π/3) m, the frequency in Hz is
qa.e: ω = 10π = 2πν → ν = 5 Hz.

qa.q: For x = 0.04 cos(10πt + π/3) m, the phase constant is
qa.e: φ is the constant added to ωt.

qa.q: A particle in SHM with amplitude 2 cm starts from the mean position moving in the +x direction. A suitable equation is
qa.a: x = 2 sin ωt
qa.e: At t = 0, x = 0 and increasing: sin ωt fits (equivalently 2 cos(ωt − π/2)).

qa.q: The angular frequency of an SHM with period 0.2 s, in units of π rad s⁻¹, is
Two SHMs have the same amplitude and period but phase constants 0 and π. Their displacements at any time are
qa.a: Equal and opposite
qa.e: cos(ωt + π) = −cos ωt.

qa.q: On an x–t graph, increasing the angular frequency of SHM
qa.a: Shortens the period, packing more cycles in the same time
qa.e: T = 2π/ω decreases.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): In SHM, the amplitude is the maximum displacement from the mean position.
Reason (R): Since |cos(ωt + φ)| ≤ 1, x = A cos(ωt + φ) never exceeds A in magnitude.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: The cosine's maximum value 1 gives |x|max = A. R explains A.

qa.q: A particle moves on a circle of radius 5 cm with angular speed π rad s⁻¹. The amplitude of the SHM of its projection on a diameter in cm is
qa.e: Amplitude = radius.

qa.q: For the same particle (ω = π rad s⁻¹), the period of the projected SHM in s is
qa.e: T = 2π/ω = 2 s.

qa.q: A particle moving anticlockwise on a reference circle starts at angle π/4 from the x-axis. The x-projection is
qa.a: A cos(ωt + π/4)
qa.e: Angle at time t is ωt + π/4.

qa.q: Uniform circular motion can be regarded as a combination of
qa.a: Two perpendicular SHMs of equal amplitude differing in phase by π/2
qa.e: x = A cos ωt and y = A sin ωt.

qa.q: A particle on a reference circle of radius 4 cm turns at 3 rev s⁻¹. The angular frequency of the SHM in units of π rad s⁻¹ is
qa.e: ω = 2π × 3 = 6π rad s⁻¹.

qa.q: Which is NOT simple harmonic?
qa.a: Uniform circular motion itself
qa.e: Only the projections are SHM.

qa.q: At t = 0 the particle is at the top of the reference circle (angle π/2) moving anticlockwise. Its x-projection at t = 0 is
qa.e: x = A cos(π/2) = 0.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The foot of the perpendicular from a particle in uniform circular motion onto a diameter executes SHM.
Reason (R): Its displacement along the diameter is A cos(ωt + φ).
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: A sinusoidal displacement is SHM by definition. R explains A.

qa.q: A particle in SHM has amplitude 4 cm and angular frequency 3 rad s⁻¹. Its maximum speed in cm s⁻¹ is
qa.e: v_max = ωA = 3 × 4 = 12 cm s⁻¹.

qa.q: For the same particle (A = 4 cm, ω = 3 rad s⁻¹), its maximum acceleration in cm s⁻² is
qa.e: a_max = ω²A = 9 × 4 = 36 cm s⁻².

qa.q: A particle in SHM (A = 10 cm, ω = 4 rad s⁻¹) is at x = 6 cm. Its speed in cm s⁻¹ is
In SHM, acceleration is
qa.a: Proportional to displacement and directed towards the mean position
qa.e: a = −ω²x.

qa.q: The phase difference between displacement and acceleration in SHM is
qa.a: π
qa.e: a = −ω²x: opposite in phase.

qa.q: In SHM, the speed is maximum at
qa.a: The mean position
qa.e: At x = 0, v = ωA.

qa.q: A particle has a = −16x (SI units) in SHM. Its period in s is (π = 3.14)

Assertion (A): The velocity of a particle in SHM is zero at the extreme positions.
Reason (R): The acceleration of a particle in SHM is zero at the extreme positions.
qa.a: A is true but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false: acceleration −ω²x is maximum at the extremes.

qa.q: A 0.25 kg mass on a spring of k = 100 N m⁻¹. The angular frequency in rad s⁻¹ is
A spring–mass system has angular frequency 20 rad s⁻¹. Its period in s is (π = 3.14)
If the mass on a spring is made 9 times larger, the period becomes how many times?
A 2 kg block is attached between two identical springs (k = 50 N m⁻¹ each) fixed to walls on either side. Its angular frequency in rad s⁻¹ is
A spring of k = 200 N m⁻¹ with a 2 kg mass oscillates with amplitude 5 cm. Its maximum acceleration in m s⁻² is
For the same system (k = 200 N m⁻¹, m = 2 kg, A = 5 cm), the maximum speed in m s⁻¹ is
The restoring force in SHM is
qa.a: Proportional to displacement and opposite to it
qa.e: F = −kx.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The period of a spring–mass oscillator does not depend on the amplitude.
Reason (R): T = 2π√(m/k) contains only the mass and the spring constant.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Amplitude does not appear, so T is the same for small or large (elastic) oscillations. R explains A.

qa.q: A particle in SHM has amplitude A. At what displacement are its KE and PE equal?
qa.e: ½kx² = ½k(A² − x²) → x² = A²/2.

qa.q: A 0.5 kg mass on a spring (k = 50 N m⁻¹) oscillates with A = 0.2 m. Its total energy in J is
For the same oscillator (E = 1 J), the kinetic energy at x = 0.1 m in J is
If the amplitude of SHM is tripled, the total energy becomes how many times?
qa.e: E ∝ A².

qa.q: The total mechanical energy of a body in SHM (no friction)
qa.a: Remains constant
qa.e: Only its split between K and U changes.

qa.q: The kinetic energy of a particle in SHM varies in time with a period of
qa.e: sin²(ωt + φ) repeats twice per cycle.

qa.q: At the extreme positions of SHM, the energy is
qa.a: All potential
qa.e: v = 0, so K = 0 and U = E.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): At the mean position of SHM, the kinetic energy is maximum.
Reason (R): At x = 0 the potential energy ½kx² is zero, so all the energy is kinetic.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: K = E − U = E at x = 0. R explains A.

qa.q: The period of a simple pendulum is
qa.e: From ω² = g/L.

qa.q: A pendulum's length is increased 4 times. Its period becomes how many times?
qa.e: T ∝ √L.

qa.q: The bob of a pendulum is replaced by one of double mass (same length). The period
qa.a: Stays the same
qa.e: T does not depend on mass.

qa.q: The motion of a simple pendulum is SHM only when
qa.a: The angular displacement is small
qa.e: Then sin θ ≈ θ and the restoring torque is proportional to θ.

qa.q: A pendulum of length 2.45 m (g = 9.8 m s⁻², π = 3.14) has a period in s of
The restoring torque on a pendulum bob displaced by θ is
qa.a: −mgL sin θ
qa.e: Only the component mg sin θ perpendicular to the string gives torque about the support.

qa.q: Two pendulums have lengths 1 m and 0.25 m. The ratio of their periods (long : short) is

Assertion (A): A simple pendulum with a heavier bob swings more slowly.
Reason (R): Both the restoring torque and the moment of inertia of the bob are proportional to its mass.
qa.a: A is false but R is true
qa.e: A is false: since both are ∝ m, mass cancels and T = 2π√(L/g). R is true.

qa.q: The time period of a seconds pendulum (in s) is
qa.e: It takes 1 s for each swing, so 2 s for a full oscillation.

qa.q: Taking g = π² m s⁻², the length of a seconds pendulum in m is
qa.e: L = gT²/(4π²) = π² × 4/(4π²) = 1 m.

qa.q: A pendulum has a period of 2 s on Earth. On the Moon (g_Moon = g/6), its period in s is about (√6 ≈ 2.45)
A pendulum is in a lift accelerating upward at 2.2 m s⁻² (g = 9.8 m s⁻²). The effective g in m s⁻² is
qa.e: g_eff = g + a = 12 m s⁻².

qa.q: In a freely falling lift, a simple pendulum
qa.a: Does not oscillate
qa.e: g_eff = 0, so there is no restoring torque (T → ∞).

qa.q: To measure g with a pendulum, plot T² against L. The slope of the line equals
qa.a: 4π²/g
qa.e: T² = (4π²/g)L.

qa.q: A student measures L = 1.0 m and T = 2.0 s. Using π² = 9.87, g in m s⁻² is

Assertion (A): The rotation of the Earth about its axis is periodic but not simple harmonic.
Reason (R): SHM requires to-and-fro motion about a mean position with a restoring force proportional to displacement.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: The Earth just turns; there is no to-and-fro motion. R explains A.

qa.q: A wave transfers
qa.a: Energy without transporting matter as a whole
qa.e: The disturbance moves; the medium stays.

qa.q: Which wave can travel through vacuum?
qa.a: Light
qa.e: Electromagnetic waves need no medium.

qa.q: Mechanical wave propagation requires the medium to have
qa.a: Elasticity and inertia
qa.e: Elastic restoring forces pass on the disturbance; inertia keeps parts moving.

qa.q: As a sound wave passes, the air molecules
qa.a: Oscillate about their mean positions
qa.e: Only the disturbance reaches the listener.

qa.q: Waves associated with moving electrons are called
qa.a: Matter waves
qa.e: They are a quantum idea (de Broglie).

qa.q: Why can't astronauts hear each other directly in space?
qa.a: There is no medium to carry sound
qa.e: Sound is a mechanical wave needing a medium.

qa.q: In a Mexican wave in a stadium, what travels around the stands?
qa.a: The pattern (disturbance), not the people
qa.e: Each person only stands and sits; the pattern moves.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Sound cannot travel through a vacuum.
Reason (R): Sound is a mechanical wave and requires a material medium for propagation.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Without particles there is nothing to oscillate. R explains A.

qa.q: In a longitudinal wave, particles of the medium oscillate
qa.a: Along the direction of wave propagation
qa.e: They form compressions and rarefactions.

qa.q: Sound waves in air are
qa.a: Longitudinal
qa.e: Air cannot resist shear; sound travels as compressions.

qa.q: Why can't transverse mechanical waves travel through the bulk of a gas?
qa.a: Gases have no shear modulus to provide a sideways restoring force
qa.e: Transverse waves need resistance to shear.

qa.q: Waves on the surface of water are
qa.a: A combination of transverse and longitudinal
qa.e: Water particles move in circular or elliptical paths.

qa.q: Regions of high pressure and density in a sound wave are called
qa.a: Compressions
qa.e: Low-pressure regions are rarefactions.

qa.q: A wave produced by plucking a stretched sitar string is
qa.a: Transverse
qa.e: The string moves perpendicular to its length.

qa.q: Earthquake S-waves cannot pass through the Earth's liquid outer core because
qa.a: They are transverse and liquids cannot support shear
qa.e: This 'S-wave shadow' revealed the liquid outer core.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Transverse mechanical waves travel along a stretched string.
Reason (R): A stretched string can provide restoring forces perpendicular to its length.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Tension pulls displaced parts back sideways, sustaining transverse waves. R explains A.

qa.q: For y = 0.02 sin(2πx − 50πt) (SI units), the wavelength in m is
qa.e: k = 2π → λ = 2π/k = 1 m.

qa.q: For y = 0.02 sin(2πx − 50πt) (SI units), the frequency in Hz is
For y = 0.02 sin(2πx − 50πt), the direction of propagation is
qa.a: +x
qa.e: The form (kx − ωt) travels towards +x.

qa.q: The unit of angular wave number k is
qa.a: rad m⁻¹
qa.e: k = 2π/λ.

qa.q: For y = 3 sin(0.5x + 4t) cm (x in cm, t in s), the amplitude in cm is
qa.e: The coefficient of the sine.

qa.q: Two points on a wave 0.25λ apart differ in phase by
qa.e: Phase difference = kΔx = (2π/λ)(λ/4) = π/2.

qa.q: For a wave with T = 0.02 s, the angular frequency in units of π rad s⁻¹ is
qa.e: ω = 2π/T = 100π rad s⁻¹.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The equation y = a sin(kx + ωt) represents a wave travelling in the −x direction.
Reason (R): A point of constant phase satisfies kx + ωt = constant, so x decreases as t increases.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: dx/dt = −ω/k < 0. R explains A.

qa.q: A wave has frequency 500 Hz and wavelength 0.68 m. Its speed in m s⁻¹ is
A string of linear mass density 0.004 kg m⁻¹ is under a tension of 16 N. The wave speed in m s⁻¹ is
If the tension in a string is increased 9 times, the wave speed becomes how many times?
qa.e: v ∝ √T.

qa.q: The speed of a wave in a given medium depends on
qa.a: The properties of the medium
qa.e: v is set by elasticity and inertia of the medium.

qa.q: For y = 0.1 sin(4x − 20t) (SI units), the wave speed in m s⁻¹ is
A sound source's frequency is doubled in the same medium. The wavelength
qa.a: Halves
qa.e: v fixed, v = νλ → λ ∝ 1/ν.

qa.q: A 5 m steel wire of mass 0.1 kg is stretched with 200 N. The time for a pulse to travel its length, in s, is

Assertion (A): A thicker string of the same material and tension carries waves more slowly.
Reason (R): Wave speed on a stretched string does not depend on its tension.
qa.a: A is true but R is false
qa.e: A is true (larger μ). R is false: v = √(T/μ) depends on tension.

qa.q: Laplace's correction to Newton's formula replaces P by
qa.a: γP
qa.e: Adiabatic bulk modulus is γP.

qa.q: The speed of sound in air at 27 °C is 340 m s⁻¹. At 1200 K (927 °C), it would be (in m s⁻¹)
If air pressure is doubled at constant temperature, the speed of sound
qa.a: Stays the same
qa.e: ρ doubles too, so P/ρ is unchanged.

qa.q: Speed of longitudinal waves in a steel rod (Y = 2 × 10¹¹ Pa, ρ = 8000 kg m⁻³) in m s⁻¹ is
Newton's formula underestimated the speed of sound because he assumed the process was
qa.a: Isothermal instead of adiabatic
qa.e: Compressions are too quick for heat to flow, so they are adiabatic.

qa.q: Speed of sound in water (B = 2.25 × 10⁹ Pa, ρ = 1000 kg m⁻³) in m s⁻¹ is
Sound travels fastest in
qa.a: Solids
qa.e: Solids have large elastic moduli compared with their density.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The speed of sound in air increases when the air pressure is increased at constant temperature.
Reason (R): The speed of sound in a gas is proportional to the square root of its absolute temperature.
qa.a: A is false but R is true
qa.e: A is false: P/ρ is unchanged at constant temperature, so v is unchanged. R is true.

qa.q: The thunder of a lightning strike is heard 5 s after the flash (v = 340 m s⁻¹). The distance of the strike in m is
qa.e: d = vt = 340 × 5 = 1700 m (light's travel time is negligible).

qa.q: A sonar pulse returns from the sea bed after 1.2 s (speed of sound in water 1500 m s⁻¹). The depth in m is
According to the principle of superposition, the resultant displacement when two waves overlap is
qa.a: The algebraic sum of the individual displacements
qa.e: y = y₁ + y₂.

qa.q: Two identical pulses, one upright and one inverted, approach each other on a string. When they exactly overlap, the string
qa.a: Is momentarily flat at those points
qa.e: Equal and opposite displacements cancel; the energy is then in the string's motion.

qa.q: After two pulses pass through each other on a string, they
qa.a: Continue unchanged
qa.e: Superposition is linear; each pulse moves on as before.

qa.q: A man hears an echo from a wall 0.4 s after clapping (v = 340 m s⁻¹). The wall's distance in m is
At a point, wave 1 gives y₁ = +4 mm and wave 2 gives y₂ = −6 mm. The resultant displacement in mm is

Assertion (A): The distance to a cliff is half the product of the speed of sound and the echo time.
Reason (R): The sound travels to the cliff and back, covering twice the distance.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Total path = 2d = vt, so d = vt/2. R explains A.

qa.q: Two waves of equal amplitude a and the same frequency superpose in phase. The resultant amplitude is
qa.a: 2a
qa.e: φ = 0: A = 2a cos 0 = 2a.

qa.q: The resultant amplitude of two equal waves (amplitude a) with phase difference π is
Two waves of amplitude 4 cm each with phase difference 2π/3 superpose. The resultant amplitude in cm is
The formula for the resultant amplitude of two equal waves with phase difference φ is
qa.a: 2a cos(φ/2)
qa.e: From adding the two sines.

qa.q: Constructive interference occurs when the phase difference is
qa.a: 0 or an even multiple of π

qa.q: Two waves of amplitude 6 mm each have phase difference π/2. The resultant amplitude in mm (√2 ≈ 1.414) is
Noise-cancelling headphones work on the principle of
qa.a: Destructive interference
qa.e: They add a wave with phase difference π to the noise.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Two waves of equal amplitude and frequency can cancel each other completely.
Reason (R): Two waves of equal amplitude always have equal frequencies.
qa.a: A is true but R is false
qa.e: A is true (phase difference π). R is false: amplitude and frequency are independent.

qa.q: When a wave is reflected from a rigid boundary, the phase change is
qa.a: π
qa.e: The fixed end forces zero displacement, inverting the pulse.

qa.q: When a wave is reflected from a free end, the phase change is
qa.e: A crest returns as a crest.

qa.q: The distance between two consecutive nodes in a standing wave is
qa.e: sin kx = 0 at x = nλ/2.

qa.q: In y = 2a sin kx cos ωt, the amplitude at position x is
qa.a: 2a sin kx
qa.e: It depends on position, not on time.

qa.q: A standing wave has λ = 0.6 m. The distance between a node and the next antinode in m is
In a standing wave on a string, adjacent antinodes are 12 cm apart. The wavelength in cm is
qa.e: Adjacent antinodes are λ/2 apart: λ = 24 cm.

qa.q: A standing wave is formed by
qa.a: Superposition of two identical waves travelling in opposite directions
qa.e: Typically an incident and a reflected wave.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): No energy is transported across a node in a standing wave.
Reason (R): Particles at a node never move, so no work is done across that point.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Zero displacement means no energy flow through a node. R explains A.

qa.q: A pipe closed at one end has length 0.85 m (v = 340 m s⁻¹). Its fundamental frequency in Hz is
A pipe closed at one end has a fundamental frequency of 100 Hz. The next higher frequency it can produce in Hz is
qa.e: Only odd harmonics: 3 × 100 = 300 Hz.

qa.q: A pipe open at both ends, 0.85 m long (v = 340 m s⁻¹), has fundamental frequency in Hz
A string fixed at both ends vibrates in its 3rd harmonic. The number of loops (segments) is
qa.e: The nth mode has n loops.

qa.q: Which harmonics are present in a pipe closed at one end?
qa.a: Only odd harmonics
qa.e: L must be an odd multiple of λ/4.

qa.q: A 1 m string has fundamental 150 Hz. The wave speed on it in m s⁻¹ is
For the same length, the ratio of fundamental frequencies of an open pipe to a closed pipe is

Assertion (A): A pipe closed at one end produces only odd harmonics.
Reason (R): The fundamental frequency of a pipe closed at one end is v/(4L).
qa.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true, but the fundamental's value doesn't explain the absence of even harmonics; the node–antinode condition L = (2n − 1)λ/4 does.

qa.q: In a resonance tube with a 480 Hz fork, successive resonances occur at 18 cm and 53.5 cm. The speed of sound in m s⁻¹ is
In a resonance tube, the difference between two successive resonance lengths equals
qa.e: From L = λ/4 to 3λ/4.

qa.q: A string 1.5 m long (both ends fixed) carries waves at 300 m s⁻¹. Its third harmonic in Hz is
A closed pipe has fundamental 120 Hz. Which frequency (in Hz) can it NOT produce?
qa.e: Only odd multiples of 120 Hz: 360, 600, 840 Hz are allowed; 240 Hz is an even multiple.

qa.q: A steel wire of length 0.5 m, μ = 0.01 kg m⁻¹, tension 100 N, is fixed at both ends. Its fundamental frequency in Hz is
An open pipe resonates at successive frequencies 400 Hz and 500 Hz. Its fundamental frequency in Hz is
qa.e: Open pipes have all harmonics: the difference of successive harmonics = ν₁ = 100 Hz.

qa.q: A closed pipe resonates at successive frequencies 750 Hz and 1050 Hz. Its fundamental frequency in Hz is
qa.e: Successive odd harmonics differ by 2ν₁: 300 = 2ν₁ → ν₁ = 150 Hz.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Using the difference of two resonance lengths gives a more accurate speed of sound than using the first length alone.
Reason (R): The end correction cancels out when one resonance length is subtracted from another.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both lengths share the same end correction, which disappears in L₂ − L₁. R explains A.

qa.q: Two tuning forks of 384 Hz and 388 Hz are sounded together. The number of beats per second is
qa.e: Beat frequency = 388 − 384 = 4 Hz.

qa.q: A 256 Hz fork gives 4 beats s⁻¹ with an unknown fork. Filing the unknown fork (raising its frequency) increases the beats. The unknown frequency in Hz was
qa.e: If it were 260, raising it moves away from 256: beats increase ✓. If 252, beats would first decrease.

qa.q: A 480 Hz fork gives 6 beats s⁻¹ with fork X. Loading X with wax increases the beats. ν_X in Hz was
qa.e: Wax lowers ν_X; beats increase only if ν_X was below 480, i.e. 474 Hz.

qa.q: Beats are heard when two sound waves
qa.a: Have slightly different frequencies
qa.e: The slow drifting phase difference makes loudness rise and fall.

qa.q: Musicians tune an instrument to a reference by
qa.a: Adjusting until the beats disappear
qa.e: Zero beats means equal frequencies.

qa.q: 20 beats are heard in 5 s between two sources. If one is 500 Hz, the other could be (in Hz)
qa.e: Beat frequency = 20/5 = 4 Hz → 504 or 496 Hz; 504 is among the options.

qa.q: Loading a prong of a tuning fork with wax
qa.a: Decreases its frequency
qa.e: Extra mass lowers the natural frequency.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Two sitar strings slightly out of tune produce a throbbing sound when plucked together.
Reason (R): Waves on plucked strings are transverse.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true, but the throbbing is explained by beats from slightly different frequencies, not by the wave being transverse.
